last_observation.worked_solution:
To find the equation of the normal line to a polar curve at a point $P,$ we follow four steps:

**Step 1**: Calculate the derivative $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

In this case, we're given that

$$
{y}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ),\,{x}^{′}(\theta )=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Find the slope of the tangent at $P:$

The slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =2\pi /3} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3})-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{2\pi }{3})}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{2\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3})} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3})-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{3})}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3})} \\  & =\frac{-\frac{1}{2}-2\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})}{2\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{2})}{(-\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2})} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P:$

We compute the $xy$-coordinates of $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}))\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}) \\  & =(1-2(-\frac{1}{2}))(-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-1 \\ {y}_{1} & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}))\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}) \\  & =(1-2(-\frac{1}{2}))\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\  & =\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(-1,\sqrt{3}).$

**Step 4**: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the normal:

We find the equation of the normal as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{m}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-\sqrt{3} & =3\sqrt{3}\cdot (x-(-1)) \\ y-\sqrt{3} & =3\sqrt{3}x+3\sqrt{3} \\ y & =3\sqrt{3}x+4\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Find the slope of the tangent at $P:$

The slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =2\pi /3} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3})-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{2\pi }{3})}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{2\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3})} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3})-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{3})}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3})} \\  & =\frac{-\frac{1}{2}-2\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})}{2\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{2})}{(-\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2})} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P:$

We compute the $xy$-coordinates of $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}))\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}) \\  & =(1-2(-\frac{1}{2}))(-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-1 \\ {y}_{1} & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}))\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}) \\  & =(1-2(-\frac{1}{2}))\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\  & =\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(-1,\sqrt{3}).$

**Step 4**: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the normal:

We find the equation of the normal as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{m}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-\sqrt{3} & =3\sqrt{3}\cdot (x-(-1)) \\ y-\sqrt{3} & =3\sqrt{3}x+3\sqrt{3} \\ y & =3\sqrt{3}x+4\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6

Find the equation of the normal line to the polar curve r=1−2cos⁡θ at θ=2π3 given that y′(θ)=cos⁡θ−2cos⁡(2θ),x′(θ)=2sin⁡(2θ)−sin⁡θ.

a
y=33x+43
b
y=−33x−43
c
y=43x+33
d
y=−43x+33
e
y=33x−43
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the equation of the normal line to a polar curve at a point P, we follow four steps:

Step 1: Calculate the derivative dydx:

In this case, we're given that

y′(θ)=cos⁡θ−2cos⁡(2θ),x′(θ)=2sin⁡(2θ)−sin⁡θ.

Therefore,

dydx=y′(θ)x′(θ)=cos⁡θ−2cos⁡(2θ)2sin⁡(2θ)−sin⁡θ

Step 2: Find the slope of the tangent at P:

The slope of the tangent line is

m=dydx|θ=2π/3=cos⁡(2π3)−2cos⁡(2⋅2π3)2sin⁡(2⋅2π3)−sin⁡(2π3)=cos⁡(2π3)−2cos⁡(4π3)2sin⁡(4π3)−sin⁡(2π3)=−12−2⋅(−12)2⋅(−32)−32=(12)(−332)=−133.

Step 3: Find the Cartesian coordinates of P:

We compute the xy-coordinates of P as follows:

x1=rcos⁡θ=(1−2cos⁡θ)cos⁡θ=(1−2cos⁡(2π3))cos⁡(2π3)=(1−2(−12))(−12)=−1y1=rsin⁡θ=(1−2cos⁡θ)sin⁡θ=(1−2cos⁡(2π3))sin⁡(2π3)=(1−2(−12))⋅32=3

Therefore, the coordinates of P are (−1,3).

Step 4: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the normal:

We find the equation of the normal as follows:

y−y1=−1m(x−x1)y−3=33⋅(x−(−1))y−3=33x+33y=33x+43

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta )=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+4\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ), \\ {x}^{′}(\theta )=2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )-4\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

The Cartesian equation of the normal line is $y=$

question.worked_solution:
To find the equation of the normal line to a polar curve at a point $P,$ we follow four steps:

**Step 1**: Calculate the derivative $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

In this case, we're given that

$$
{y}^{′}(\theta )=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+4\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ),\,{x}^{′}(\theta )=2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )-4\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+4\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )-4\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Find the slope of the tangent at $P:$

The slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})+4\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})}{2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})-4\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})} \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}{2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})} \\  & =\frac{2}{2-\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P:$

We compute the $xy$-coordinates of $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\pi \cdot {(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2} \\ {y}_{1} & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}).$

**Step 4**: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the normal:

We find the equation of the normal as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{m}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-\frac{\pi }{2} & =\frac{\pi -2}{2}(x-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\ y & =\frac{\pi -2}{2}\,x+\frac{\pi (4-\pi )}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the equation of the normal line to a polar curve at a point $P,$ we follow four steps:

**Step 1**: Calculate the derivative $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

In this case, we're given that

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{tan}⁡(2\theta ).
$$

**Step 2**: Find the slope of the tangent at $P:$

The slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =\pi /6} \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P:$

We compute the $xy$-coordinates of $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =4\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\  & =\sqrt{3} \\ {y}_{1} & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =4\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(\sqrt{3},1).$

**Step 4**: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the normal:

We find the equation of the normal as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{m}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-1 & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(x-\sqrt{3}) \\ y-1 & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}x+1 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\,x+2\end{aligned}

question.worked_solution:
To find the equation of the normal line to a polar curve at a point $P,$ we follow four steps:

**Step 1**: Calculate the derivative $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

In this case, we're given that

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.
$$

**Step 2**: Find the slope of the tangent at $P:$

The slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =3\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})+\frac{3\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}))}{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})-\frac{3\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}))} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot (-1)+\frac{3\pi }{2}\cdot 0}{(2\cdot 0-\frac{3\pi }{2}\cdot (-1))} \\  & =\frac{-2}{(\frac{3\pi }{2})} \\  & =-\frac{4}{3\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P:$

We compute the $xy$-coordinates of $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={\theta }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={(\frac{3\pi }{2})}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & ={(\frac{3\pi }{2})}^{2}\cdot 0 \\  & =0 \\ {y}_{1} & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={\theta }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={(\frac{3\pi }{2})}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & ={(\frac{3\pi }{2})}^{2}\cdot (-1) \\  & =-\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(0,-\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}).$

**Step 4**: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the normal:

We find the equation of the normal as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{m}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}) & =\frac{3\pi }{4}\cdot (x-0) \\ y+\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4} & =\frac{3\pi }{4}\,x \\ y & =\frac{3\pi }{4}x-\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9

Find the equation of the normal line to the polar curve r=θ2 at θ=3π2, given that dydx=2sin⁡θ+θcos⁡θ2cos⁡θ−θsin⁡θ.

a
y=3π2x−9π24
b
y=3π4x−3π4
c
y=3π4x−3π2
d
y=3π4x−9π24
e
y=3π2x−3π4
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To find the equation of the normal line to a polar curve at a point P, we follow four steps:

Step 1: Calculate the derivative dydx:

In this case, we're given that

dydx=2sin⁡θ+θcos⁡θ2cos⁡θ−θsin⁡θ.

Step 2: Find the slope of the tangent at P:

The slope of the tangent line is

m=dydx|θ=3π/2=(2sin⁡(3π2)+3π2cos⁡(3π2))(2cos⁡(3π2)−3π2sin⁡(3π2))=2⋅(−1)+3π2⋅0(2⋅0−3π2⋅(−1))=−2(3π2)=−43π.

Step 3: Find the Cartesian coordinates of P:

We compute the xy-coordinates of P as follows:

x1=rcos⁡θ=θ2cos⁡θ=(3π2)2cos⁡(3π2)=(3π2)2⋅0=0y1=rsin⁡θ=θ2sin⁡θ=(3π2)2sin⁡(3π2)=(3π2)2⋅(−1)=−9π24

Therefore, the coordinates of P are (0,−9π24).

Step 4: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the normal:

We find the equation of the normal as follows:

y−y1=−1m(x−x1)y−(−9π24)=3π4⋅(x−0)y+9π24=3π4xy=3π4x−9π24

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding Normal Lines to Polar Curves
last_observation.worked_solution:
To find the equation of the normal line to a polar curve at a point $P,$ we follow four steps:

**Step 1**: Calculate the derivative $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

In this case, we're given that

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.
$$

**Step 2**: Find the slope of the tangent at $P:$

The slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =3\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})+\frac{3\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}))}{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})-\frac{3\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}))} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot (-1)+\frac{3\pi }{2}\cdot 0}{(2\cdot 0-\frac{3\pi }{2}\cdot (-1))} \\  & =\frac{-2}{(\frac{3\pi }{2})} \\  & =-\frac{4}{3\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P:$

We compute the $xy$-coordinates of $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={\theta }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={(\frac{3\pi }{2})}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & ={(\frac{3\pi }{2})}^{2}\cdot 0 \\  & =0 \\ {y}_{1} & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={\theta }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={(\frac{3\pi }{2})}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & ={(\frac{3\pi }{2})}^{2}\cdot (-1) \\  & =-\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(0,-\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}).$

**Step 4**: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the normal:

We find the equation of the normal as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{m}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}) & =\frac{3\pi }{4}\cdot (x-0) \\ y+\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4} & =\frac{3\pi }{4}\,x \\ y & =\frac{3\pi }{4}x-\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.
$$

b

EXPLANATION

To find the equation of the normal line to a polar curve at a point P, we follow four steps:

Step 1: Calculate the derivative dydx:

In this case, we're given that

dydx=2sin⁡θ+θcos⁡θ2cos⁡θ−θsin⁡θ.

Step 2: Find the slope of the tangent at P:

The slope of the tangent line is

m=dydx|θ=3π/2=(2sin⁡(3π2)+3π2cos⁡(3π2))(2cos⁡(3π2)−3π2sin⁡(3π2))=2⋅(−1)+3π2⋅0(2⋅0−3π2⋅(−1))=−2(3π2)=−43π.

Step 3: Find the Cartesian coordinates of P:

We compute the xy-coordinates of P as follows:

x1=rcos⁡θ=θ2cos⁡θ=(3π2)2cos⁡(3π2)=(3π2)2⋅0=0y1=rsin⁡θ=θ2sin⁡θ=(3π2)2sin⁡(3π2)=(3π2)2⋅(−1)=−9π24

Therefore, the coordinates of P are (0,−9π24).

Step 4: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the normal:

We find the equation of the normal as follows:

y−y1=−1m(x−x1)y−(−9π24)=3π4⋅(x−0)y+9π24=3π4xy=3π4x−9π24

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.

feedback.worked_solution:
To find the equation of the normal line to a polar curve at a point $P,$ we follow four steps:

**Step 1**: Calculate the derivative $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

In this case, we're given that

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.
$$

**Step 2**: Find the slope of the tangent at $P:$

The slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =3\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})+\frac{3\pi }{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}))}{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})-\frac{3\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}))} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot (-1)+\frac{3\pi }{2}\cdot 0}{(2\cdot 0-\frac{3\pi }{2}\cdot (-1))} \\  & =\frac{-2}{(\frac{3\pi }{2})} \\  & =-\frac{4}{3\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P:$

We compute the $xy$-coordinates of $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={\theta }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={(\frac{3\pi }{2})}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & ={(\frac{3\pi }{2})}^{2}\cdot 0 \\  & =0 \\ {y}_{1} & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={\theta }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={(\frac{3\pi }{2})}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & ={(\frac{3\pi }{2})}^{2}\cdot (-1) \\  & =-\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(0,-\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}).$

**Step 4**: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the normal:

We find the equation of the normal as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{m}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}) & =\frac{3\pi }{4}\cdot (x-0) \\ y+\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4} & =\frac{3\pi }{4}\,x \\ y & =\frac{3\pi }{4}x-\frac{9{\pi }^{2}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the equation of the normal line to a polar curve at a point $P,$ we follow four steps:

**Step 1**: Calculate the derivative $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

In this case, we're given that

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta )-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }.
$$

**Step 2**: Find the slope of the tangent at $P:$

The slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =3\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{9\pi }{4})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}))}{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{9\pi }{4})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}))} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}{(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}+(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}))} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{2})}{(\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{2})} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P:$

We compute the $xy$-coordinates of $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}) \\  & =(-1)\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ {y}_{1} & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}) \\  & =(-1)\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}).$

**Step 4**: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the normal:

We find the equation of the normal as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{m}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) & =-1\cdot (x-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\ y+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & =-x+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ y & =-x\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

Find the equation of the normal line to the polar curve r=sin⁡(2θ) at θ=3π4, given that dydx=3sin⁡(3θ)−sin⁡θ3cos⁡(3θ)+cos⁡θ.

a
y=−2x
b
y=−x
c
y=x−2
d
y=x+2
e
y=−x+2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the equation of the normal line to a polar curve at a point P, we follow four steps:

Step 1: Calculate the derivative dydx:

In this case, we're given that

dydx=3sin⁡(3θ)−sin⁡θ3cos⁡(3θ)+cos⁡θ.

Step 2: Find the slope of the tangent at P:

The slope of the tangent line is

m=dydx|θ=3π/4=(3sin⁡(9π4)−sin⁡(3π4))(3cos⁡(9π4)+cos⁡(3π4))=(322−22)(322+(−22))=(222)(222)=1.

Step 3: Find the Cartesian coordinates of P:

We compute the xy-coordinates of P as follows:

x1=rcos⁡θ=sin⁡(2θ)cos⁡θ=sin⁡(3π2)cos⁡(3π4)=(−1)⋅(−22)=22y1=rsin⁡θ=sin⁡(2θ)sin⁡θ=sin⁡(3π2)sin⁡(3π4)=(−1)⋅(22)=−22

Therefore, the coordinates of P are (22,−22).

Step 4: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the normal:

We find the equation of the normal as follows:

y−y1=−1m(x−x1)y−(−22)=−1⋅(x−22)y+22=−x+22y=−x

feedback.problem:
Find the equation of the **normal** line to the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )$ at $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{4},$ given that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta )-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }.
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
To find the equation of the normal line to a polar curve at a point $P,$ we follow four steps:

**Step 1**: Calculate the derivative $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

In this case, we're given that

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta )-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }.
$$

**Step 2**: Find the slope of the tangent at $P:$

The slope of the tangent line is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{\theta =3\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{9\pi }{4})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}))}{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{9\pi }{4})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}))} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}{(\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}+(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}))} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{2})}{(\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{2})} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Find the Cartesian coordinates of $P:$

We compute the $xy$-coordinates of $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}) \\  & =(-1)\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ {y}_{1} & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}) \\  & =(-1)\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}).$

**Step 4**: Using point-slope form, find the equation of the normal:

We find the equation of the normal as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{m}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) & =-1\cdot (x-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\ y+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & =-x+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ y & =-x\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.worked_solution:
The "square of a sum" formula states that

$$
{x}^{2}+2ax+{a}^{2}=(x+a)^{2}.
$$

We will use this formula to factor the given trinomial. Our trinomial is

$$
{x}^{2}+18x+81.
$$

First, we write the constant term as a perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+18x+{9}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we factor a $2$ out of the linear term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2\cdot 9x+{9}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the trinomial using the square of sum formula with $a=9.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+9)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We take each term of the first binomial and multiply it by the second binomial. Then, we simplify by collecting like terms.

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-3y)({x}^{2}+4y) & = \\ x({x}^{2}+4y)-3y({x}^{2}+4y) & = \\ {x}^{3}+4xy-3{x}^{2}y-12{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We cannot simplify the above expression any further because there are no like terms.

8.Linear Equations Requiring Multiplication by a Negative Integer?
If 115=−m3, then m=

Wed, Oct 14th @ 11:52 PM|Elapsed: 1:10Correct

answer_fields.input_html: −15

questions.worked_solution:
First, let's swap the left and right-hand sides so that the variable is on the left-hand side.

$$
-\frac{m}{3}=\frac{1}{15}
$$

Then, we remove the negative sign from the variable. To do this, we multiply both sides of the equation by $-1.$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{m}{3} & =\frac{1}{15} \\ (-1)\cdot (-\frac{m}{3}) & =(-1)\cdot \frac{1}{15} \\ \frac{m}{3} & =-\frac{1}{15}\end{aligned}
$$

In the equation above, $m$ is being divided by $3.$ To isolate $m$, we can perform the opposite operation, which is *multiplying* by $3.$ So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $3$ and simplify.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{m}{3} & =-\frac{1}{15} \\ 3\cdot \frac{m}{3} & =3\cdot (-\frac{1}{15}) \\ \frac{3m}{3} & =-\frac{3}{15} \\ \frac{\cancel{3}m}{\cancel{3}} & =-\frac{1}{5} \\ m & =-\frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

answer_fields.input_html: 10.245

questions.worked_solution:
Our measurement is given to the nearest $0.01\,\text{mL}.$ So, the greatest possible error of this measurement is

$$
\frac{0.01\,\text{mL}}{2}=0.005\,\text{mL}.
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the lower and upper bounds of this measurement as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{lower bound} & =10.25\,\text{mL}-0.005\,\text{mL} \\  & =10.245\,\text{mL} \\ \text{upper bound} & =10.25\,\text{mL}+0.005\,\text{mL} \\  & =10.255\,\text{mL}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the exact value of $v$ lies between the lower and upper bound, we conclude that

$$
10.245\,\text{mL}\le v<10.255\,\text{mL}.
$$

feedback.problem: If $\frac{1}{15}=-\frac{m}{3},$ then $m=${{field-1}}.
feedback.worked_solution:
First, let's swap the left and right-hand sides so that the variable is on the left-hand side.

$$
-\frac{m}{3}=\frac{1}{15}
$$

Then, we remove the negative sign from the variable. To do this, we multiply both sides of the equation by $-1.$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{m}{3} & =\frac{1}{15} \\ (-1)\cdot (-\frac{m}{3}) & =(-1)\cdot \frac{1}{15} \\ \frac{m}{3} & =-\frac{1}{15}\end{aligned}
$$

In the equation above, $m$ is being divided by $3.$ To isolate $m$, we can perform the opposite operation, which is *multiplying* by $3.$ So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $3$ and simplify.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{m}{3} & =-\frac{1}{15} \\ 3\cdot \frac{m}{3} & =3\cdot (-\frac{1}{15}) \\ \frac{3m}{3} & =-\frac{3}{15} \\ \frac{\cancel{3}m}{\cancel{3}} & =-\frac{1}{5} \\ m & =-\frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
Our measurement is given to the nearest $0.01\,\text{mL}.$ So, the greatest possible error of this measurement is

$$
\frac{0.01\,\text{mL}}{2}=0.005\,\text{mL}.
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the lower and upper bounds of this measurement as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{lower bound} & =10.25\,\text{mL}-0.005\,\text{mL} \\  & =10.245\,\text{mL} \\ \text{upper bound} & =10.25\,\text{mL}+0.005\,\text{mL} \\  & =10.255\,\text{mL}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the exact value of $v$ lies between the lower and upper bound, we conclude that

$$
10.245\,\text{mL}\le v<10.255\,\text{mL}.
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: The volume of a cylinder decreases at a rate that's proportional to the square of its radius. Write down a differential equation describing the rate of change of the radius, $r(t),$ in this process. Assume that the height of the cylinder does not change and that $K>0.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*The **volume** of a cylinder **decreases** at a rate that's **proportional** to the **square of its radius**.*

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *volume $V$ of a cylinder* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}$ *decreases* at a rate that's *proportional to the square of its radius.* Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=-k{r}^{2},
$$

where $k>0.$

We wish to use this information to find an expression for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$

The volume $V$ of a cylinder is given by

$$
V=\pi {r}^{2}h.
$$

Differentiating this equation with respect to $t,$ and the fact that the height of the cylinder does not change, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}h) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =2\pi hr\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =-k{r}^{2} \\ 2\pi hr\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-k{r}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{k{r}^{2}}{2\pi hr} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{kr}{2\pi h}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now introduce a new constant:

$$
K=\frac{k}{2\pi h}>0
$$

 

Therefore, our equation becomes

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-Kr.
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
The volume of a cylinder decreases at a rate proportional to its volume. Write down a differential equation describing the rate of change of the height, $h(t),$ in this process. 
Assume that the radius of the cylinder does not change and that $k>0.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*The **volume** of a cylinder **decreases** at a rate **proportional** to its **volume**. *

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *volume $V$ of a cylinder* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}$ *decreases* at a rate *proportional to the volume.* Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=-kV,
$$

where $k>0.$

We wish to use this information to find an expression for $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.$

The volume $V$ of a cylinder is given by

$$
V=\pi {r}^{2}h.
$$

Differentiating this equation with respect to $t,$ and using the fact that the radius of the cylinder does not change, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}h) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\pi {r}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =-kV \\ \pi {r}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-k(\pi {r}^{2}h) \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{k\pi {r}^{2}h}{\pi {r}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-kh.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.raw_html:
2.Expressing Three-Dimensional Related Rates Using Differential Equations?

The volume of a cylinder decreases at a rate proportional to its volume. Write down a differential equation describing the rate of change of the height, h(t), in this process. Assume that the radius of the cylinder does not change and that k>0.

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: The area of a circle decreases at a rate that's proportional to the cube of its radius. Write down a differential equation describing the rate of change of the radius, $r(t),$ in this process. Assume that $K>0.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*The **area** of a circle **decreases** at a **rate** that's **proportional** to the cube of its **radius**. *

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *area $A$ of a circle* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ *decreases* at a rate that's *proportional* to the cube of its *radius.* In other words,

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=-k{r}^{3}
$$

where $k>0.$

We wish to use this information to find an expression for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$

The area of a circle is given by 

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}.
$$

 

Differentiating this equation with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =2\pi r\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-k{r}^{3} \\ 2\pi r\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-k{r}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{k{r}^{3}}{2\pi r} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{k{r}^{2}}{2\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

We now introduce a new constant:

$$
K=\frac{k}{2\pi }>0
$$

 

Therefore, our equation becomes

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-K{r}^{2}.
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: At each point $P$ on a particular curve, the derivative ${y}^{′}(x)$ is proportional to the shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis. The derivative at the point $(3,-5)$ equals $24.$ What differential equation describes this curve?
questions.worked_solution:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*At each point $P$ on a particular curve, the **derivative** ${y}^{′}(x)$ is **proportional** to the **shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis**.*

We note the following:

- The *shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis* is given by $|x|.$

- Since the *derivative* is *proportional to* the shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis, we have 

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=k\cdot |x|
$$

where $k$ is a constant.

So, our differential equation is

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=k|x|.
$$

In addition, we're told that ${y}^{′}(x)=24$ when at the point $(3,-5).$ We can use this to determine the value of the coefficient $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}24=k|3|\,⟹\,k=8\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the differential equation describing the curve is

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=8|x|.
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: At each point $P$ on a particular curve, the derivative ${y}^{′}(x)$ is **inversely** proportional to the shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis. The derivative at the point $(2,8)$ equals $5.$ What differential equation describes this curve?
questions.worked_solution:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*At each point $P$ on a particular curve, the **derivative** ${y}^{′}(x)$ is **inversely proportional** to the **shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis**.*

We note the following:

- The *shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis* is given by $|x|.$

- Since the *derivative* is *inversely proportional* to the shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis, we have 

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=k\cdot \frac{1}{|x|}
$$

where $k$ is a constant.

So, our differential equation is

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=\frac{k}{|x|}.
$$

In addition, we're told that ${y}^{′}(x)=5$ when at the point $(2,8).$ We can use this to determine the value of the coefficient $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}5=\frac{k}{|2|}\,⟹\,k=10\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the differential equation describing the curve is

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=\frac{10}{|x|}.
$$

questions.raw_html:
5.Translating Coordinate Plane Problems Into Differential Equations ?

At each point P on a particular curve, the derivative y′(x) is inversely proportional to the shortest distance from P to the y-axis. The derivative at the point (2,8) equals 5. What differential equation describes this curve?

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*The **volume** of a cylinder **decreases** at a rate that's **proportional** to the **square of its radius**.*

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *volume $V$ of a cylinder* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}$ *decreases* at a rate that's *proportional to the square of its radius.* Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=-k{r}^{2},
$$

where $k>0.$

We wish to use this information to find an expression for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$

The volume $V$ of a cylinder is given by

$$
V=\pi {r}^{2}h.
$$

Differentiating this equation with respect to $t,$ and the fact that the height of the cylinder does not change, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}h) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =2\pi hr\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =-k{r}^{2} \\ 2\pi hr\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-k{r}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{k{r}^{2}}{2\pi hr} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{kr}{2\pi h}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now introduce a new constant:

$$
K=\frac{k}{2\pi h}>0
$$

 

Therefore, our equation becomes

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-Kr.
$$

Question 1
?

The volume of a cylinder decreases at a rate that's proportional to the square of its radius. Write down a differential equation describing the rate of change of the radius, r(t), in this process. Assume that the height of the cylinder does not change and that K>0.

a
 drdt=−Kr
b
 drdt=−Kr2
c
 drdt=−Kr
d
 drdt=Kr2
e
 drdt=K−r
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

The volume of a cylinder decreases at a rate that's proportional to the square of its radius.

We note the following:

  • The question describes the rate at which the volume V of a cylinder varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity dVdt.

  • We're told that dVdt decreases at a rate that's proportional to the square of its radius. Therefore, dVdt=−kr2, where k>0.

We wish to use this information to find an expression for drdt.

The volume V of a cylinder is given by V=πr2h.

Differentiating this equation with respect to t, and the fact that the height of the cylinder does not change, we get dVdt=ddt(πr2h)dVdt=2πhrdrdt.

Therefore, dVdt=−kr22πhrdrdt=−kr2drdt=−kr22πhrdrdt=−kr2πh.

We now introduce a new constant: K=k2πh>0

Therefore, our equation becomes drdt=−Kr.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*The **volume** of a cylinder **decreases** at a rate **proportional** to its **volume**. *

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *volume $V$ of a cylinder* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}$ *decreases* at a rate *proportional to the volume.* Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=-kV,
$$

where $k>0.$

We wish to use this information to find an expression for $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.$

The volume $V$ of a cylinder is given by

$$
V=\pi {r}^{2}h.
$$

Differentiating this equation with respect to $t,$ and using the fact that the radius of the cylinder does not change, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}h) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\pi {r}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =-kV \\ \pi {r}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-k(\pi {r}^{2}h) \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{k\pi {r}^{2}h}{\pi {r}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-kh.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

The volume of a cylinder decreases at a rate proportional to its volume. Write down a differential equation describing the rate of change of the height, h(t), in this process. Assume that the radius of the cylinder does not change and that k>0.

a
dhdt=k−h
b
dhdt=−kh
c
dhdt=−kh2
d
dhdt=−k
e
dhdt=−kh
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

The volume of a cylinder decreases at a rate proportional to its volume.

We note the following:

  • The question describes the rate at which the volume V of a cylinder varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity dVdt.

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *area $A$ of a circle* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ *decreases* at a rate that's *proportional* to the cube of its *radius.* In other words,

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=-k{r}^{3}
$$

where $k>0.$

We wish to use this information to find an expression for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$

The area of a circle is given by 

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}.
$$

 

Differentiating this equation with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =2\pi r\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-k{r}^{3} \\ 2\pi r\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-k{r}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{k{r}^{3}}{2\pi r} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{k{r}^{2}}{2\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

We now introduce a new constant:

$$
K=\frac{k}{2\pi }>0
$$

 

Therefore, our equation becomes

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-K{r}^{2}.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*At each point $P$ on a particular curve, the **derivative** ${y}^{′}(x)$ is **proportional** to the **shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis**.*

We note the following:

- The *shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis* is given by $|x|.$

- Since the *derivative* is *proportional to* the shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis, we have 

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=k\cdot |x|
$$

where $k$ is a constant.

So, our differential equation is

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=k|x|.
$$

In addition, we're told that ${y}^{′}(x)=24$ when at the point $(3,-5).$ We can use this to determine the value of the coefficient $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}24=k|3|\,⟹\,k=8\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the differential equation describing the curve is

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=8|x|.
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

At each point P on a particular curve, the derivative y′(x) is proportional to the shortest distance from P to the y-axis. The derivative at the point (3,−5) equals 24. What differential equation describes this curve?

a
y′(x)=x2+y23
b
y′(x)=8|x|
c
y′(x)=3|x|
d
y′(x)=4x2+y2
e
y′(x)=24|y|5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

At each point P on a particular curve, the derivative y′(x) is proportional to the shortest distance from P to the y-axis.

We note the following:

  • The shortest distance from P to the y-axis is given by |x|.

  • Since the derivative is proportional to the shortest distance from P to the y-axis, we have y′(x)=k⋅|x| where k is a constant.

So, our differential equation is

y′(x)=k|x|.

In addition, we're told that y′(x)=24 when at the point (3,−5). We can use this to determine the value of the coefficient k:

24=k|3|⟹k=8

Finally, the differential equation describing the curve is y′(x)=8|x|.

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*At each point $P$ on a particular curve, the **derivative** ${y}^{′}(x)$ is **inversely proportional** to the **shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis**.*

We note the following:

- The *shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis* is given by $|x|.$

- Since the *derivative* is *inversely proportional* to the shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis, we have 

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=k\cdot \frac{1}{|x|}
$$

where $k$ is a constant.

So, our differential equation is

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=\frac{k}{|x|}.
$$

In addition, we're told that ${y}^{′}(x)=5$ when at the point $(2,8).$ We can use this to determine the value of the coefficient $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}5=\frac{k}{|2|}\,⟹\,k=10\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the differential equation describing the curve is

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=\frac{10}{|x|}.
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

At each point P on a particular curve, the derivative y′(x) is inversely proportional to the shortest distance from P to the y-axis. The derivative at the point (2,8) equals 5. What differential equation describes this curve?

a
y′(x)=10|x|
b
y′(x)=5|y|2
c
y′(x)=5|x|
d
y′(x)=40|y|
e
y′(x)=|x|5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

At each point P on a particular curve, the derivative y′(x) is inversely proportional to the shortest distance from P to the y-axis.

We note the following:

  • The shortest distance from P to the y-axis is given by |x|.

  • Since the derivative is inversely proportional to the shortest distance from P to the y-axis, we have y′(x)=k⋅1|x| where k is a constant.

So, our differential equation is

y′(x)=k|x|.

In addition, we're told that y′(x)=5 when at the point (2,8). We can use this to determine the value of the coefficient k:

5=k|2|⟹k=10

Finally, the differential equation describing the curve is y′(x)=10|x|.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: The volume of a cylinder decreases at a rate that's proportional to the square of its radius. Write down a differential equation describing the rate of change of the radius, $r(t),$ in this process. Assume that the height of the cylinder does not change and that $K>0.$
question.worked_solution:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*The **volume** of a cylinder **decreases** at a rate that's **proportional** to the **square of its radius**.*

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *volume $V$ of a cylinder* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}$ *decreases* at a rate that's *proportional to the square of its radius.* Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=-k{r}^{2},
$$

where $k>0.$

We wish to use this information to find an expression for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$

The volume $V$ of a cylinder is given by

$$
V=\pi {r}^{2}h.
$$

Differentiating this equation with respect to $t,$ and the fact that the height of the cylinder does not change, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}h) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =2\pi hr\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =-k{r}^{2} \\ 2\pi hr\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-k{r}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{k{r}^{2}}{2\pi hr} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{kr}{2\pi h}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now introduce a new constant:

$$
K=\frac{k}{2\pi h}>0
$$

 

Therefore, our equation becomes

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-Kr.
$$

Question 1
?

The volume of a cylinder decreases at a rate that's proportional to the square of its radius. Write down a differential equation describing the rate of change of the radius, r(t), in this process. Assume that the height of the cylinder does not change and that K>0.

a
 drdt=−Kr
b
 drdt=−Kr2
c
 drdt=−Kr
d
 drdt=Kr2
e
 drdt=K−r
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

The volume of a cylinder decreases at a rate that's proportional to the square of its radius.

We note the following:

  • The question describes the rate at which the volume V of a cylinder varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity dVdt.

  • We're told that dVdt decreases at a rate that's proportional to the square of its radius. Therefore, dVdt=−kr2, where k>0.

We wish to use this information to find an expression for drdt.

The volume V of a cylinder is given by V=πr2h.

Differentiating this equation with respect to t, and the fact that the height of the cylinder does not change, we get dVdt=ddt(πr2h)dVdt=2πhrdrdt.

Therefore, dVdt=−kr22πhrdrdt=−kr2drdt=−kr22πhrdrdt=−kr2πh.

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.worked_solution:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*The **volume** of a cylinder **decreases** at a rate that's **proportional** to the **square of its radius**.*

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *volume $V$ of a cylinder* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}$ *decreases* at a rate that's *proportional to the square of its radius.* Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=-k{r}^{2},
$$

where $k>0.$

We wish to use this information to find an expression for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$

The volume $V$ of a cylinder is given by

$$
V=\pi {r}^{2}h.
$$

Differentiating this equation with respect to $t,$ and the fact that the height of the cylinder does not change, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}h) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =2\pi hr\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =-k{r}^{2} \\ 2\pi hr\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-k{r}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{k{r}^{2}}{2\pi hr} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{kr}{2\pi h}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now introduce a new constant:

$$
K=\frac{k}{2\pi h}>0
$$

 

Therefore, our equation becomes

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-Kr.
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

The volume of a cylinder decreases at a rate that's proportional to the square of its radius. Write down a differential equation describing the rate of change of the radius, r(t), in this process. Assume that the height of the cylinder does not change and that K>0.

a
 drdt=−Kr
b
 drdt=−Kr2
c
 drdt=−Kr
d
 drdt=Kr2
e
 drdt=K−r
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

The volume of a cylinder decreases at a rate that's proportional to the square of its radius.

We note the following:

  • The question describes the rate at which the volume V of a cylinder varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity dVdt.

  • We're told that dVdt decreases at a rate that's proportional to the square of its radius. Therefore, dVdt=−kr2, where k>0.

We wish to use this information to find an expression for drdt.

The volume V of a cylinder is given by V=πr2h.

Differentiating this equation with respect to t, and the fact that the height of the cylinder does not change, we get dVdt=ddt(πr2h)dVdt=2πhrdrdt.

Therefore, dVdt=−kr22πhrdrdt=−kr2drdt=−kr22πhrdrdt=−kr2πh.

We now introduce a new constant: K=k2πh>0

Therefore, our equation becomes drdt=−Kr.

solution.reasoning: With constant height h, V=\pi h r^2, so dV/dt=2\pi h r\,dr/dt. The stated decrease means dV/dt=-k r^2 for k>0. Therefore dr/dt=-[k/(2\pi h)]r=-Kr after absorbing the constant factor into K>0. Choice c is mathematically correct; no Math Academy answer-key evidence was captured.

feedback.problem: The volume of a cylinder decreases at a rate that's proportional to the square of its radius. Write down a differential equation describing the rate of change of the radius, $r(t),$ in this process. Assume that the height of the cylinder does not change and that $K>0.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*The **volume** of a cylinder **decreases** at a rate that's **proportional** to the **square of its radius**.*

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *volume $V$ of a cylinder* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}$ *decreases* at a rate that's *proportional to the square of its radius.* Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=-k{r}^{2},
$$

where $k>0.$

We wish to use this information to find an expression for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$

The volume $V$ of a cylinder is given by

$$
V=\pi {r}^{2}h.
$$

Differentiating this equation with respect to $t,$ and the fact that the height of the cylinder does not change, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}h) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =2\pi hr\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =-k{r}^{2} \\ 2\pi hr\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-k{r}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{k{r}^{2}}{2\pi hr} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{kr}{2\pi h}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now introduce a new constant:

$$
K=\frac{k}{2\pi h}>0
$$

 

Therefore, our equation becomes

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-Kr.
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
The volume of a cylinder decreases at a rate proportional to its volume. Write down a differential equation describing the rate of change of the height, $h(t),$ in this process. 
Assume that the radius of the cylinder does not change and that $k>0.$
question.worked_solution:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*The **volume** of a cylinder **decreases** at a rate **proportional** to its **volume**. *

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *volume $V$ of a cylinder* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}$ *decreases* at a rate *proportional to the volume.* Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=-kV,
$$

where $k>0.$

We wish to use this information to find an expression for $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.$

The volume $V$ of a cylinder is given by

$$
V=\pi {r}^{2}h.
$$

Differentiating this equation with respect to $t,$ and using the fact that the radius of the cylinder does not change, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}h) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\pi {r}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =-kV \\ \pi {r}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-k(\pi {r}^{2}h) \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{k\pi {r}^{2}h}{\pi {r}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-kh.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

The volume of a cylinder decreases at a rate proportional to its volume. Write down a differential equation describing the rate of change of the height, h(t), in this process. Assume that the radius of the cylinder does not change and that k>0.

a
dhdt=k−h
b
dhdt=−kh
c
dhdt=−kh2
d
dhdt=−k
e
dhdt=−kh
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

The volume of a cylinder decreases at a rate proportional to its volume.

We note the following:

  • The question describes the rate at which the volume V of a cylinder varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity dVdt.

  • We're told that dVdt decreases at a rate proportional to the volume. Therefore, dVdt=−kV, where k>0.

We wish to use this information to find an expression for dhdt.

The volume V of a cylinder is given by V=πr2h.

Differentiating this equation with respect to t, and using the fact that the radius of the cylinder does not change, we get dVdt=ddt(πr2h)dVdt=πr2dhdt.

Therefore, dVdt=−kVπr2dhdt=−k(πr2h)dhdt=−kπr2hπr2dhdt=−kh.

last_observation.worked_solution:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*The **volume** of a cylinder **decreases** at a rate **proportional** to its **volume**. *

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *volume $V$ of a cylinder* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}$ *decreases* at a rate *proportional to the volume.* Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=-kV,
$$

where $k>0.$

We wish to use this information to find an expression for $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.$

The volume $V$ of a cylinder is given by

$$
V=\pi {r}^{2}h.
$$

Differentiating this equation with respect to $t,$ and using the fact that the radius of the cylinder does not change, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}h) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\pi {r}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =-kV \\ \pi {r}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-k(\pi {r}^{2}h) \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{k\pi {r}^{2}h}{\pi {r}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-kh.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
The volume of a cylinder decreases at a rate proportional to its volume. Write down a differential equation describing the rate of change of the height, $h(t),$ in this process. 
Assume that the radius of the cylinder does not change and that $k>0.$
question.worked_solution:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*The **volume** of a cylinder **decreases** at a rate **proportional** to its **volume**. *

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *volume $V$ of a cylinder* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}$ *decreases* at a rate *proportional to the volume.* Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=-kV,
$$

where $k>0.$

We wish to use this information to find an expression for $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.$

The volume $V$ of a cylinder is given by

$$
V=\pi {r}^{2}h.
$$

Differentiating this equation with respect to $t,$ and using the fact that the radius of the cylinder does not change, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}h) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\pi {r}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =-kV \\ \pi {r}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-k(\pi {r}^{2}h) \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{k\pi {r}^{2}h}{\pi {r}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-kh.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

The volume of a cylinder decreases at a rate proportional to its volume. Write down a differential equation describing the rate of change of the height, h(t), in this process. Assume that the radius of the cylinder does not change and that k>0.

a
dhdt=k−h
b
dhdt=−kh
c
dhdt=−kh2
d
dhdt=−k
e
dhdt=−kh
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

The volume of a cylinder decreases at a rate proportional to its volume.

We note the following:

  • The question describes the rate at which the volume V of a cylinder varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity dVdt.

  • We're told that dVdt decreases at a rate proportional to the volume. Therefore, dVdt=−kV, where k>0.

We wish to use this information to find an expression for dhdt.

The volume V of a cylinder is given by V=πr2h.

Differentiating this equation with respect to t, and using the fact that the radius of the cylinder does not change, we get dVdt=ddt(πr2h)dVdt=πr2dhdt.

Therefore, dVdt=−kVπr2dhdt=−k(πr2h)dhdt=−kπr2hπr2dhdt=−kh.

solution.reasoning: For fixed radius r, V=\pi r^2h and dV/dt=\pi r^2 dh/dt. Proportional volume decrease gives dV/dt=-kV=-k\pi r^2h. Dividing by \pi r^2 yields dh/dt=-kh, choice e. No Math Academy answer-key evidence was provided.

Question 2

The volume of a cylinder decreases at a rate proportional to its volume. Write down a differential equation describing the rate of change of the height, h(t), in this process. Assume that the radius of the cylinder does not change and that k>0.

a
dhdt=k−h
b
dhdt=−kh
c
dhdt=−kh2
d
dhdt=−k
e
dhdt=−kh
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

The volume of a cylinder decreases at a rate proportional to its volume.

We note the following:

  • The question describes the rate at which the volume V of a cylinder varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity dVdt.

  • We're told that dVdt decreases at a rate proportional to the volume. Therefore, dVdt=−kV, where k>0.

We wish to use this information to find an expression for dhdt.

The volume V of a cylinder is given by V=πr2h.

Differentiating this equation with respect to t, and using the fact that the radius of the cylinder does not change, we get dVdt=ddt(πr2h)dVdt=πr2dhdt.

Therefore, dVdt=−kVπr2dhdt=−k(πr2h)dhdt=−kπr2hπr2dhdt=−kh.

question.problem: The area of a circle decreases at a rate that's proportional to the cube of its radius. Write down a differential equation describing the rate of change of the radius, $r(t),$ in this process. Assume that $K>0.$
question.worked_solution:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*The **area** of a circle **decreases** at a **rate** that's **proportional** to the cube of its **radius**. *

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *area $A$ of a circle* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ *decreases* at a rate that's *proportional* to the cube of its *radius.* In other words,

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=-k{r}^{3}
$$

where $k>0.$

We wish to use this information to find an expression for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$

The area of a circle is given by 

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}.
$$

 

Differentiating this equation with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =2\pi r\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-k{r}^{3} \\ 2\pi r\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-k{r}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{k{r}^{3}}{2\pi r} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{k{r}^{2}}{2\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

We now introduce a new constant:

$$
K=\frac{k}{2\pi }>0
$$

 

Therefore, our equation becomes

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-K{r}^{2}.
$$

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.worked_solution:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*The **area** of a circle **decreases** at a **rate** that's **proportional** to the cube of its **radius**. *

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *area $A$ of a circle* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ *decreases* at a rate that's *proportional* to the cube of its *radius.* In other words,

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=-k{r}^{3}
$$

where $k>0.$

We wish to use this information to find an expression for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$

The area of a circle is given by 

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}.
$$

 

Differentiating this equation with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =2\pi r\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-k{r}^{3} \\ 2\pi r\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-k{r}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{k{r}^{3}}{2\pi r} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{k{r}^{2}}{2\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

We now introduce a new constant:

$$
K=\frac{k}{2\pi }>0
$$

 

Therefore, our equation becomes

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-K{r}^{2}.
$$

The area of a circle decreases at a rate that's proportional to the cube of its radius. Write down a differential equation describing the rate of change of the radius, r(t), in this process. Assume that K>0.

a
drdt=−Kr2
b
drdt=−Kr
c
drdt=−Kr2

drdt=−Kr
e
drdt=−K

EXPLANATION

Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

The area of a circle decreases at a rate that's proportional to the cube of its radius.

We note the following:

  • The question describes the rate at which the area A of a circle varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity dAdt.

  • We're told that dAdt decreases at a rate that's proportional to the cube of its radius. In other words, dAdt=−kr3 where k>0.

We wish to use this information to find an expression for drdt.

The area of a circle is given by A=πr2.

Differentiating this equation with respect to t, we get dAdt=ddt(πr2)dAdt=2πrdrdt.

Therefore,

dAdt=−kr32πrdrdt=−kr3drdt=−kr32πrdrdt=−kr22π.

We now introduce a new constant: K=k2π>0

Therefore, our equation becomes drdt=−Kr2.

solution.reasoning: Since A=\pi r^2, dA/dt=2\pi r\,dr/dt. The stated decrease gives dA/dt=-kr^3 for k>0, hence dr/dt=-(k/(2\pi))r^2=-Kr^2 with K>0. Thus choice c is mathematically correct. No captured Math Academy answer evidence establishes its key.

feedback.problem: The area of a circle decreases at a rate that's proportional to the cube of its radius. Write down a differential equation describing the rate of change of the radius, $r(t),$ in this process. Assume that $K>0.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*The **area** of a circle **decreases** at a **rate** that's **proportional** to the cube of its **radius**. *

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *area $A$ of a circle* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ *decreases* at a rate that's *proportional* to the cube of its *radius.* In other words,

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=-k{r}^{3}
$$

where $k>0.$

We wish to use this information to find an expression for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$

The area of a circle is given by 

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}.
$$

 

Differentiating this equation with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =2\pi r\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-k{r}^{3} \\ 2\pi r\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-k{r}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{k{r}^{3}}{2\pi r} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{k{r}^{2}}{2\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

We now introduce a new constant:

$$
K=\frac{k}{2\pi }>0
$$

 

Therefore, our equation becomes

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-K{r}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, our equation becomes drdt=−Kr2.

*At each point $P$ on a particular curve, the **derivative** ${y}^{′}(x)$ is **proportional** to the **shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis**.*

- The *shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis* is given by $|x|.$

- Since the *derivative* is *proportional to* the shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis, we have 

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=k\cdot |x|
$$

where $k$ is a constant.

So, our differential equation is

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=k|x|.

$$
\begin{aligned}24=k|3|\,⟹\,k=8\end{aligned}

{y}^{′}(x)=8|x|.

Question 4
?

At each point P on a particular curve, the derivative y′(x) is proportional to the shortest distance from P to the y-axis. The derivative at the point (3,−5) equals 24. What differential equation describes this curve?

a
y′(x)=x2+y23
b
y′(x)=8|x|
c
y′(x)=3|x|
d
y′(x)=4x2+y2
e
y′(x)=24|y|5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

At each point P on a particular curve, the derivative y′(x) is proportional to the shortest distance from P to the y-axis.

We note the following:

  • The shortest distance from P to the y-axis is given by |x|.

  • Since the derivative is proportional to the shortest distance from P to the y-axis, we have y′(x)=k⋅|x| where k is a constant.

So, our differential equation is

y′(x)=k|x|.

In addition, we're told that y′(x)=24 when at the point (3,−5). We can use this to determine the value of the coefficient k:

24=k|3|⟹k=8

Finally, the differential equation describing the curve is y′(x)=8|x|.

last_observation.worked_solution:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*At each point $P$ on a particular curve, the **derivative** ${y}^{′}(x)$ is **proportional** to the **shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis**.*

We note the following:

- The *shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis* is given by $|x|.$

- Since the *derivative* is *proportional to* the shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis, we have 

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=k\cdot |x|
$$

where $k$ is a constant.

So, our differential equation is

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=k|x|.
$$

In addition, we're told that ${y}^{′}(x)=24$ when at the point $(3,-5).$ We can use this to determine the value of the coefficient $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}24=k|3|\,⟹\,k=8\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the differential equation describing the curve is

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=8|x|.
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

At each point P on a particular curve, the derivative y′(x) is proportional to the shortest distance from P to the y-axis. The derivative at the point (3,−5) equals 24. What differential equation describes this curve?

a
y′(x)=x2+y23
b
y′(x)=8|x|
c
y′(x)=3|x|
d
y′(x)=4x2+y2
e
y′(x)=24|y|5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

At each point P on a particular curve, the derivative y′(x) is proportional to the shortest distance from P to the y-axis.

We note the following:

  • The shortest distance from P to the y-axis is given by |x|.

  • Since the derivative is proportional to the shortest distance from P to the y-axis, we have y′(x)=k⋅|x| where k is a constant.

So, our differential equation is

y′(x)=k|x|.

In addition, we're told that y′(x)=24 when at the point (3,−5). We can use this to determine the value of the coefficient k:

24=k|3|⟹k=8

Finally, the differential equation describing the curve is y′(x)=8|x|.

solution.reasoning: The shortest distance from (x,y) to the y-axis is |x|, so y′(x)=k|x|. At (3,-5), 24=3k, giving k=8. Thus choice b is mathematically correct. No Math Academy answer-key evidence was provided.

Question 4
?

At each point P on a particular curve, the derivative y′(x) is proportional to the shortest distance from P to the y-axis. The derivative at the point (3,−5) equals 24. What differential equation describes this curve?

a
y′(x)=x2+y23
b
y′(x)=8|x|
c
y′(x)=3|x|
d
y′(x)=4x2+y2
e
y′(x)=24|y|5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

At each point P on a particular curve, the derivative y′(x) is proportional to the shortest distance from P to the y-axis.

We note the following:

  • The shortest distance from P to the y-axis is given by |x|.

  • Since the derivative is proportional to the shortest distance from P to the y-axis, we have y′(x)=k⋅|x| where k is a constant.

So, our differential equation is

y′(x)=k|x|.

In addition, we're told that y′(x)=24 when at the point (3,−5). We can use this to determine the value of the coefficient k:

24=k|3|⟹k=8

Finally, the differential equation describing the curve is y′(x)=8|x|.

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: At each point $P$ on a particular curve, the derivative ${y}^{′}(x)$ is **inversely** proportional to the shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis. The derivative at the point $(2,8)$ equals $5.$ What differential equation describes this curve?
question.worked_solution:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*At each point $P$ on a particular curve, the **derivative** ${y}^{′}(x)$ is **inversely proportional** to the **shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis**.*

We note the following:

- The *shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis* is given by $|x|.$

- Since the *derivative* is *inversely proportional* to the shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis, we have 

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=k\cdot \frac{1}{|x|}
$$

where $k$ is a constant.

So, our differential equation is

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=\frac{k}{|x|}.
$$

In addition, we're told that ${y}^{′}(x)=5$ when at the point $(2,8).$ We can use this to determine the value of the coefficient $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}5=\frac{k}{|2|}\,⟹\,k=10\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the differential equation describing the curve is

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=\frac{10}{|x|}.
$$

Question 5
?

At each point P on a particular curve, the derivative y′(x) is inversely proportional to the shortest distance from P to the y-axis. The derivative at the point (2,8) equals 5. What differential equation describes this curve?

a
y′(x)=10|x|
b
y′(x)=5|y|2
c
y′(x)=5|x|
d
y′(x)=40|y|
e
y′(x)=|x|5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

At each point P on a particular curve, the derivative y′(x) is inversely proportional to the shortest distance from P to the y-axis.

We note the following:

  • The shortest distance from P to the y-axis is given by |x|.

  • Since the derivative is inversely proportional to the shortest distance from P to the y-axis, we have y′(x)=k⋅1|x| where k is a constant.

So, our differential equation is

y′(x)=k|x|.

In addition, we're told that y′(x)=5 when at the point (2,8). We can use this to determine the value of the coefficient k:

5=k|2|⟹k=10

Finally, the differential equation describing the curve is y′(x)=10|x|.

question.html:
Question 5
?

At each point P on a particular curve, the derivative y′(x) is inversely proportional to the shortest distance from P to the y-axis. The derivative at the point (2,8) equals 5. What differential equation describes this curve?

a
y′(x)=10|x|
b
y′(x)=5|y|2
c
y′(x)=5|x|
d
y′(x)=40|y|
e
y′(x)=|x|5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

At each point P on a particular curve, the derivative y′(x) is inversely proportional to the shortest distance from P to the y-axis.

We note the following:

  • The shortest distance from P to the y-axis is given by |x|.

  • Since the derivative is inversely proportional to the shortest distance from P to the y-axis, we have y′(x)=k⋅1|x| where k is a constant.

So, our differential equation is

y′(x)=k|x|.

In addition, we're told that y′(x)=5 when at the point (2,8). We can use this to determine the value of the coefficient k:

5=k|2|⟹k=10

Finally, the differential equation describing the curve is y′(x)=10|x|.

solution.reasoning: The shortest distance to the y-axis is |x|. Inverse proportionality gives y′(x)=k/|x|. At (2,8), 5=k/2, so k=10. Thus choice a is mathematically correct, for x≠0. No Math Academy answer-key evidence was provided.

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem: At each point $P$ on a particular curve, the derivative ${y}^{′}(x)$ is **inversely** proportional to the shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis. The derivative at the point $(2,8)$ equals $5.$ What differential equation describes this curve?
feedback.worked_solution:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*At each point $P$ on a particular curve, the **derivative** ${y}^{′}(x)$ is **inversely proportional** to the **shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis**.*

We note the following:

- The *shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis* is given by $|x|.$

- Since the *derivative* is *inversely proportional* to the shortest distance from $P$ to the $y$-axis, we have 

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=k\cdot \frac{1}{|x|}
$$

where $k$ is a constant.

So, our differential equation is

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=\frac{k}{|x|}.
$$

In addition, we're told that ${y}^{′}(x)=5$ when at the point $(2,8).$ We can use this to determine the value of the coefficient $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}5=\frac{k}{|2|}\,⟹\,k=10\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the differential equation describing the curve is

$$
{y}^{′}(x)=\frac{10}{|x|}.
$$

Question 5
?

At each point P on a particular curve, the derivative y′(x) is inversely proportional to the shortest distance from P to the y-axis. The derivative at the point (2,8) equals 5. What differential equation describes this curve?

a
y′(x)=10|x|
b
y′(x)=5|y|2
c
y′(x)=5|x|
d
y′(x)=40|y|
e
y′(x)=|x|5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

At each point P on a particular curve, the derivative y′(x) is inversely proportional to the shortest distance from P to the y-axis.

We note the following:

  • The shortest distance from P to the y-axis is given by |x|.

  • Since the derivative is inversely proportional to the shortest distance from P to the y-axis, we have y′(x)=k⋅1|x| where k is a constant.

So, our differential equation is

y′(x)=k|x|.

In addition, we're told that y′(x)=5 when at the point (2,8). We can use this to determine the value of the coefficient k:

5=k|2|⟹k=10

Finally, the differential equation describing the curve is y′(x)=10|x|.

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14224903/assets/b82ed81f724322dc05a2c65d3635ac74f5ca92ff413e9d7e5131ebb604269f26.png)

Determine the equation of the trend line shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the trend line passes through the points $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(-4,6)$ and $({x}_{2},{y}_{2})=(4,3).$

We will write the equation of the line in the slope-intercept form 

$$
y=mx+b.
$$

First, we compute the slope $m$ of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\  & =\frac{3-6}{4-(-4)} \\  & =\frac{-3}{8} \\  & =-\frac{3}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $m=-\frac{3}{8}$ into the slope-intercept form above, we get

$$
y=-\frac{3}{8}x+b.
$$

We now need to find the $y$-intercept $b.$ We can find this by substituting the coordinates of a point on the line. Any point will do, so let's substitute $(-4,6):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{3}{8}x+b \\ 6 & =-\frac{3}{8}(-4)+b \\ 6 & =\frac{3}{2}+b \\ 12 & =3+2b \\ b & =\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the line is 

$$
y=-\frac{3}{8}x+\frac{9}{2}.
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14224903/assets/1c9f30692222eaaed4cda6b608dcc1ccb01eefd6b5fa7730b5b8bb29c9f528b1.png)

Determine the equation of the trend line shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the trend line passes through the points $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(2,2)$ and $({x}_{2},{y}_{2})=(7,8).$

We will write the equation of the line in the slope-intercept form 

$$
y=mx+b.
$$

First, we compute the slope $m$ of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\  & =\frac{8-2}{7-2} \\  & =\frac{6}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $m=\frac{6}{5}$ into the slope-intercept form above, we get

$$
y=\frac{6}{5}x+b.
$$

We now need to find the $y$-intercept $b.$ We can find this by substituting the coordinates of a point on the line. Any point will do, so let's substitute $(2,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{6}{5}x+b \\ 2 & =\frac{6}{5}(2)+b \\ 2 & =\frac{12}{5}+b \\ 10 & =12+5b \\ -2 & =5b \\ b & =-\frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the line is 

$$
y=\frac{6}{5}x-\frac{2}{5}.
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =0.5x+b \\ 4 & =0.5(2)+b \\ 4 & =1+b \\ 3 & =b \\ b & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the line is 

$$
y=0.5x+3.
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14224903/assets/e4b948bc417deab7c83cb40f53ad4b55fbfb169fc4ec761a9365856a9457a8f5.png)

Estimate the equation of the trend line for the scatter plot above. Round both the slope and the $y$-intercept to the nearest $0.5.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's draw an approximate trend line for our scatter plot:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14224903/assets/fd3ce3de75fa9296c721e3f3a28bef241eae6350819c4cc7a54707921c0c1fe4.png)

It seems that the trend line passes through $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})≈(2,7)$ and $({x}_{2},{y}_{2})≈(8,4).$

We will write the equation of the line in the slope-intercept form 

$$
y=mx+b.
$$

First, we estimate the slope $m$ of the line as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ≈\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\  & =\frac{4-7}{8-2} \\  & =\frac{-3}{6} \\  & =-0.5\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $m=-0.5$ into the slope-intercept form above, we get

$$
y=-0.5x+b.
$$

We now need to estimate the $y$-intercept $b.$ We can do this by substituting the coordinates of a point on the line. Any point will do, so let's substitute $(2,7):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-0.5x+b \\ 7 & =-0.5(2)+b \\ 7 & =-1+b \\ 8 & =b \\ b & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the line is 

$$
y=-0.5x+8.
$$
