question.html:
Question 13
?

Given that x1 and x2 are the solutions to sin⁡(3x−π4)=−22 for 0≤x≤π2, what is the value of x1+x2?

a
π2
b
π3
c
5π4
d
2π3
e
3π4
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will find the general solution to the equation, and then generate all of the solutions in the required domain.

The general solution to our equation is

3x−π4=5π4+2nπ,3x−π4=7π4+2nπ.

Solving the two equations above for x gives:

3x=3π2+2nπ3x=2π+2nπx=π2+2nπ3x=2π3+2nπ3x=π(4n+3)6x=2(n+1)π3

We set n=0,±1,±2,…, until we have generated all solutions in the domain 0≤x≤π2.

  • Setting n=0 gives x=π2 and x=2π3 (too big)

  • Setting n=−1 gives x=−π6 (too small) and x=0.

All other values of n generate solutions outside the domain 0≤x<2π3. So, the solutions x1,x2 are

x=0,π2.

Finally,

x1+x2=0+π2=π2.

last_observation.worked_solution:
We will find the general solution to the equation, and then generate all of the solutions in the required domain.

The general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-\frac{\pi }{4} & =\frac{5\pi }{4}+2n\pi , & \, & \, & 3x-\frac{\pi }{4} & =\frac{7\pi }{4}+2n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the two equations above for $x$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x & =\frac{3\pi }{2}+2n\pi  & \, & \, & 3x & =2\pi +2n\pi  \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{2}+\frac{2n\pi }{3} & \, & \, & x & =\frac{2\pi }{3}+\frac{2n\pi }{3} \\ x & =\frac{\pi (4n+3)}{6} & \, & \, & x & =\frac{2(n+1)\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

We set $n=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…,$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain $0\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

- Setting $n=0$ gives $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $x=\frac{2\pi }{3}$ (too big)

- Setting $n=-1$ gives $x=-\frac{\pi }{6}$ (too small) and $x=0.$

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain $0\le x<\frac{2\pi }{3}.$ So, the solutions ${x}_{1},{x}_{2}$ are

$$
x=0,\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Finally, 

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Consider the equation $\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x-\frac{\pi }{4})=-\frac{1}{2}$ for $0\le x<\pi .$ If the solutions ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3},{x}_{4}$ are written in **ascending order**, what are their values? Express your answers in terms of $\pi .$

${x}_{2}=${{field-2}}$,\,$
${x}_{3}=${{field-3}}$,\,$

question.worked_solution:
We will find the general solution to the equation, and then generate all of the solutions in the required domain.

The general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}4x-\frac{\pi }{4} & =\frac{7\pi }{6}+2n\pi , & \, & \, & 4x-\frac{\pi }{4} & =\frac{11\pi }{6}+2n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the two equations above for $x$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}4x & =\frac{7\pi }{6}+\frac{\pi }{4}+2n\pi  & \, & \, & 4x & =\frac{11\pi }{6}+\frac{\pi }{4}+2n\pi  \\ 4x & =\frac{17\pi }{12}+2n\pi  & \, & \, & 4x & =\frac{25\pi }{12}+2n\pi  \\ x & =\frac{17\pi }{48}+\frac{n\pi }{2} & \, & \, & x & =\frac{25\pi }{48}+\frac{n\pi }{2} \\ x & =\frac{17\pi }{48}+\frac{24n\pi }{48} & \, & \, & x & =\frac{25\pi }{48}+\frac{24n\pi }{48} \\ x & =\frac{(24n+17)\pi }{48} & \, & \, & x & =\frac{(24n+25)\pi }{48}\end{aligned}
$$

We set $n=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…,$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain $0\le x<\pi .$

- Setting $n=0$ gives $x=\frac{17\pi }{48}$ and $x=\frac{25\pi }{48}$

- Setting $n=-1$ gives $x=-\frac{7\pi }{48}$ (too small) and $x=\frac{\pi }{48}$

- Setting $n=1$ gives $x=\frac{41\pi }{48}$ and $x=\frac{49\pi }{48}$ (too big)

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain $0\le x<\pi .$ So, the solutions ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3},{x}_{4}$ (written in ascending order) are

$$
x=\frac{\pi }{48},\frac{17\pi }{48},\frac{25\pi }{48},\frac{41\pi }{48}.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that:

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{\pi }{48},\,{x}_{2}=\frac{17\pi }{48},\,{x}_{3}=\frac{25\pi }{48},\,{x}_{4}=\frac{41\pi }{48}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Solve the inequality $\operatorname{ln}⁡(4-x)-1\ge 0.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we isolate the logarithm:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(4-x)-1 & \ge 0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(4-x) & \ge 1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $e.$ We get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4-x)} & \ge {e}^{1} \\ 4-x & \ge e \\ -x & \ge e-4 \\ x & \le 4-e\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithm, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
4-x>0\,⇒\,x<4
$$

Our solution is $x\le 4-e,$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,4-e].$ Additionally, the domain of the logarithm is $x<4,$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,4).$ To find the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty ,4-e]\cap (-\infty ,4)=(-\infty ,4-e]
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (-\infty ,4-e],$ which can also be written as $x\le 4-e.$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Solve the inequality $10{log}_{2}⁡(x-6)-3<2.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we isolate the logarithm:

$$
\begin{aligned}10{log}_{2}⁡(x-6)-3 & <2 \\ 10{log}_{2}⁡(x-6) & <5 \\ {log}_{2}⁡(x-6) & <\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $2.$ We get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{{log}_{2}⁡(x-6)} & <{2}^{1/2} \\ x-6 & <\sqrt{2} \\ x & <6+\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithm, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
x-6>0\,⇒\,x>6
$$

Our solution is $x<6+\sqrt{2},$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,6+\sqrt{2}).$ Additionally, the domain of the logarithm is $x>6,$ which can be expressed as $(6,\infty ).$ To find the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty ,6+\sqrt{2})\cap (6,\infty )=(6,6+\sqrt{2})
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (6,6+\sqrt{2}),$ which can also be written as $6<x<6+\sqrt{2}.$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.worked_solution:
First, we isolate the logarithm:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{log}_{2}⁡(x+4)-2 & >0 \\ 5{log}_{2}⁡(x+4) & >2 \\ {log}_{2}⁡(x+4) & >\frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $2.$ We get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{{log}_{2}⁡(x+4)} & >{2}^{2/5} \\ x+4 & >\sqrt[5]{4} \\ x & >\sqrt[5]{4}-4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithm, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
x+4>0\,⇒\,x>-4
$$

Our solution is $x>\sqrt[5]{4}-4,$ which can be expressed as $(\sqrt[5]{4}-4,\infty ).$ Additionally, the domain of the logarithm is $x>-4,$ which can be expressed as $(-4,\infty ).$ To find the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm, we take the intersection:

$$
(\sqrt[5]{4}-4,\infty )\cap (-4,\infty )=(\sqrt[5]{4}-4,\infty )
$$

Therefore, the solution is 

$$
x\in (\sqrt[5]{4}-4,\infty ),\text{ which can also be written as }x>\sqrt[5]{4}-4.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we isolate the logarithm:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+4)-6 & >0 \\ \frac{3}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+4) & >6 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+4) & >10\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $e.$ We get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+4)} & >{e}^{10} \\ x+4 & >{e}^{10} \\ x & >{e}^{10}-4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithm, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
x+4>0\,⇒\,x>-4
$$

Our solution is $x>{e}^{10}-4,$ which can be expressed as $({e}^{10}-4,\infty ).$ Additionally, the domain of the logarithm is $x>-4,$ which can be expressed as $(-4,\infty ).$ To find the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm, we take the intersection:

$$
({e}^{10}-4,\infty )\cap (-4,\infty )=({e}^{10}-4,\infty )
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in ({e}^{10}-4,\infty ),$ which can also be written as $x>{e}^{10}-4.$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: Solve the inequality $3{log}_{3}⁡(x-1)-5<7.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we isolate the logarithm:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{log}_{3}⁡(x-1)-5 & <7 \\ 3{log}_{3}⁡(x-1) & <12 \\ {log}_{3}⁡(x-1) & <4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $3.$ We get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{{log}_{3}⁡(x-1)} & <{3}^{4} \\ x-1 & <81 \\ x & <82\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithm, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
x-1>0\,⇒\,x>1
$$

Our solution is $x<82,$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,82).$ Additionally, the domain of the logarithm is $x>1,$ which can be expressed as $(1,\infty ).$ To find the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty ,82)\cap (1,\infty )=(1,82)
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (1,82),$ which can also be written as $1<x<82.$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.worked_solution:
We use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $10.$ This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{10}^{\operatorname{log}⁡(3x-4)} & \le {10}^{\operatorname{log}⁡(x+8)} \\ {10}^{\operatorname{log}⁡(3x-4)} & \le {10}^{\operatorname{log}⁡(x+8)} \\ 3x-4 & \le x+8 \\ 2x & \le 12 \\ x & \le 6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-4 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >\frac{4}{3} \\ x+8 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >-8\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x\le 6,$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,6].$ Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are $x>\frac{4}{3}$ and $x>-8,$ which can be expressed as $(\frac{4}{3},\infty )$ and $(-8,\infty )$ respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty ,6]\cap (\frac{4}{3},\infty )\cap (-8,\infty )=(\frac{4}{3},6]
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (\frac{4}{3},6],$ which can also be written as $\frac{4}{3}<x\le 6.$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem: Solve the inequality $\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x-1)<\operatorname{ln}⁡(5-4x).$
questions.worked_solution:
We use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $e.$ This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x-1)} & <{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5-4x)} \\ 3x-1 & <5-4x \\ 7x & <6 \\ x & <\frac{6}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-1 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >\frac{1}{3} \\ 5-4x & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & <\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x<\frac{6}{7},$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,\frac{6}{7}).$ Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are $x>\frac{1}{3}$ and $x<\frac{5}{4},$ which can be expressed as $(\frac{1}{3},\infty )$ and $(-\infty ,\frac{5}{4}),$ respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty ,\frac{6}{7})\cap (\frac{1}{3},\infty )\cap (-\infty ,\frac{5}{4})=(\frac{1}{3},\frac{6}{7})
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (\frac{1}{3},\frac{6}{7}),$ which can also be written as $\frac{1}{3}<x<\frac{6}{7}.$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.worked_solution:
We use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $10.$ This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{10}^{\operatorname{log}⁡(2x-7)-1} & \le {10}^{\operatorname{log}⁡(x+3)} \\ {10}^{\operatorname{log}⁡(2x-7)}\cdot {10}^{-1} & \le {10}^{\operatorname{log}⁡(x+3)} \\ (2x-7)\cdot \frac{1}{10} & \le x+3 \\ 2x-7 & \le 10x+30 \\ -8x & \le 37 \\ x & \ge -\frac{37}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-7 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >\frac{7}{2} \\ x+3 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >-3\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x\ge -\frac{37}{8},$ which can be expressed as $[-\frac{37}{8},\infty ).$ Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are $x>\frac{7}{2}$ and $x>-3,$ which can be expressed as $(\frac{7}{2},\infty )$ and $(-3,\infty )$ respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection:

$$
[-\frac{37}{8},\infty )\cap (\frac{7}{2},\infty )\cap (-3,\infty )=(\frac{7}{2},\infty )
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (\frac{7}{2},\infty ),$ which can also be written as $x>\frac{7}{2}.$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.worked_solution:
We use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $e.$ This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+4)-1} & <{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)} \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+4)}\cdot {e}^{-1} & <{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)} \\ (2x+4)\cdot \frac{1}{e} & <x-2 \\ 2x+4 & <xe-2e \\ 4+2e & <xe-2x \\ 4+2e & <x(e-2) \\ x & >\frac{4+2e}{e-2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+4 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >-2 \\ x-2 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >2\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x>\frac{4+2e}{e-2},$ which can be expressed as $(\frac{4+2e}{e-2},\infty ).$ Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are $x>-2$ and $x>2,$ which can be expressed as $(-2,\infty )$ and $(2,\infty )$ respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection:

$$
(\frac{4+2e}{e-2},\infty )\cap (-2,\infty )\cap (2,\infty )=(\frac{4+2e}{e-2},\infty )
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (\frac{4+2e}{e-2},\infty ),$ which can also be written as 

$$
x>\frac{4+2e}{e-2}.
$$

questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem: Solve the inequality $\operatorname{ln}⁡(2-x)>\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-7).$
questions.worked_solution:
We use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $e.$ This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2-x)} & >{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-7)} \\ 2-x & >x-7 \\ -2x & >-9 \\ x & <\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}2-x & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & <2 \\ x-7 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >7\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x<\frac{9}{2},$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,\frac{9}{2}).$ Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are $x<2$ and $x>7,$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,2)$ and $(7,\infty )$ respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty ,\frac{9}{2})\cap (-\infty ,2)\cap (7,\infty )=∅
$$

The intersection is empty. Therefore, there is no solution.

Example: 
                    Solving an Inequality Involving One Logarithmic Function
canonical_examples.problem: Solve the inequality $\dfrac{3}{5} \ln(x+2) +1 \leq 0.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we isolate the logarithm:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2)+1 & \le 0 \\ \frac{3}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2) & \le -1 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2) & \le -\frac{5}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $e.$ We get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2)} & \le {e}^{-5/3} \\ x+2 & \le {e}^{-5/3} \\ x & \le {e}^{-5/3}-2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithm, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
x+2> 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad x > -2
$$

Our solution is $x \leq e^{-5/3}-2,$ which can be expressed as $\left(-\infty, e^{-5/3}-2\right].$ Additionally, the domain of the logarithm is $x > -2,$ which can be expressed as $(-2, \infty).$ To find the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm, we take the intersection:

$$
\left(-\infty, e^{-5/3}-2\right] \cap (-2, \infty) = \left(-2,e^{-5/3}-2 \right]
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x \in \left(-2, e^{-5/3}-2\right],$ which can also be written as $-2<  x \leq e^{-5/3}-2.$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
When we have a logarithm in an inequality with base $n > 1,$ we can use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $n.$

However, there is a catch: when we solve the resulting inequality, we must remember to remove extraneous solutions. We can do this by keeping only the solutions that are in the domain of the original logarithm.

For example, to solve the inequality

$$
\log_2 (x-1) < 4,
$$

we write each side of the inequality as an exponent of $2,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{{log}_{2}⁡(x-1)} & <{2}^{4} \\ x-1 & <16 \\ x & <17.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithm, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
x-1 > 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad x > 1
$$

Our solution is $x < 17,$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty, 17).$ But the domain of the logarithm is $x > 1,$ which can be expressed as $(1, \infty).$ To find the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty, 17) \cap (1, \infty) = (1, 17)
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x \in (1,17),$ which can also be written as $1 < x < 17.$

tutorials.name: The Reason Why We Can Use Each Side as an Exponent
tutorials.problem:
We're allowed to use each side of an inequality as the exponent of a number $n>1.$ But why are we allowed to do this?

The reason is that this operation preserves the ordering of numbers. That is to say, if $a < b$ and $n>1,$ then $n^a < n^b.$

To see this concretely, consider the following order of numbers:

$$
-2 < -1 < 0 < 0.5 < 1 < 2 < 3
$$

If we raise $2$ to the power of these numbers, the results stay in the same order:

$$
\underbrace{0.25}_{ 2^{-2} } < \underbrace{0.5}_{ 2^{-1} } < \underbrace{1}_{ 2^0 } < \underbrace{\,\, 1.41\ldots \,\,}_{ 2^{0.5} } < \underbrace{2}_{ 2^1 } < \underbrace{4}_{ 2^2 } < \underbrace{8}_{ 2^3 }
$$

tutorials.name: Inequalities with Two Logarithms
tutorials.problem:
When we have two logarithms in an inequality, we can use the same solution procedure as before: we use each side of the inequality as an exponent of the base of the logarithm.

Just remember that we still need to remove extraneous solutions. We can do this by keeping only the solutions that are in the domains of *all* the logarithms in the original inequality.

observed_steps.name: Example: Solving an Inequality Involving One Logarithmic Function
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we isolate the logarithm:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2)+1 & \le 0 \\ \frac{3}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2) & \le -1 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2) & \le -\frac{5}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $e.$ We get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2)} & \le {e}^{-5/3} \\ x+2 & \le {e}^{-5/3} \\ x & \le {e}^{-5/3}-2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithm, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
x+2> 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad x > -2
$$

Our solution is $x \leq e^{-5/3}-2,$ which can be expressed as $\left(-\infty, e^{-5/3}-2\right].$ Additionally, the domain of the logarithm is $x > -2,$ which can be expressed as $(-2, \infty).$ To find the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm, we take the intersection:

$$
\left(-\infty, e^{-5/3}-2\right] \cap (-2, \infty) = \left(-2,e^{-5/3}-2 \right]
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x \in \left(-2, e^{-5/3}-2\right],$ which can also be written as $-2<  x \leq e^{-5/3}-2.$

First, we isolate the logarithm:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(4-x)-1 & \ge 0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(4-x) & \ge 1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $e.$ We get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4-x)} & \ge {e}^{1} \\ 4-x & \ge e \\ -x & \ge e-4 \\ x & \le 4-e\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithm, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
4-x>0\,⇒\,x<4
$$

Our solution is $x\le 4-e,$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,4-e].$ Additionally, the domain of the logarithm is $x<4,$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,4).$ To find the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty ,4-e]\cap (-\infty ,4)=(-\infty ,4-e]
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (-\infty ,4-e],$ which can also be written as $x\le 4-e.$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Solve the inequality 3log3⁡(x−1)−5<7.

a
x>82
b
1<x<82
c
x<81
d
−1<x<82
e
2<x<81
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we isolate the logarithm:

3log3⁡(x−1)−5<73log3⁡(x−1)<12log3⁡(x−1)<4

Now, we use each side of the inequality as an exponent of 3. We get the following:

3log3⁡(x−1)<34x−1<81x<82

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithm, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

x−1>0⇒x>1

Our solution is x<82, which can be expressed as (−∞,82). Additionally, the domain of the logarithm is x>1, which can be expressed as (1,∞). To find the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm, we take the intersection:

(−∞,82)∩(1,∞)=(1,82)

Therefore, the solution is x∈(1,82), which can also be written as 1<x<82.

tutorial.problem:
When we have two logarithms in an inequality, we can use the same solution procedure as before: we use each side of the inequality as an exponent of the base of the logarithm.

Just remember that we still need to remove extraneous solutions. We can do this by keeping only the solutions that are in the domains of *all* the logarithms in the original inequality.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
We use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $10.$ This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{10}^{\operatorname{log}⁡(3x-4)} & \le {10}^{\operatorname{log}⁡(x+8)} \\ {10}^{\operatorname{log}⁡(3x-4)} & \le {10}^{\operatorname{log}⁡(x+8)} \\ 3x-4 & \le x+8 \\ 2x & \le 12 \\ x & \le 6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-4 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >\frac{4}{3} \\ x+8 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >-8\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x\le 6,$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,6].$ Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are $x>\frac{4}{3}$ and $x>-8,$ which can be expressed as $(\frac{4}{3},\infty )$ and $(-8,\infty )$ respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty ,6]\cap (\frac{4}{3},\infty )\cap (-8,\infty )=(\frac{4}{3},6]
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (\frac{4}{3},6],$ which can also be written as $\frac{4}{3}<x\le 6.$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
We use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $e.$ This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x-1)} & <{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5-4x)} \\ 3x-1 & <5-4x \\ 7x & <6 \\ x & <\frac{6}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-1 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >\frac{1}{3} \\ 5-4x & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & <\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x<\frac{6}{7},$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,\frac{6}{7}).$ Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are $x>\frac{1}{3}$ and $x<\frac{5}{4},$ which can be expressed as $(\frac{1}{3},\infty )$ and $(-\infty ,\frac{5}{4}),$ respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty ,\frac{6}{7})\cap (\frac{1}{3},\infty )\cap (-\infty ,\frac{5}{4})=(\frac{1}{3},\frac{6}{7})
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (\frac{1}{3},\frac{6}{7}),$ which can also be written as $\frac{1}{3}<x<\frac{6}{7}.$

Solve the inequality ln⁡(3x−1)<ln⁡(5−4x).

x<67

13<x<54
e
x>13

EXPLANATION

We use each side of the inequality as an exponent of e. This gives the following: eln⁡(3x−1)<eln⁡(5−4x)3x−1<5−4x7x<6x<67

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive: 3x−1>0⇒x>135−4x>0⇒x<54

Our solution is x<67, which can be expressed as (−∞,67). Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are x>13 and x<54, which can be expressed as (13,∞) and (−∞,54), respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection: (−∞,67)∩(13,∞)∩(−∞,54)=(13,67)

Therefore, the solution is x∈(13,67), which can also be written as 13<x<67.

We use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $10.$ This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{10}^{\operatorname{log}⁡(2x-7)-1} & \le {10}^{\operatorname{log}⁡(x+3)} \\ {10}^{\operatorname{log}⁡(2x-7)}\cdot {10}^{-1} & \le {10}^{\operatorname{log}⁡(x+3)} \\ (2x-7)\cdot \frac{1}{10} & \le x+3 \\ 2x-7 & \le 10x+30 \\ -8x & \le 37 \\ x & \ge -\frac{37}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-7 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >\frac{7}{2} \\ x+3 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >-3\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x\ge -\frac{37}{8},$ which can be expressed as $[-\frac{37}{8},\infty ).$ Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are $x>\frac{7}{2}$ and $x>-3,$ which can be expressed as $(\frac{7}{2},\infty )$ and $(-3,\infty )$ respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection:

$$
[-\frac{37}{8},\infty )\cap (\frac{7}{2},\infty )\cap (-3,\infty )=(\frac{7}{2},\infty )
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (\frac{7}{2},\infty ),$ which can also be written as $x>\frac{7}{2}.$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Solve the inequality $\operatorname{ln}⁡(4-x)-1\ge 0.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we isolate the logarithm:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(4-x)-1 & \ge 0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(4-x) & \ge 1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $e.$ We get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4-x)} & \ge {e}^{1} \\ 4-x & \ge e \\ -x & \ge e-4 \\ x & \le 4-e\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithm, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
4-x>0\,⇒\,x<4
$$

Our solution is $x\le 4-e,$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,4-e].$ Additionally, the domain of the logarithm is $x<4,$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,4).$ To find the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty ,4-e]\cap (-\infty ,4)=(-\infty ,4-e]
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (-\infty ,4-e],$ which can also be written as $x\le 4-e.$

Therefore, the solution is x∈(−∞,4−e], which can also be written as x≤4−e.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Solve the inequality $10{log}_{2}⁡(x-6)-3<2.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we isolate the logarithm:

$$
\begin{aligned}10{log}_{2}⁡(x-6)-3 & <2 \\ 10{log}_{2}⁡(x-6) & <5 \\ {log}_{2}⁡(x-6) & <\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $2.$ We get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{{log}_{2}⁡(x-6)} & <{2}^{1/2} \\ x-6 & <\sqrt{2} \\ x & <6+\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithm, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
x-6>0\,⇒\,x>6
$$

Our solution is $x<6+\sqrt{2},$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,6+\sqrt{2}).$ Additionally, the domain of the logarithm is $x>6,$ which can be expressed as $(6,\infty ).$ To find the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty ,6+\sqrt{2})\cap (6,\infty )=(6,6+\sqrt{2})
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (6,6+\sqrt{2}),$ which can also be written as $6<x<6+\sqrt{2}.$

$$

$$

Now, we use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $2.$ We get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{{log}_{2}⁡(x-6)} & <{2}^{1/2} \\ x-6 & <\sqrt{2} \\ x & <6+\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithm, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
x-6>0\,⇒\,x>6
$$

Our solution is $x<6+\sqrt{2},$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,6+\sqrt{2}).$ Additionally, the domain of the logarithm is $x>6,$ which can be expressed as $(6,\infty ).$ To find the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty ,6+\sqrt{2})\cap (6,\infty )=(6,6+\sqrt{2})
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (6,6+\sqrt{2}),$ which can also be written as $6<x<6+\sqrt{2}.$

$$

Now, we use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $3.$ We get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{{log}_{3}⁡(x-1)} & <{3}^{4} \\ x-1 & <81 \\ x & <82\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithm, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
x-1>0\,⇒\,x>1
$$

Our solution is $x<82,$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,82).$ Additionally, the domain of the logarithm is $x>1,$ which can be expressed as $(1,\infty ).$ To find the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty ,82)\cap (1,\infty )=(1,82)
$$

$$

$$

Now, we use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $3.$ We get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{{log}_{3}⁡(x-1)} & <{3}^{4} \\ x-1 & <81 \\ x & <82\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithm, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
x-1>0\,⇒\,x>1
$$

Our solution is $x<82,$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,82).$ Additionally, the domain of the logarithm is $x>1,$ which can be expressed as $(1,\infty ).$ To find the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty ,82)\cap (1,\infty )=(1,82)
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (1,82),$ which can also be written as $1<x<82.$

question.problem: Solve the inequality $\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x-1)<\operatorname{ln}⁡(5-4x).$
question.worked_solution:
We use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $e.$ This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x-1)} & <{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5-4x)} \\ 3x-1 & <5-4x \\ 7x & <6 \\ x & <\frac{6}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-1 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >\frac{1}{3} \\ 5-4x & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & <\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x<\frac{6}{7},$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,\frac{6}{7}).$ Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are $x>\frac{1}{3}$ and $x<\frac{5}{4},$ which can be expressed as $(\frac{1}{3},\infty )$ and $(-\infty ,\frac{5}{4}),$ respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty ,\frac{6}{7})\cap (\frac{1}{3},\infty )\cap (-\infty ,\frac{5}{4})=(\frac{1}{3},\frac{6}{7})
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (\frac{1}{3},\frac{6}{7}),$ which can also be written as $\frac{1}{3}<x<\frac{6}{7}.$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Solving an Inequality Involving Two Logarithmic Functions
last_observation.worked_solution:
We use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $e.$ This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x-1)} & <{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5-4x)} \\ 3x-1 & <5-4x \\ 7x & <6 \\ x & <\frac{6}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-1 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >\frac{1}{3} \\ 5-4x & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & <\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x<\frac{6}{7},$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,\frac{6}{7}).$ Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are $x>\frac{1}{3}$ and $x<\frac{5}{4},$ which can be expressed as $(\frac{1}{3},\infty )$ and $(-\infty ,\frac{5}{4}),$ respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty ,\frac{6}{7})\cap (\frac{1}{3},\infty )\cap (-\infty ,\frac{5}{4})=(\frac{1}{3},\frac{6}{7})
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (\frac{1}{3},\frac{6}{7}),$ which can also be written as $\frac{1}{3}<x<\frac{6}{7}.$

Solve the inequality ln⁡(3x−1)<ln⁡(5−4x).

a
13<x<67
b
67<x<54
c
x<67
d
13<x<54
e
x>13
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We use each side of the inequality as an exponent of e. This gives the following: eln⁡(3x−1)<eln⁡(5−4x)3x−1<5−4x7x<6x<67

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive: 3x−1>0⇒x>135−4x>0⇒x<54

Our solution is x<67, which can be expressed as (−∞,67). Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are x>13 and x<54, which can be expressed as (13,∞) and (−∞,54), respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection: (−∞,67)∩(13,∞)∩(−∞,54)=(13,67)

Therefore, the solution is x∈(13,67), which can also be written as 13<x<67.

$$

$$
[-\frac{37}{8},\infty )\cap (\frac{7}{2},\infty )\cap (-3,\infty )=(\frac{7}{2},\infty )
$$

$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (\frac{4+2e}{e-2},\infty ),$ which can also be written as

question.html:
Question 10
?

Solve the inequality ln⁡(2−x)>ln⁡(x−7).

a
x<2
b
92<x<7
c
2<x<92
d
No solution
e
x<92
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We use each side of the inequality as an exponent of e. This gives the following: eln⁡(2−x)>eln⁡(x−7)2−x>x−7−2x>−9x<92

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive: 2−x>0⇒x<2x−7>0⇒x>7

Our solution is x<92, which can be expressed as (−∞,92). Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are x<2 and x>7, which can be expressed as (−∞,2) and (7,∞) respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection: (−∞,92)∩(−∞,2)∩(7,∞)=∅

The intersection is empty. Therefore, there is no solution.

solution.reasoning: The logarithms require 2-x>0 and x-7>0 simultaneously, meaning x<2 and x>7. These conditions cannot both hold, so there is no real solution: option d. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 10
feedback.problem: Solve the inequality $\operatorname{ln}⁡(2-x)>\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-7).$
feedback.worked_solution:
We use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $e.$ This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2-x)} & >{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-7)} \\ 2-x & >x-7 \\ -2x & >-9 \\ x & <\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}2-x & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & <2 \\ x-7 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >7\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x<\frac{9}{2},$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,\frac{9}{2}).$ Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are $x<2$ and $x>7,$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,2)$ and $(7,\infty )$ respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty ,\frac{9}{2})\cap (-\infty ,2)\cap (7,\infty )=∅
$$

The intersection is empty. Therefore, there is no solution.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
In **ascending order**, rounded to two decimal places in radians, the solutions to the equation $2\operatorname{sin}⁡x=10\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ for $0\le x<2\pi ,$ are

${x}_{1}≈$
 {{field-1}}$,\,{x}_{2}≈$ 
{{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We divide both sides of the equation by $\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and use the identity $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =10\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =\frac{10\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\ \frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =\frac{10\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} \\ 2\operatorname{tan}⁡x & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we rearrange the equation and isolate $\operatorname{tan}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{tan}⁡x & =10 \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =\frac{10}{2} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(5)≈1.373\,40\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $5$ decimal places.

To find the other solution in the given interval, we add $\pi $ to the principal value. Hence,

$$
x≈1.373\,40+\pi ≈4.514\,99
$$

rounded to $5$ decimal places. 

So, in ascending order, rounded to two decimal places, the solutions are 

$$
{x}_{1}≈1.37,\,{x}_{2}≈4.51.
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions to the equation $5\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x=0$ for $0\le x<2\pi ,$ what is the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2},$ rounded to $1$ decimal place?
questions.worked_solution:
We divide both sides of the equation by $\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and use the identity $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}5\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0 \\ \frac{5\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =0 \\ \frac{5\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\frac{2\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} & =0 \\ 5\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-2 & =0 \\ 5\operatorname{tan}⁡x-2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we rearrange the equation and isolate $\operatorname{tan}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}5\operatorname{tan}⁡x & =2 \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =\frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{2}{5})=0.380\,506…≈0.380\,5\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $4$ decimal places. 

Since $0.380\,5$ lies inside the given domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}=0.380\,5.$

To find the other solution in the given interval, we add $\pi $ to the principal value. Hence,

$$
{x}_{2}=0.380\,506…+\pi =3.522\,099…≈3.522\,1
$$

rounded to $4$ decimal places. 

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}≈0.380\,5\cdot 3.522\,1≈1.3
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions to the equation $2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+9\operatorname{cos}⁡x=0$ for $0\le x<2\pi ,$ what is the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2},$ rounded to $3$ decimal places?
questions.worked_solution:
We divide both sides of the equation by $\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and use the identity $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+9\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0 \\ \frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}+\frac{9\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =0 \\ \frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}+\frac{9\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} & =0 \\ 2\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}+9 & =0 \\ 2\operatorname{tan}⁡x+9 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we rearrange the equation and isolate $\operatorname{tan}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{tan}⁡x & =-9 \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =-\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-\frac{9}{2})=-1.352\,127\,380\,…≈-1.352\,127\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $6$ decimal places. 

Since $-1.352\,127$ lies outside the given domain, it is not a solution.
To generate the solutions, we add integer multiples of $\pi .$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =-1.352\,127\,380\,…+\pi =1.789\,465\,272\,…≈1.789\,465 \\ {x}_{2} & =-1.352\,127\,380\,…+2\pi =4.931\,057\,926\,…≈4.931\,058\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $6$ decimal places.

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}≈1.789\,466\cdot 4.931\,058≈8.824
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

$$

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{\pi }{4},\,{x}_{2}=\frac{5\pi }{4}.

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions to the equation $4\operatorname{sin}⁡x-15\operatorname{cos}⁡x=0$ for ${0}^{∘}\le x<{360}^{∘},$ what is the numerical value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2},$ rounded to the nearest integer?
questions.worked_solution:
We divide both sides of the equation by $\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and use the identity $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}4\operatorname{sin}⁡x-15\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0 \\ \frac{4\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\frac{15\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =0 \\ \frac{4\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\frac{15\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} & =0 \\ 4\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-15 & =0 \\ 4\operatorname{tan}⁡x-15 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we rearrange the equation and isolate $\operatorname{tan}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4\operatorname{tan}⁡x & =15 \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =\frac{15}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal value:

$$
x=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{15}{4})=75.068\,582{…}^{∘}≈{75.069}^{∘}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Since ${75.069}^{∘}$ lies inside the given domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}={75.069}^{∘}.$

To generate more solutions, we add integer multiples of ${180}^{∘}.$ Hence,

$$
{x}_{2}={x}_{1}+{180}^{∘}=75.068\,582{…}^{∘}+{180}^{∘}≈255.069\,{…}^{∘}.
$$

Finally, the numerical value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$ is $75.069\cdot 255.069≈19\,148$
rounded to the nearest integer.

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
In **ascending order**, the exact solutions in radians to the equation $\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x=0,$ for $-\pi \le x<\pi ,$ are

${x}_{1}=$
{{field-1}}$,\,{x}_{2}=$
{{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We divide each term of the equation by $\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and use the identity $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0 \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}+\frac{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =0 \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x+\sqrt{3} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we rearrange the equation and isolate $\operatorname{tan}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡x & =-\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-\sqrt{3})=-\frac{\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-\frac{\pi }{3}$ is inside the given domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{3}.$

To generate the solutions, we add integer multiples of $\pi .$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =-\frac{\pi }{3}+\pi =\frac{2\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, in ascending order, the solutions are

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{3},\,{x}_{2}=\frac{2\pi }{3}.
$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions to the equation $\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-5\operatorname{cos}⁡x=0$ for $-\pi <x\le \pi ,$  what is the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2},$ rounded to $3$ decimal places?
questions.worked_solution:
We divide both sides of the equation by $\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and use the identity $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-5\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0 \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\frac{5\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =0 \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\frac{5\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-5 & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡x-5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we rearrange the equation and isolate $\operatorname{tan}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡x-5 & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡x & =5 \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(10)=1.471\,127\,674…≈1.471\,128\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $6$ decimal places. 

To find the other solution in the given interval, we substract $\pi $ from the principal value. Hence,

$$
{x}_{2}=1.471\,128-\pi ≈-1.670\,465
$$

rounded to $6$ decimal places. 

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}≈(1.471\,128)\cdot (-1.670\,465)≈-2.457
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem:
In **ascending order**, the exact solutions in radians to the equation $\operatorname{sin}⁡x=\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ for $-\pi \le x<\pi ,$ are

${x}_{1}=$
{{field-1}}$,\,{x}_{2}=$
{{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We divide both sides of the equation by $\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and use the identity $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3})=\frac{\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\frac{\pi }{3}$ is inside the given domain, one solution is ${x}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{3}.$

To find another solution in the domain, we subtract $\pi :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{\pi }{3}-\pi =-\frac{2\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, in ascending order, the solutions are

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{2\pi }{3},\,{x}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{3}.
$$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions of the equation $\operatorname{sin}⁡x=-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ for $-\pi <x\le \pi ,$ what is the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We divide both sides of the equation by $\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and use the identity $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =-\sqrt{3} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =-\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-\sqrt{3})=-\frac{\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-\frac{\pi }{3}$ lies inside the given domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{3}.$

To find the other solution, we add $\pi $ to the principal value. Hence,

$$
{x}_{2}=-\frac{\pi }{3}+\pi =\frac{2\pi }{3}
$$

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=-\frac{\pi }{3}\cdot \frac{2\pi }{3}=-\frac{2{\pi }^{2}}{9}.
$$

questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions of the equation $3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x=0$ for $-\pi <x\le \pi ,$ what is the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We divide both sides of the equation by $\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and use the identity $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0 \\ \frac{3\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\frac{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =0 \\ \frac{3\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\frac{\sqrt{3}\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} & =0 \\ 3\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\sqrt{3} & =0 \\ 3\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\sqrt{3} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we rearrange the equation and isolate $\operatorname{tan}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\sqrt{3} & =0 \\ 3\operatorname{tan}⁡x & =\sqrt{3} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})=\frac{\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\frac{\pi }{6}$ lies inside the given domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}=\frac{\pi }{6}.$

To find the other solution, we subtract $\pi $ from the principal value. Hence,

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{6}-\pi =-\frac{5\pi }{6}.
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=-\frac{5\pi }{6},\,\frac{\pi }{6}.$

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=-\frac{5\pi }{6}\cdot \frac{\pi }{6}=-\frac{5{\pi }^{2}}{36}.
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Solving Trigonometric Equations Using the Sin-Cos-Tan Identity
canonical_examples.problem: Calculate, in degrees to the nearest degree, the solutions to the equation $5\sin x = -7\cos x$ for $0^\circ \leq x < 360^\circ.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We divide each term of the equation by $\cos x$ and use the identity $\tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}5\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =-7\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{5\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =-\frac{7\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\ \frac{5\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =-\frac{7\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} \\ 5\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =-7 \\ 5\operatorname{tan}⁡x & =-7\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we rearrange the equation and isolate $\tan x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\tan x = -\dfrac{7}{5}
$$

The length of the interval for $x$ is $2\pi$, so we will likely require $2$ solutions. 

We can immediately calculate the principal value $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
x = \arctan\left(-\dfrac{7}{5}\right) \approx -54.46
$$

This value is outside the domain $0^\circ \leq x < 360^\circ.$ To get a value that's inside the domain, we add $180^\circ\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-\frac{7}{5})+{180}^{∘} \\  & ≈-{54.46}^{∘}+{180}^{∘} \\  & ={125.54}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the other solution inside the given interval, we add $180^\circ$ to $x_1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}+{180}^{∘} \\  & ≈{125.54}^{∘}+{180}^{∘} \\  & ={305.54}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the solutions, rounded to the nearest degree, are $x= 126^\circ, 306^\circ.$

Example: 
                    Solving Trigonometric Equations Using the Sin-Cos-Tan Identity Under a Modified Domain
canonical_examples.problem: Calculate, in degrees to the nearest degree, the solutions to the equation $3\sin x + 12\cos x = 0$ for $-180^\circ <  x \leq 180^\circ.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We divide each term of the equation by $\cos x$ and use the identity $\tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡x+12\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0 \\ \frac{3\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}+\frac{12\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =0 \\ \frac{3\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}+\frac{12\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} & =0 \\ 3\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}+12 & =0 \\ 3\operatorname{tan}⁡x+12 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we rearrange the equation and isolate $\tan x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{tan}⁡x & =-12 \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

We can immediately calculate the principal value $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
x = \arctan(-4) \approx -75.96^\circ
$$

Since this value lies inside the given domain, our first solution is $x_1 = -75.96^\circ.$

To find the other solution in the given interval, we *add* $180^\circ.$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}+{180}^{∘} \\  & ≈-{75.96}^{∘}+{180}^{∘} \\  & ={104.04}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the solutions, rounded to the nearest degree, are $x= -76^\circ, 104^\circ.$

tutorials.problem:
Suppose we want to find all of the solutions to the equation

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14225097/assets/039f2eaa5fc29449de1795a64aeb80391087cbbad093f0b1b8e3533bb024687f.svg)

To calculate a solution, we can reduce the equation to a more convenient form by dividing through by $\cos x,$ and then use the identity $\tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$ to simplify. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0 \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\frac{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =0 \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\frac{\sqrt{3}\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} & =0 \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\sqrt{3} & =0 \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x-\sqrt{3} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we rearrange the equation and isolate $\tan x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\tan x = \sqrt{3}
$$

We can immediately calculate the principal value $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
x = \arctan(\sqrt{3}) = \dfrac{\pi}{3}
$$

Since $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ lies inside the given domain, our first solution is $x_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{3}.$

To find the other solution in the given interval, we add $\pi\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}+\pi  \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}+\pi  \\  & =\frac{4\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

So the solutions are $x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}, \dfrac{4\pi}{3}.$

tutorials.problem:
Let's find all the solutions to the equation
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14225097/assets/cd3dc7a1fd4373b4448b79bf449892ef5eb7056fa762edc25aef73539f427ecc.svg)

Notice that this time, the domain is $-\pi <  x \leq \pi.$

First, we divide each term of the equation by $\cos x$ and use the identity $\tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$ to simplify. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0 \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =0 \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\frac{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} & =0 \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-1 & =0 \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x-1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we rearrange the equation and isolate $\tan x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\tan x = 1
$$

We can immediately calculate the principal value $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
x =  \arctan(1) = \dfrac{\pi}{4}
$$

Since $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ lies inside the given domain, our first solution is $x_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.$

To find the other solution in the given interval, we *subtract* $\pi.$ Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-\pi  \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}-\pi  \\  & =-\frac{3\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

So the solutions are $x = -\dfrac{3\pi}{4} , \dfrac{\pi}{4} .$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
We divide both sides of the equation by $\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and use the identity $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =10\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =\frac{10\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\ \frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =\frac{10\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} \\ 2\operatorname{tan}⁡x & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we rearrange the equation and isolate $\operatorname{tan}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{tan}⁡x & =10 \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =\frac{10}{2} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(5)≈1.373\,40\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $5$ decimal places.

To find the other solution in the given interval, we add $\pi $ to the principal value. Hence,

$$
x≈1.373\,40+\pi ≈4.514\,99
$$

rounded to $5$ decimal places. 

So, in ascending order, rounded to two decimal places, the solutions are 

$$
{x}_{1}≈1.37,\,{x}_{2}≈4.51.
$$

\begin{aligned}4\operatorname{sin}⁡x-15\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0 \\ \frac{4\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\frac{15\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =0 \\ \frac{4\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\frac{15\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} & =0 \\ 4\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-15 & =0 \\ 4\operatorname{tan}⁡x-15 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we rearrange the equation and isolate $\operatorname{tan}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4\operatorname{tan}⁡x & =15 \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =\frac{15}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal value:

$$
x=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{15}{4})=75.068\,582{…}^{∘}≈{75.069}^{∘}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Since ${75.069}^{∘}$ lies inside the given domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}={75.069}^{∘}.$

To generate more solutions, we add integer multiples of ${180}^{∘}.$ Hence,

$$
{x}_{2}={x}_{1}+{180}^{∘}=75.068\,582{…}^{∘}+{180}^{∘}≈255.069\,{…}^{∘}.
$$

Finally, the numerical value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$ is $75.069\cdot 255.069≈19\,148$
rounded to the nearest integer.

Question 5
?

Given that x1 and x2 are the solutions to the equation 4sin⁡x−15cos⁡x=0 for 0∘≤x<360∘, what is the numerical value of x1⋅x2, rounded to the nearest integer?

a
18198
b
19148
c
14198
d
16184
e
13184
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We divide both sides of the equation by cos⁡x and use the identity tan⁡x=sin⁡xcos⁡x.

4sin⁡x−15cos⁡x=04sin⁡xcos⁡x−15cos⁡xcos⁡x=04sin⁡xcos⁡x−15cos⁡xcos⁡x=04⋅sin⁡xcos⁡x−15=04tan⁡x−15=0

Now, we rearrange the equation and isolate tan⁡x:

4tan⁡x=15tan⁡x=154

Next, we find the principal value:

x=arctan⁡(154)=75.068582…∘≈75.069∘

rounded to 3 decimal places.

Since 75.069∘ lies inside the given domain, our first solution is x1=75.069∘.

To generate more solutions, we add integer multiples of 180∘. Hence,

x2=x1+180∘=75.068582…∘+180∘≈255.069…∘.

Finally, the numerical value of x1⋅x2 is 75.069⋅255.069≈19148 rounded to the nearest integer.

tutorial.problem:
Let's find all the solutions to the equation
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14225097/assets/01883003f4801b8ef1e11419587801e9b3db1f4ffda27da5a5f834210171d329.svg)

Notice that this time, the domain is $-\pi <  x \leq \pi.$

First, we divide each term of the equation by $\cos x$ and use the identity $\tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$ to simplify. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0 \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =0 \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\frac{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} & =0 \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-1 & =0 \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x-1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we rearrange the equation and isolate $\tan x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\tan x = 1
$$

We can immediately calculate the principal value $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
x =  \arctan(1) = \dfrac{\pi}{4}
$$

Since $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ lies inside the given domain, our first solution is $x_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.$

To find the other solution in the given interval, we *subtract* $\pi.$ Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-\pi  \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}-\pi  \\  & =-\frac{3\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

So the solutions are $x = -\dfrac{3\pi}{4} , \dfrac{\pi}{4} .$

question.html:
Question 7
?

Given that x1 and x2 are the solutions to the equation 12sin⁡x−5cos⁡x=0 for −π<x≤π, what is the value of x1⋅x2, rounded to 3 decimal places?

a
−1.671
b
−1.471
c
−2.457
d
−6.785
e
−2.465
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We divide both sides of the equation by cos⁡x and use the identity tan⁡x=sin⁡xcos⁡x.

12sin⁡x−5cos⁡x=0sin⁡x2cos⁡x−5cos⁡xcos⁡x=0sin⁡x2cos⁡x−5cos⁡xcos⁡x=012⋅sin⁡xcos⁡x−5=012tan⁡x−5=0

Now, we rearrange the equation and isolate tan⁡x:

12tan⁡x−5=012tan⁡x=5tan⁡x=10

Next, we find the principal value:

x=arctan⁡(10)=1.471127674…≈1.471128 rounded to 6 decimal places.

To find the other solution in the given interval, we substract π from the principal value. Hence, x2=1.471128−π≈−1.670465 rounded to 6 decimal places.

Finally, x1⋅x2≈(1.471128)⋅(−1.670465)≈−2.457 rounded to three decimal places.

observed_steps.name: Question 8
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Solving Trigonometric Equations Using the Sin-Cos-Tan Identity Under a Modified Domain
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We divide both sides of the equation by $\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and use the identity $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3})=\frac{\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\frac{\pi }{3}$ is inside the given domain, one solution is ${x}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{3}.$

To find another solution in the domain, we subtract $\pi :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{\pi }{3}-\pi =-\frac{2\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, in ascending order, the solutions are

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{2\pi }{3},\,{x}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{3}.
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
We divide both sides of the equation by $\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and use the identity $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =-\sqrt{3} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =-\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-\sqrt{3})=-\frac{\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-\frac{\pi }{3}$ lies inside the given domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{3}.$

To find the other solution, we add $\pi $ to the principal value. Hence,

$$
{x}_{2}=-\frac{\pi }{3}+\pi =\frac{2\pi }{3}
$$

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=-\frac{\pi }{3}\cdot \frac{2\pi }{3}=-\frac{2{\pi }^{2}}{9}.
$$

Question 9
?

Given that x1 and x2 are the solutions of the equation sin⁡x=−3cos⁡x for −π<x≤π, what is the value of x1⋅x2?

a
−2π29
b
5π4
c
−π23
d
π4
e
−3π281
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We divide both sides of the equation by cos⁡x and use the identity tan⁡x=sin⁡xcos⁡x.

sin⁡x=−3cos⁡xsin⁡xcos⁡x=−3cos⁡xcos⁡xsin⁡xcos⁡x=−3cos⁡xcos⁡xsin⁡xcos⁡x=−3tan⁡x=−3

Next, we find the principal value:

x=arctan⁡(−3)=−π3

Since −π3 lies inside the given domain, our first solution is x1=−π3.

To find the other solution, we add π to the principal value. Hence, x2=−π3+π=2π3

Finally, x1⋅x2=−π3⋅2π3=−2π29.

observed_steps.name: Question 10
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Solving Trigonometric Equations Using the Sin-Cos-Tan Identity Under a Modified Domain
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We divide both sides of the equation by $\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and use the identity $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0 \\ \frac{3\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\frac{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =0 \\ \frac{3\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\frac{\sqrt{3}\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} & =0 \\ 3\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\sqrt{3} & =0 \\ 3\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\sqrt{3} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we rearrange the equation and isolate $\operatorname{tan}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\sqrt{3} & =0 \\ 3\operatorname{tan}⁡x & =\sqrt{3} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})=\frac{\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\frac{\pi }{6}$ lies inside the given domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}=\frac{\pi }{6}.$

To find the other solution, we subtract $\pi $ from the principal value. Hence,

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{6}-\pi =-\frac{5\pi }{6}.
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=-\frac{5\pi }{6},\,\frac{\pi }{6}.$

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=-\frac{5\pi }{6}\cdot \frac{\pi }{6}=-\frac{5{\pi }^{2}}{36}.
$$

question.html:
Question 10
?

Given that x1 and x2 are the solutions of the equation 3sin⁡x−3cos⁡x=0 for −π<x≤π, what is the value of x1⋅x2?

a
−π212
b
−π236
c
−7π236
d
−π24
e
−5π236
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We divide both sides of the equation by cos⁡x and use the identity tan⁡x=sin⁡xcos⁡x.

3sin⁡x−3cos⁡x=03sin⁡xcos⁡x−3cos⁡xcos⁡x=03sin⁡xcos⁡x−3cos⁡xcos⁡x=03⋅sin⁡xcos⁡x−3=03tan⁡x−3=0

Now, we rearrange the equation and isolate tan⁡x:

3tan⁡x−3=03tan⁡x=3tan⁡x=33

Next, we find the principal value:

x=arctan⁡(33)=π6

Since π6 lies inside the given domain, our first solution is x1=π6.

To find the other solution, we subtract π from the principal value. Hence, x2=π6−π=−5π6.

Therefore, the solutions are x=−5π6,π6.

Finally, x1⋅x2=−5π6⋅π6=−5π236.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
In **ascending order**, rounded to two decimal places in radians, the solutions to the equation $2\operatorname{sin}⁡x=10\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ for $0\le x<2\pi ,$ are

${x}_{1}≈$
 {{field-1}}$,\,{x}_{2}≈$ 
{{field-2}}.
question.worked_solution:
We divide both sides of the equation by $\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and use the identity $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =10\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =\frac{10\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\ \frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =\frac{10\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} \\ 2\operatorname{tan}⁡x & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we rearrange the equation and isolate $\operatorname{tan}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{tan}⁡x & =10 \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =\frac{10}{2} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(5)≈1.373\,40\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $5$ decimal places.

To find the other solution in the given interval, we add $\pi $ to the principal value. Hence,

$$
x≈1.373\,40+\pi ≈4.514\,99
$$

rounded to $5$ decimal places. 

So, in ascending order, rounded to two decimal places, the solutions are 

$$
{x}_{1}≈1.37,\,{x}_{2}≈4.51.
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions to the equation $5\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x=0$ for $0\le x<2\pi ,$ what is the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2},$ rounded to $1$ decimal place?
question.worked_solution:
We divide both sides of the equation by $\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and use the identity $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}5\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0 \\ \frac{5\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =0 \\ \frac{5\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\frac{2\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} & =0 \\ 5\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-2 & =0 \\ 5\operatorname{tan}⁡x-2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we rearrange the equation and isolate $\operatorname{tan}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}5\operatorname{tan}⁡x & =2 \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =\frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{2}{5})=0.380\,506…≈0.380\,5\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $4$ decimal places. 

Since $0.380\,5$ lies inside the given domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}=0.380\,5.$

To find the other solution in the given interval, we add $\pi $ to the principal value. Hence,

$$
{x}_{2}=0.380\,506…+\pi =3.522\,099…≈3.522\,1
$$

rounded to $4$ decimal places. 

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}≈0.380\,5\cdot 3.522\,1≈1.3
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Given that x1 and x2 are the solutions to the equation 5sin⁡x−2cos⁡x=0 for 0≤x<2π, what is the value of x1⋅x2, rounded to 1 decimal place?

a
1.1
b
1.7
c
1.5
d
1.9
e
1.3
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We divide both sides of the equation by cos⁡x and use the identity tan⁡x=sin⁡xcos⁡x.

5sin⁡x−2cos⁡x=05sin⁡xcos⁡x−2cos⁡xcos⁡x=05sin⁡xcos⁡x−2cos⁡xcos⁡x=05⋅sin⁡xcos⁡x−2=05tan⁡x−2=0

Now, we rearrange the equation and isolate tan⁡x:

5tan⁡x=2tan⁡x=25

Next, we find the principal value:

x=arctan⁡(25)=0.380506…≈0.3805 rounded to 4 decimal places.

Since 0.3805 lies inside the given domain, our first solution is x1=0.3805.

To find the other solution in the given interval, we add π to the principal value. Hence,

x2=0.380506…+π=3.522099…≈3.5221 rounded to 4 decimal places.

Finally, x1⋅x2≈0.3805⋅3.5221≈1.3 rounded to one decimal place.

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Solving Trigonometric Equations Using the Sin-Cos-Tan Identity
last_observation.worked_solution:
We divide both sides of the equation by $\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and use the identity $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}5\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0 \\ \frac{5\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =0 \\ \frac{5\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\frac{2\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} & =0 \\ 5\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-2 & =0 \\ 5\operatorname{tan}⁡x-2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we rearrange the equation and isolate $\operatorname{tan}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}5\operatorname{tan}⁡x & =2 \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =\frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{2}{5})=0.380\,506…≈0.380\,5\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $4$ decimal places. 

Since $0.380\,5$ lies inside the given domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}=0.380\,5.$

To find the other solution in the given interval, we add $\pi $ to the principal value. Hence,

$$
{x}_{2}=0.380\,506…+\pi =3.522\,099…≈3.522\,1
$$

rounded to $4$ decimal places. 

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}≈0.380\,5\cdot 3.522\,1≈1.3
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions to the equation $2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+9\operatorname{cos}⁡x=0$ for $0\le x<2\pi ,$ what is the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2},$ rounded to $3$ decimal places?
question.worked_solution:
We divide both sides of the equation by $\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and use the identity $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+9\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0 \\ \frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}+\frac{9\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =0 \\ \frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}+\frac{9\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} & =0 \\ 2\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}+9 & =0 \\ 2\operatorname{tan}⁡x+9 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we rearrange the equation and isolate $\operatorname{tan}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{tan}⁡x & =-9 \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =-\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-\frac{9}{2})=-1.352\,127\,380\,…≈-1.352\,127\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $6$ decimal places. 

Since $-1.352\,127$ lies outside the given domain, it is not a solution.
To generate the solutions, we add integer multiples of $\pi .$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =-1.352\,127\,380\,…+\pi =1.789\,465\,272\,…≈1.789\,465 \\ {x}_{2} & =-1.352\,127\,380\,…+2\pi =4.931\,057\,926\,…≈4.931\,058\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $6$ decimal places.

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}≈1.789\,466\cdot 4.931\,058≈8.824

question.html:
Question 3
?

Given that x1 and x2 are the solutions to the equation 2sin⁡x+9cos⁡x=0 for 0≤x<2π, what is the value of x1⋅x2, rounded to 3 decimal places?

a
8.280
b
8.824
c
4.284
d
4.804
e
4.842
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We divide both sides of the equation by cos⁡x and use the identity tan⁡x=sin⁡xcos⁡x.

2sin⁡x+9cos⁡x=02sin⁡xcos⁡x+9cos⁡xcos⁡x=02sin⁡xcos⁡x+9cos⁡xcos⁡x=02⋅sin⁡xcos⁡x+9=02tan⁡x+9=0

Now, we rearrange the equation and isolate tan⁡x:

2tan⁡x=−9tan⁡x=−92

Next, we find the principal value:

x=arctan⁡(−92)=−1.352127380…≈−1.352127 rounded to 6 decimal places.

Since −1.352127 lies outside the given domain, it is not a solution. To generate the solutions, we add integer multiples of π. Hence,

x1=−1.352127380…+π=1.789465272…≈1.789465x2=−1.352127380…+2π=4.931057926…≈4.931058 rounded to 6 decimal places.

Finally, x1⋅x2≈1.789466⋅4.931058≈8.824 rounded to three decimal places.

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Solving Trigonometric Equations Using the Sin-Cos-Tan Identity
last_observation.worked_solution:
We divide both sides of the equation by $\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and use the identity $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+9\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0 \\ \frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}+\frac{9\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =0 \\ \frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}+\frac{9\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} & =0 \\ 2\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}+9 & =0 \\ 2\operatorname{tan}⁡x+9 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we rearrange the equation and isolate $\operatorname{tan}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{tan}⁡x & =-9 \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =-\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-\frac{9}{2})=-1.352\,127\,380\,…≈-1.352\,127\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $6$ decimal places. 

Since $-1.352\,127$ lies outside the given domain, it is not a solution.
To generate the solutions, we add integer multiples of $\pi .$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =-1.352\,127\,380\,…+\pi =1.789\,465\,272\,…≈1.789\,465 \\ {x}_{2} & =-1.352\,127\,380\,…+2\pi =4.931\,057\,926\,…≈4.931\,058\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $6$ decimal places.

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}≈1.789\,466\cdot 4.931\,058≈8.824
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions to the equation $4\operatorname{sin}⁡x-15\operatorname{cos}⁡x=0$ for ${0}^{∘}\le x<{360}^{∘},$ what is the numerical value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2},$ rounded to the nearest integer?
question.worked_solution:
We divide both sides of the equation by $\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and use the identity $\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}4\operatorname{sin}⁡x-15\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0 \\ \frac{4\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\frac{15\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =0 \\ \frac{4\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\frac{15\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} & =0 \\ 4\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-15 & =0 \\ 4\operatorname{tan}⁡x-15 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we rearrange the equation and isolate $\operatorname{tan}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4\operatorname{tan}⁡x & =15 \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =\frac{15}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal value:

$$
x=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{15}{4})=75.068\,582{…}^{∘}≈{75.069}^{∘}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Since ${75.069}^{∘}$ lies inside the given domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}={75.069}^{∘}.$

To generate more solutions, we add integer multiples of ${180}^{∘}.$ Hence,

$$
{x}_{2}={x}_{1}+{180}^{∘}=75.068\,582{…}^{∘}+{180}^{∘}≈255.069\,{…}^{∘}.
$$

Finally, the numerical value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$ is $75.069\cdot 255.069≈19\,148$
rounded to the nearest integer.

question.html:
Question 5
?

Given that x1 and x2 are the solutions to the equation 4sin⁡x−15cos⁡x=0 for 0∘≤x<360∘, what is the numerical value of x1⋅x2, rounded to the nearest integer?

a
18198
b
19148
c
14198
d
16184
e
13184
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We divide both sides of the equation by cos⁡x and use the identity tan⁡x=sin⁡xcos⁡x.

4sin⁡x−15cos⁡x=04sin⁡xcos⁡x−15cos⁡xcos⁡x=04sin⁡xcos⁡x−15cos⁡xcos⁡x=04⋅sin⁡xcos⁡x−15=04tan⁡x−15=0

Now, we rearrange the equation and isolate tan⁡x:

4tan⁡x=15tan⁡x=154

Next, we find the principal value:

x=arctan⁡(154)=75.068582…∘≈75.069∘

rounded to 3 decimal places.

Since 75.069∘ lies inside the given domain, our first solution is x1=75.069∘.

To generate more solutions, we add integer multiples of 180∘. Hence,

x2=x1+180∘=75.068582…∘+180∘≈255.069…∘.

Finally, the numerical value of x1⋅x2 is 75.069⋅255.069≈19148 rounded to the nearest integer.

$$
\begin{aligned}4\operatorname{sin}⁡x-15\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0 \\ \frac{4\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\frac{15\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =0 \\ \frac{4\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-\frac{15\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}} & =0 \\ 4\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-15 & =0 \\ 4\operatorname{tan}⁡x-15 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we rearrange the equation and isolate $\operatorname{tan}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4\operatorname{tan}⁡x & =15 \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =\frac{15}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
x=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{15}{4})=75.068\,582{…}^{∘}≈{75.069}^{∘}

question.problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions to the equation $\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-5\operatorname{cos}⁡x=0$ for $-\pi <x\le \pi ,$  what is the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2},$ rounded to $3$ decimal places?

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡x-5 & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡x & =5 \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =10\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

rounded to $6$ decimal places.

$$
