feedback.html:
Question 15
?

The maximum value of Q(x)=x12−4x1x2+4x22, when 9x12+4x22=36, is 40. Which of the following is a vector x at which the maximum is attained?

a
12[−23]
b
15[−26]
c
110[−29]
d
110[−13]
e
15[−12]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[1−2−24]

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

x1222+x2232=1

This is an ellipse with semiaxes a=2 (along the x1-axis) and b=3 (along the x2-axis). If we introduce new variables

y1=x12 and y2=x23,

the equation of the ellipse will transform into y12+y22=1 or ‖y‖=1.

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix

P=[2003],

we obtain that x=Py. Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

Q(x)=xTAx=(Py)TA(Py)=yT(PTAP)y=Q′(y).

As a result, since PT=P, the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is

B=PTAP=PAP=[2003][1−2−24][2003]=[2−4−612][2003]=[4−12−1236].

Now, we maximize Q′(y) when ‖y‖=1, as usual.

Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is 40, we have

max{Q′(y)|‖y‖=1}=λmax=40.

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue λmax=40:

B−40I=[4−12−1236]−40[1001]=[−36−12−12−4] Seeking a non-zero solution of (B−40I)y=0 gives the eigenvector v=[−13]. Dividing v by its norm ‖v‖=10, we get

umax=v‖v‖=110[−13].

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

xmax=Pumax=[2003]⋅110[−13]=110[−29]

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
$$ \{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2y(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(1) \\ y(1)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].$*
$[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c,
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2(t-1)} & (t-1){e}^{2(t-1)} \\ 0 & {e}^{2(t-1)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\,{e}^{2(t-1)}\, \\ \,0\,\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=8y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-8x(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(8t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(8t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(8t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(8t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 8 \\ -8 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 8 \\ -8 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 8 \\ -8 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(8t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(8t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(8t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(8t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(8t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(8t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(8t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(8t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(8t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(8t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(8t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(8t)\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.$

questions.raw_html:
2.Finding the General Solution of a Homogeneous System Using a Given Matrix Exponential?

{x′(t)=8y(t)y′(t)=−8x(t) Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

Hint: eAt=[cos⁡(8t)sin⁡(8t)−sin⁡(8t)cos⁡(8t)], where A=[08−80].

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=4y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=4x(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,x(0),
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $x(0)$ is the initial condition vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ 2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
$$ \{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=3y(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(2) \\ y(2)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & t{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{3t}\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}].$*
$[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c,
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-2)}\,x(2) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3(t-2)} & (t-2){e}^{3(t-2)} \\ 0 & {e}^{3(t-2)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\,(t-2){e}^{3(t-2)}\, \\ \,{e}^{3(t-2)}\,\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Consider the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ is the unique solution to the initial value problem

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)\,c$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(0)=c$

$\text{L6}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}\,x(0)$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the 
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by 
{{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}$ by 
{{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is a fundamental matrix for the system, any solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c.
$$

Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{properties of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ From $\text{L2}$ we have

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c.
$$

Evaluating this identity at $t=0$ gives

$$
x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c,
$$

which is precisely line $\text{L3}.$ Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{evaluating both sides at }t=0.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$, $\text{L4},$ and $\text{L5}.$ From $\text{L3}$ we know

$$
x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c,
$$

and from $\text{L4}$ we know ${Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.$ Replacing ${Φ}_{0}(0)$ with ${I}_{n}$ in the equation $x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c$ gives

$$
x(0)={I}_{n}c=c,
$$

which is line $\text{L5}.$ Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}$ by $\text{replacing }{Φ}_{0}(0)\text{ with }{I}_{n}\text{ in }x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c.$

questions.raw_html:
5.Proving the Matrix Exponential Formula for IVP Solution: Homogeneous Systems?

Consider the homogeneous system x′(t)=Ax(t), where A is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix Φ0(t) is the unique solution to the initial value problem Φ0′(t)=AΦ0(t),Φ0(0)=In. A derivation of the formula for the solution x(t) passing through x(0) is presented below.

L1: Let Φ0(t)=eAt

L2: x(t)=Φ0(t)c for some constant vector c

L3: x(0)=Φ0(0)c

L4: Φ0(0)=In

L5: x(0)=c

L6: x(t)=eAtx(0)

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

Line L2 follows from L1 by the
properties of a fundamental matrix
properties of a fundamental matrix
definition of matrix multiplication
properties of the determinant
definition of a solution curve
.

Line L3 follows from L2 by
evaluating both sides at t=0
evaluating both sides at t=0
differentiating the equation
using diagonalization of Φ0(t)
applying the chain rule
.

Line L5 follows from lines L3 and L4 by
replacing Φ0(0) with In in x(0)=Φ0(0)c
replacing Φ0(0) with In in x(0)=Φ0(0)c
differentiating x(0)=Φ0(0)c
using properties of det(Φ0(0))
applying the chain rule
.

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c,
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2(t-1)} & (t-1){e}^{2(t-1)} \\ 0 & {e}^{2(t-1)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\,{e}^{2(t-1)}\, \\ \,0\,\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 8 \\ -8 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 8 \\ -8 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(8t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(8t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(8t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(8t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(8t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(8t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(8t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(8t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(8t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(8t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(8t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(8t)\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.$

Question 2
?

{x′(t)=8y(t)y′(t)=−8x(t) Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

Hint: eAt=[cos⁡(8t)sin⁡(8t)−sin⁡(8t)cos⁡(8t)], where A=[08−80].

a
x(t)=c1[cos⁡(8t)−sin⁡(8t)]+c2[−sin⁡(8t)cos⁡(8t)]
b
x(t)=c1[cos⁡(8t)−sin⁡(8t)]+c2[sin⁡(8t)cos⁡(8t)]
c
x(t)=c1[cos⁡(8t)−sin⁡(8t)]e−8t+c2[sin⁡(8t)cos⁡(8t)]
d
x(t)=c1[cos⁡(8t)−sin⁡(8t)]e8t+c2[sin⁡(8t)cos⁡(8t)]
e
x(t)=c1[cos⁡(8t)−sin⁡(8t)]+c2[sin⁡(8t)cos⁡(8t)]e8t
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Writing our system in matrix form, we get x′(t)=[08−80]x(t), where x(t)=[x(t)y(t)]. So, the matrix of the system is A=[08−80].

Given the system x′(t)=Ax(t), where A is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as x(t)=Φ(t)c, where Φ(t) is a fundamental matrix of the system, and c is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix Φ0(t) of the system is given by Φ0(t)=eAt=[cos⁡(8t)sin⁡(8t)−sin⁡(8t)cos⁡(8t)].

Therefore, the general solution is

x(t)=Φ0(t)c=eAtc=[cos⁡(8t)sin⁡(8t)−sin⁡(8t)cos⁡(8t)][c1c2]=c1[cos⁡(8t)−sin⁡(8t)]+c2[sin⁡(8t)cos⁡(8t)],

where c1,c2∈R.

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,x(0),
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $x(0)$ is the initial condition vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ 2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Hint: eAt=[cosh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)cosh⁡(4t)], where A=[0440].

EXPLANATION

Writing our system in matrix form, we get x′(t)=[0440]x(t), where x(t)=[x(t)y(t)]. So, the matrix of the system is A=[0440].

Given the system x′(t)=Ax(t), where A is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as x(t)=Φ0(t)x(0), where Φ0(t)=eAt is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and x(0) is the initial condition vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix Φ0(t) of the system is given by

Φ0(t)=eAt=[cosh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)cosh⁡(4t)].

Therefore, the solution is

x(t)=eAtx(0)=[cosh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)cosh⁡(4t)][02]=[2sinh⁡(4t)2cosh⁡(4t)].

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c,
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-2)}\,x(2) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3(t-2)} & (t-2){e}^{3(t-2)} \\ 0 & {e}^{3(t-2)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\,(t-2){e}^{3(t-2)}\, \\ \,{e}^{3(t-2)}\,\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is a fundamental matrix for the system, any solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c.
$$

Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{properties of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ From $\text{L2}$ we have

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c.
$$

Evaluating this identity at $t=0$ gives

$$
x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c,
$$

which is precisely line $\text{L3}.$ Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{evaluating both sides at }t=0.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$, $\text{L4},$ and $\text{L5}.$ From $\text{L3}$ we know

$$
x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c,
$$

and from $\text{L4}$ we know ${Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.$ Replacing ${Φ}_{0}(0)$ with ${I}_{n}$ in the equation $x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c$ gives

$$
x(0)={I}_{n}c=c,
$$

which is line $\text{L5}.$ Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}$ by $\text{replacing }{Φ}_{0}(0)\text{ with }{I}_{n}\text{ in }x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c.$

Question 5
?
Consider the homogeneous system x′(t)=Ax(t), where A is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix Φ0(t) is the unique solution to the initial value problem Φ0′(t)=AΦ0(t),Φ0(0)=In. A derivation of the formula for the solution x(t) passing through x(0) is presented below.

L1: Let Φ0(t)=eAt

L2: x(t)=Φ0(t)c for some constant vector c

L3: x(0)=Φ0(0)c

L4: Φ0(0)=In

L5: x(0)=c

L6: x(t)=eAtx(0)

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

Line L2 follows from L1 by the
properties of a fundamental matrix
definition of a solution curve
definition of matrix multiplication
properties of the determinant
properties of a fundamental matrix
.

Line L3 follows from L2 by
evaluating both sides at t=0
using diagonalization of Φ0(t)
differentiating the equation
evaluating both sides at t=0
applying the chain rule
.

Line L5 follows from lines L3 and L4 by
replacing Φ0(0) with In in x(0)=Φ0(0)c
differentiating x(0)=Φ0(0)c
replacing Φ0(0) with In in x(0)=Φ0(0)c
applying the chain rule
using properties of det(Φ0(0))
.

Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's justify each of the selected steps.

  • We first consider lines L1 and L2. Since Φ0(t)=eAt is a fundamental matrix for the system, any solution of the system can be written as x(t)=Φ0(t)c. Thus, L2 follows from L1 by the properties of a fundamental matrix.

  • Next, we consider lines L2 and L3. From L2 we have x(t)=Φ0(t)c. Evaluating this identity at t=0 gives x(0)=Φ0(0)c, which is precisely line L3. Thus, L3 follows from L2 by evaluating both sides at t=0.

  • Finally, we consider lines L3, L4, and L5. From L3 we know x(0)=Φ0(0)c, and from L4 we know Φ0(0)=In. Replacing Φ0(0) with In in the equation x(0)=Φ0(0)c gives x(0)=Inc=c, which is line L5. Therefore, L5 follows from lines L3 and L4 by replacing Φ0(0) with In in x(0)=Φ0(0)c.

question.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c,
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2(t-1)} & (t-1){e}^{2(t-1)} \\ 0 & {e}^{2(t-1)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\,{e}^{2(t-1)}\, \\ \,0\,\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(8t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(8t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(8t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(8t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 8 \\ -8 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
question.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 8 \\ -8 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 8 \\ -8 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(8t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(8t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(8t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(8t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(8t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(8t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(8t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(8t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(8t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(8t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(8t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(8t)\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.$

Question 2
?

{x′(t)=8y(t)y′(t)=−8x(t) Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

Hint: eAt=[cos⁡(8t)sin⁡(8t)−sin⁡(8t)cos⁡(8t)], where A=[08−80].

a
x(t)=c1[cos⁡(8t)−sin⁡(8t)]+c2[−sin⁡(8t)cos⁡(8t)]
b
x(t)=c1[cos⁡(8t)−sin⁡(8t)]+c2[sin⁡(8t)cos⁡(8t)]
c
x(t)=c1[cos⁡(8t)−sin⁡(8t)]e−8t+c2[sin⁡(8t)cos⁡(8t)]
d
x(t)=c1[cos⁡(8t)−sin⁡(8t)]e8t+c2[sin⁡(8t)cos⁡(8t)]
e
x(t)=c1[cos⁡(8t)−sin⁡(8t)]+c2[sin⁡(8t)cos⁡(8t)]e8t
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Writing our system in matrix form, we get x′(t)=[08−80]x(t), where x(t)=[x(t)y(t)]. So, the matrix of the system is A=[08−80].

Given the system x′(t)=Ax(t), where A is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as x(t)=Φ(t)c, where Φ(t) is a fundamental matrix of the system, and c is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix Φ0(t) of the system is given by Φ0(t)=eAt=[cos⁡(8t)sin⁡(8t)−sin⁡(8t)cos⁡(8t)].

Therefore, the general solution is

x(t)=Φ0(t)c=eAtc=[cos⁡(8t)sin⁡(8t)−sin⁡(8t)cos⁡(8t)][c1c2]=c1[cos⁡(8t)−sin⁡(8t)]+c2[sin⁡(8t)cos⁡(8t)],

where c1,c2∈R.

question.html:
Question 2
?

{x′(t)=8y(t)y′(t)=−8x(t) Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

Hint: eAt=[cos⁡(8t)sin⁡(8t)−sin⁡(8t)cos⁡(8t)], where A=[08−80].

a
x(t)=c1[cos⁡(8t)−sin⁡(8t)]+c2[−sin⁡(8t)cos⁡(8t)]
b
x(t)=c1[cos⁡(8t)−sin⁡(8t)]+c2[sin⁡(8t)cos⁡(8t)]
c
x(t)=c1[cos⁡(8t)−sin⁡(8t)]e−8t+c2[sin⁡(8t)cos⁡(8t)]
d
x(t)=c1[cos⁡(8t)−sin⁡(8t)]e8t+c2[sin⁡(8t)cos⁡(8t)]
e
x(t)=c1[cos⁡(8t)−sin⁡(8t)]+c2[sin⁡(8t)cos⁡(8t)]e8t
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Writing our system in matrix form, we get x′(t)=[08−80]x(t), where x(t)=[x(t)y(t)]. So, the matrix of the system is A=[08−80].

Given the system x′(t)=Ax(t), where A is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as x(t)=Φ(t)c, where Φ(t) is a fundamental matrix of the system, and c is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix Φ0(t) of the system is given by Φ0(t)=eAt=[cos⁡(8t)sin⁡(8t)−sin⁡(8t)cos⁡(8t)].

Therefore, the general solution is

x(t)=Φ0(t)c=eAtc=[cos⁡(8t)sin⁡(8t)−sin⁡(8t)cos⁡(8t)][c1c2]=c1[cos⁡(8t)−sin⁡(8t)]+c2[sin⁡(8t)cos⁡(8t)],

where c1,c2∈R.

solution.reasoning: Multiplying e^{At} by the arbitrary constant vector gives x(t)=c_1\cos(8t)+c_2\sin(8t) and y(t)=-c_1\sin(8t)+c_2\cos(8t), which satisfy x'=8y and y'=-8x. Thus option b is mathematically correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=8y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-8x(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(8t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(8t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(8t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(8t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 8 \\ -8 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
feedback.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 8 \\ -8 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 8 \\ -8 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(8t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(8t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(8t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(8t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(8t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(8t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(8t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(8t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(8t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(8t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(8t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(8t)\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=4y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=4x(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
question.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,x(0),
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $x(0)$ is the initial condition vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ 2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

{x′(t)=4y(t)y′(t)=4x(t),[x(0)y(0)]=[02] Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

Hint: eAt=[cosh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)cosh⁡(4t)], where A=[0440].

a
[2sinh⁡(4t)cosh⁡(4t)]
b
[2sinh⁡(4t)−2cosh⁡(4t)]
c
[4sinh⁡(4t)2cosh⁡(4t)]
d
[2sinh⁡(4t)2cosh⁡(4t)]
e
[−2sinh⁡(4t)2cosh⁡(4t)]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Writing our system in matrix form, we get x′(t)=[0440]x(t), where x(t)=[x(t)y(t)]. So, the matrix of the system is A=[0440].

Given the system x′(t)=Ax(t), where A is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as x(t)=Φ0(t)x(0), where Φ0(t)=eAt is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and x(0) is the initial condition vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix Φ0(t) of the system is given by

Φ0(t)=eAt=[cosh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)cosh⁡(4t)].

Therefore, the solution is

x(t)=eAtx(0)=[cosh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)cosh⁡(4t)][02]=[2sinh⁡(4t)2cosh⁡(4t)].

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,x(0),
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $x(0)$ is the initial condition vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ 2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

{x′(t)=4y(t)y′(t)=4x(t),[x(0)y(0)]=[02] Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

Hint: eAt=[cosh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)cosh⁡(4t)], where A=[0440].

a
[2sinh⁡(4t)cosh⁡(4t)]
b
[2sinh⁡(4t)−2cosh⁡(4t)]
c
[4sinh⁡(4t)2cosh⁡(4t)]
d
[2sinh⁡(4t)2cosh⁡(4t)]
e
[−2sinh⁡(4t)2cosh⁡(4t)]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Writing our system in matrix form, we get x′(t)=[0440]x(t), where x(t)=[x(t)y(t)]. So, the matrix of the system is A=[0440].

Given the system x′(t)=Ax(t), where A is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as x(t)=Φ0(t)x(0), where Φ0(t)=eAt is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and x(0) is the initial condition vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix Φ0(t) of the system is given by

Φ0(t)=eAt=[cosh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)cosh⁡(4t)].

Therefore, the solution is

x(t)=eAtx(0)=[cosh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)cosh⁡(4t)][02]=[2sinh⁡(4t)2cosh⁡(4t)].

solution.reasoning: Multiplying e^{At} by the initial vector (0,2) gives x(t)=2\sinh(4t) and y(t)=2\cosh(4t). Their derivatives satisfy x'=4y and y'=4x, and their initial values are (0,2). Thus option d is mathematically correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=4y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=4x(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
feedback.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,x(0),
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $x(0)$ is the initial condition vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ 2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$ \{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=3y(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(2) \\ y(2)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & t{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{3t}\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}].$*
$[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
question.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c,
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-2)}\,x(2) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3(t-2)} & (t-2){e}^{3(t-2)} \\ 0 & {e}^{3(t-2)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\,(t-2){e}^{3(t-2)}\, \\ \,{e}^{3(t-2)}\,\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Consider the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ is the unique solution to the initial value problem

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)\,c$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(0)=c$

$\text{L6}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}\,x(0)$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the 
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by 
{{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}$ by 
{{field-3}}.
question.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is a fundamental matrix for the system, any solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c.
$$

Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{properties of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ From $\text{L2}$ we have

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c.
$$

Evaluating this identity at $t=0$ gives

$$
x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c,
$$

which is precisely line $\text{L3}.$ Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{evaluating both sides at }t=0.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$, $\text{L4},$ and $\text{L5}.$ From $\text{L3}$ we know

$$
x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c,
$$

and from $\text{L4}$ we know ${Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.$ Replacing ${Φ}_{0}(0)$ with ${I}_{n}$ in the equation $x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c$ gives

$$
x(0)={I}_{n}c=c,
$$

which is line $\text{L5}.$ Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}$ by $\text{replacing }{Φ}_{0}(0)\text{ with }{I}_{n}\text{ in }x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c.$

Question 5
?
Consider the homogeneous system x′(t)=Ax(t), where A is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix Φ0(t) is the unique solution to the initial value problem Φ0′(t)=AΦ0(t),Φ0(0)=In. A derivation of the formula for the solution x(t) passing through x(0) is presented below.

L1: Let Φ0(t)=eAt

L2: x(t)=Φ0(t)c for some constant vector c

L3: x(0)=Φ0(0)c

L4: Φ0(0)=In

L5: x(0)=c

L6: x(t)=eAtx(0)

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

Line L2 follows from L1 by the
properties of a fundamental matrix
definition of a solution curve
definition of matrix multiplication
properties of the determinant
properties of a fundamental matrix
.

Line L3 follows from L2 by
evaluating both sides at t=0
using diagonalization of Φ0(t)
differentiating the equation
evaluating both sides at t=0
applying the chain rule
.

Line L5 follows from lines L3 and L4 by
replacing Φ0(0) with In in x(0)=Φ0(0)c
differentiating x(0)=Φ0(0)c
replacing Φ0(0) with In in x(0)=Φ0(0)c
applying the chain rule
using properties of det(Φ0(0))
.

Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's justify each of the selected steps.

  • We first consider lines L1 and L2. Since Φ0(t)=eAt is a fundamental matrix for the system, any solution of the system can be written as x(t)=Φ0(t)c. Thus, L2 follows from L1 by the properties of a fundamental matrix.

  • Next, we consider lines L2 and L3. From L2 we have x(t)=Φ0(t)c. Evaluating this identity at t=0 gives x(0)=Φ0(0)c, which is precisely line L3. Thus, L3 follows from L2 by evaluating both sides at t=0.

  • Finally, we consider lines L3, L4, and L5. From L3 we know x(0)=Φ0(0)c, and from L4 we know Φ0(0)=In. Replacing Φ0(0) with In in the equation x(0)=Φ0(0)c gives x(0)=Inc=c, which is line L5. Therefore, L5 follows from lines L3 and L4 by replacing Φ0(0) with In in x(0)=Φ0(0)c.

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is a fundamental matrix for the system, any solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c.
$$

Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{properties of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ From $\text{L2}$ we have

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c.
$$

Evaluating this identity at $t=0$ gives

$$
x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c,
$$

which is precisely line $\text{L3}.$ Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{evaluating both sides at }t=0.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$, $\text{L4},$ and $\text{L5}.$ From $\text{L3}$ we know

$$
x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c,
$$

and from $\text{L4}$ we know ${Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.$ Replacing ${Φ}_{0}(0)$ with ${I}_{n}$ in the equation $x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c$ gives

$$
x(0)={I}_{n}c=c,
$$

which is line $\text{L5}.$ Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}$ by $\text{replacing }{Φ}_{0}(0)\text{ with }{I}_{n}\text{ in }x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c.$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Consider the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ is the unique solution to the initial value problem

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)\,c$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(0)=c$

$\text{L6}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}\,x(0)$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the 
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by 
{{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}$ by 
{{field-3}}.

Consider the homogeneous system x′(t)=Ax(t), where A is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix Φ0(t) is the unique solution to the initial value problem Φ0′(t)=AΦ0(t),Φ0(0)=In. A derivation of the formula for the solution x(t) passing through x(0) is presented below.

L1: Let Φ0(t)=eAt

L2: x(t)=Φ0(t)c for some constant vector c

L3: x(0)=Φ0(0)c

L4: Φ0(0)=In

EXPLANATION

Let's justify each of the selected steps.

  • We first consider lines L1 and L2. Since Φ0(t)=eAt is a fundamental matrix for the system, any solution of the system can be written as x(t)=Φ0(t)c. Thus, L2 follows from L1 by the properties of a fundamental matrix.

  • Next, we consider lines L2 and L3. From L2 we have x(t)=Φ0(t)c. Evaluating this identity at t=0 gives x(0)=Φ0(0)c, which is precisely line L3. Thus, L3 follows from L2 by evaluating both sides at t=0.

  • Finally, we consider lines L3, L4, and L5. From L3 we know x(0)=Φ0(0)c, and from L4 we know Φ0(0)=In. Replacing Φ0(0) with In in the equation x(0)=Φ0(0)c gives x(0)=Inc=c, which is line L5. Therefore, L5 follows from lines L3 and L4 by replacing Φ0(0) with In in x(0)=Φ0(0)c.

Substituting Φ₀(0)=Iₙ then gives x(0)=Iₙc=c, establishing L5. These choices are mathematically determined, but no Math Academy answer or grading evidence is supplied.

feedback.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is a fundamental matrix for the system, any solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c.
$$

Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{properties of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ From $\text{L2}$ we have

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c.
$$

Evaluating this identity at $t=0$ gives

$$
x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c,
$$

which is precisely line $\text{L3}.$ Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{evaluating both sides at }t=0.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$, $\text{L4},$ and $\text{L5}.$ From $\text{L3}$ we know

$$
x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c,
$$

and from $\text{L4}$ we know ${Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.$ Replacing ${Φ}_{0}(0)$ with ${I}_{n}$ in the equation $x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c$ gives

$$
x(0)={I}_{n}c=c,
$$

which is line $\text{L5}.$ Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}$ by $\text{replacing }{Φ}_{0}(0)\text{ with }{I}_{n}\text{ in }x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c.$

feedback.html:
5.Proving the Matrix Exponential Formula for IVP Solution: Homogeneous Systems?

Consider the homogeneous system x′(t)=Ax(t), where A is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix Φ0(t) is the unique solution to the initial value problem Φ0′(t)=AΦ0(t),Φ0(0)=In. A derivation of the formula for the solution x(t) passing through x(0) is presented below.

L1: Let Φ0(t)=eAt

L2: x(t)=Φ0(t)c for some constant vector c

L3: x(0)=Φ0(0)c

L4: Φ0(0)=In

L5: x(0)=c

L6: x(t)=eAtx(0)

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

Line L2 follows from L1 by the
properties of a fundamental matrix
properties of a fundamental matrix
definition of matrix multiplication
properties of the determinant
definition of a solution curve
.

Line L3 follows from L2 by
evaluating both sides at t=0
evaluating both sides at t=0
differentiating the equation
using diagonalization of Φ0(t)
applying the chain rule
.

Line L5 follows from lines L3 and L4 by
replacing Φ0(0) with In in x(0)=Φ0(0)c
replacing Φ0(0) with In in x(0)=Φ0(0)c
differentiating x(0)=Φ0(0)c
using properties of det(Φ0(0))
applying the chain rule
.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Solve the inequality $-9<-3x+8<-5.$
questions.worked_solution:
We isolate $x$ by applying the addition and multiplication principles, as usual. 

First, we apply the addition principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}-9 & <-3x+8<-5 \\ -9-8 & <-3x+8-8<-5-8 \\ -17 & <-3x<-13\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide by $-3.$ Note that since we are dividing by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality signs.

$$
\begin{aligned}-17 & <-3x<-13 \\ \frac{-17}{-3} & >\frac{-3x}{-3}>\frac{-13}{-3} \\ \frac{17}{3} & >x>\frac{13}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

 

The solution can be written as $\frac{17}{3}>x>\frac{13}{3}$, but this is somewhat difficult to read because the larger number is on the left rather than the right. So, we will rewrite the solution by reversing the order of the numbers: 

$$
\frac{13}{3}<x<\frac{17}{3}
$$
questions.html:
1.Compound Inequalities That Require Flipping the Inequality Sign?

Solve the inequality −9<−3x+8<−5.

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Which of the following number lines gives the solution to $-3\le 2x-1\le 5?$
questions.worked_solution:
We isolate $x$  by applying the addition and multiplication principles, as usual.

$$
\begin{aligned}-3 & \le 2x-1\le 5 \\ -3+1 & \le 2x-1+1\le 5+1 \\ -2 & \le 2x\le 6 \\ \frac{-2}{2} & \le \frac{2x}{2}\le \frac{6}{2} \\ -1 & \le x\le 3\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Which of the following number lines gives the solution to $-5\le -2x+3\le 5?$
questions.worked_solution:
We isolate $x$ by applying the addition and multiplication principles, as usual. 

First, we apply the addition principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}-5 & \le -2x+3\le 5 \\ -5-3 & \le -2x+3-3\le 5-3 \\ -8 & \le -2x\le 2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide by $-2.$ Note that since we are dividing by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality signs. 

$$
\begin{aligned}-8 & \le -2x\le 2 \\ \frac{-8}{-2} & \ge \frac{-2x}{-2}\ge \frac{2}{-2} \\ \frac{8}{2} & \ge x\ge -\frac{2}{2} \\ 4 & \ge x\ge -1\end{aligned}
$$

The solution can be written as $4\ge x\ge -1$, but this is somewhat difficult to read because the larger number is on the left rather than the right. So, we will rewrite the solution by reversing the order of the numbers: 

$$
-1\le x\le 4
$$

We can represent this solution using a number line, as follows.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Which of the following number lines gives the solution to $-5\le -2x+3\le 5?$
question.worked_solution:
We isolate $x$ by applying the addition and multiplication principles, as usual. 

First, we apply the addition principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}-5 & \le -2x+3\le 5 \\ -5-3 & \le -2x+3-3\le 5-3 \\ -8 & \le -2x\le 2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide by $-2.$ Note that since we are dividing by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality signs. 

$$
\begin{aligned}-8 & \le -2x\le 2 \\ \frac{-8}{-2} & \ge \frac{-2x}{-2}\ge \frac{2}{-2} \\ \frac{8}{2} & \ge x\ge -\frac{2}{2} \\ 4 & \ge x\ge -1\end{aligned}
$$

The solution can be written as $4\ge x\ge -1$, but this is somewhat difficult to read because the larger number is on the left rather than the right. So, we will rewrite the solution by reversing the order of the numbers: 

$$
-1\le x\le 4
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Which of the following number lines gives the solution to $-5\le -2x+3\le 5?$
question.worked_solution:
We isolate $x$ by applying the addition and multiplication principles, as usual. 

First, we apply the addition principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}-5 & \le -2x+3\le 5 \\ -5-3 & \le -2x+3-3\le 5-3 \\ -8 & \le -2x\le 2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide by $-2.$ Note that since we are dividing by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality signs. 

$$
\begin{aligned}-8 & \le -2x\le 2 \\ \frac{-8}{-2} & \ge \frac{-2x}{-2}\ge \frac{2}{-2} \\ \frac{8}{2} & \ge x\ge -\frac{2}{2} \\ 4 & \ge x\ge -1\end{aligned}
$$

The solution can be written as $4\ge x\ge -1$, but this is somewhat difficult to read because the larger number is on the left rather than the right. So, we will rewrite the solution by reversing the order of the numbers: 

$$
-1\le x\le 4
$$

We can represent this solution using a number line, as follows.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Find $x+y$ if the midpoint of the line segment with endpoints $(x,y)$ and $(5,-4)$ is $(0,6).$
questions.worked_solution:
The given points are ${{(x,y)}_{⏟}}_{\text{(}{x}_{1},\,{y}_{1})}$, ${{(5,-4)}_{⏟}}_{\text{(}{x}_{2},\,{y}_{2})}$ and ${{(0,6)}_{⏟}}_{\text{(}{x}_{m},\,{y}_{m})}.$

First, the $x$-coordinate of the midpoint's  must be the average of the $x$-coordinates of the endpoints: 

$$
0=\frac{x+5}{2}\,⇒\,x=-5.
$$

Similarly, the $y$-coordinate of the midpoint must be the average of the $y$-coordinates of the endpoints: 

$$
6=\frac{y+(-4)}{2}\,⇒\,y=16.
$$

Therefore, $(x,y)=(-5,16)$ and $x+y=11.$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Expressed in terms of common logarithms, what value of $x$ satisfies the equation ${10}^{x-2}={3}^{x}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the common logarithm $(log)$ of both sides of the equation: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{10}^{x-2} & ={3}^{x} \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({10}^{x-2}) & =\operatorname{log}⁡({3}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that ${log}_{b}⁡({b}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
x-2=\operatorname{log}⁡({3}^{x})
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
x-2=x\operatorname{log}⁡(3)
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-2 & =x\operatorname{log}⁡(3) \\ x-x\operatorname{log}⁡(3) & =2 \\ x(1-\operatorname{log}⁡(3)) & =2 \\ x & =\frac{2}{1-\operatorname{log}⁡(3)}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take ${log}_{5}$ on both sides of the equation: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{x+4} & ={2}^{2-x} \\ {log}_{5}⁡({5}^{x+4}) & ={log}_{5}⁡({2}^{2-x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that ${log}_{b}⁡({b}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side:

$$
x+4={log}_{5}⁡({2}^{2-x})
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
x+4=(2-x){log}_{5}⁡(2)
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+4 & =(2-x){log}_{5}⁡(2) \\ x+4 & =2{log}_{5}⁡(2)-x{log}_{5}⁡(2) \\ x+x{log}_{5}⁡(2) & =2{log}_{5}⁡(2)-4 \\ x(1+{log}_{5}⁡(2)) & =2{log}_{5}⁡(2)-4 \\ x & =\frac{2{log}_{5}⁡(2)-4}{1+{log}_{5}⁡(2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the change of base formula, we have

$$
{log}_{5}⁡(2)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}≈0.430\,677.
$$

Finally, we can approximate $x$ as

$$
x≈\frac{2\cdot 0.430\,677-4}{1+0.430\,677}≈-2.194,
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Given that ${5}^{y}={4}^{y+1},$ what is the value of $y?$ Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take ${log}_{5}$ on both sides of the equation: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{y}={4}^{y+1} \\ {log}_{5}⁡({5}^{y}) & ={log}_{5}⁡({4}^{y+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that ${log}_{b}⁡({b}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={log}_{5}⁡({4}^{y+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =(y+1){log}_{5}⁡4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $y,$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =(y+1){log}_{5}⁡4 \\ y & =y{log}_{5}⁡4+{log}_{5}⁡4 \\ y-y{log}_{5}⁡4 & ={log}_{5}⁡4 \\ y(1-{log}_{5}⁡4) & ={log}_{5}⁡4 \\ y & =\frac{{log}_{5}⁡4}{1-{log}_{5}⁡4}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the change of base formula, we have

$$
{log}_{5}⁡(4)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}≈0.861\,353.
$$

Finally, then, we can approximate $y$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}y≈\frac{0.861\,353}{1-0.861\,353}≈6.213,\end{aligned}
$$

to $3$ decimal places.

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: Given that $\frac{{3}^{x}}{5}=3\cdot {4}^{x},$ what is the value of $x?$ Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that, by multiplying by $5$ on both sides,  the given equation is equivalent to

$$
{3}^{x}=15\cdot {4}^{x}
$$

Now, we take ${log}_{3}$ on both sides of the equation: 

$$
{log}_{3}⁡({3}^{x})={log}_{3}⁡(15\cdot {4}^{x})
$$

Then, we use the fact that ${log}_{b}⁡({b}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={log}_{3}⁡(15\cdot {4}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use  the product law and the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={log}_{3}⁡(15\cdot {4}^{x}) \\  & ={log}_{3}⁡(15)+{log}_{3}⁡({4}^{x}) \\  & ={log}_{3}⁡(15)+x{log}_{3}⁡4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={log}_{3}⁡(15)+x{log}_{3}⁡4 \\ x-x{log}_{3}⁡4 & ={log}_{3}⁡(15) \\ x(1-{log}_{3}⁡4) & ={log}_{3}⁡(15) \\ x & =\frac{{log}_{3}⁡(15)}{1-{log}_{3}⁡4}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the change of base formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{3}⁡(15)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡15}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}≈2.464\,974, \\ {log}_{3}⁡4=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}≈1.261\,860.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can approximate $x$ as

$$
x≈\frac{2.464\,974}{1-1.261\,860}≈-9.413,
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: Expressed in terms of common logarithms, what value of $x$ satisfies the equation ${10}^{x+1}={3}^{x+2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the common logarithm $(log)$ of both sides of the equation:   

$$
\begin{aligned}{10}^{x+1} & ={3}^{x+2} \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({10}^{x+1}) & =\operatorname{log}⁡({3}^{x+2})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that ${log}_{b}⁡({b}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
x+1=\operatorname{log}⁡({3}^{x+2})
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =(x+2)\operatorname{log}⁡(3) \\ x+1 & =x\operatorname{log}⁡(3)+2\operatorname{log}⁡(3)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x\operatorname{log}⁡(3)+2\operatorname{log}⁡(3) \\ x-x\operatorname{log}⁡(3) & =2\operatorname{log}⁡(3)-1 \\ x(1-\operatorname{log}⁡(3)) & =2\operatorname{log}⁡(3)-1 \\ x & =\frac{2\operatorname{log}⁡(3)-1}{1-\operatorname{log}⁡(3)}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2x-1} & =3\cdot {8}^{x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2x-1}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3\cdot {8}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{a})=a$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives

$$
2x-1=\operatorname{ln}⁡(3\cdot {8}^{x}).
$$

Next, we use the power and product laws of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-1 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+\operatorname{ln}⁡({8}^{x}) \\ 2x-1 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-1 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) \\ 2x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)+1 \\ 2x-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+1 \\ x(2-\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+1 \\ x & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+1}{2-\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{3x+1} & ={2}^{x-1} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{3x+1}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{x-1})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that ${log}_{b}⁡({b}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+1 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{x-1}).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+1 & =(x-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+1 & =(x-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ 3x+1 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ 3x-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-1 \\ x(3-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)) & =-(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+1) \\ x & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+1}{3-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x-3} & =5\cdot {8}^{2x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x-3}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5\cdot {8}^{2x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{a})=a$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives

$$
x-3=\operatorname{ln}⁡(5\cdot {8}^{2x}).
$$

Next, we use the power and product laws of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-3 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+\operatorname{ln}⁡({8}^{2x}) \\ x-3 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-3 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) \\ x-2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) & =3+\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x(1-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)) & =3+\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x & =\frac{3+\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}{1-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem: Expressed in terms of natural logarithms, what value of $x$ satisfies the equation ${e}^{x+2}=5\cdot {6}^{x}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x+2} & =5\cdot {6}^{x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x+2}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5\cdot {6}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{a})=a$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
x+2=\operatorname{ln}⁡(5\cdot {6}^{x})\,
$$

Next, we use the power and product laws of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+\operatorname{ln}⁡({6}^{x}) \\ x+2 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ x-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-2 \\ x(1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-2 \\ x & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-2}{1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)}\end{aligned}
$$

9.?

Expressed in terms of natural logarithms, what value of x satisfies the equation ex+2=5⋅6x?

questions.name: Question 10
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{3x-1} & ={6}^{2x+1} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{3x-1}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({6}^{2x+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{a})=a$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives

$$
3x-1=\operatorname{ln}⁡({6}^{2x+1}).
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
3x-1=(2x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-1 & =(2x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ 3x-1 & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ 3x-2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) & =1+\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ x(3-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)) & =1+\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ x & =\frac{1+\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)}{3-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{4x+1} & ={6}^{7x+5} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({5}^{4x+1}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({6}^{7x+5})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives

$$
(4x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)=(7x+5)\operatorname{ln}⁡(6).
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(4x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =(7x+5)\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ 4x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =7x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)+5\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ 4x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-7x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x(4\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-7\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)) & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x & =\frac{5\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-7\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 12
questions.problem: Find the solution of ${3}^{x+5}={7}^{6-2x}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{x+5} & ={7}^{6-2x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{x+5}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({7}^{6-2x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+5)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =(6-2x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+5)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =(6-2x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(7) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+5\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =6\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)-2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(7) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(7) & =6\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)-5\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\ x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)) & =6\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)-5\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\ x & =\frac{6\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)-5\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 13
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{4}^{3x-1} & ={9}^{x+6} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({4}^{3x-1}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({9}^{x+6})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives

$$
(3x-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)=(x+6)\operatorname{ln}⁡(9).
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(3x-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(4) & =(x+6)\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) \\ 3x\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(4) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)+6\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) \\ 3x\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)+6\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) \\ x(3\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)+6\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) \\ x & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)+6\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 14
questions.problem: Find the solution of ${5}^{x+3}={2}^{5-4x}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{x+3} & ={2}^{5-4x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({5}^{x+3}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{5-4x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =(5-4x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =(5-4x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-4x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+4x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)) & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x & =\frac{5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 15
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{6x+1} & ={6}^{x+7} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{6x+1}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({6}^{x+7})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives

$$
(6x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)=(x+7)\operatorname{ln}⁡(6).
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(6x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) & =(x+7)\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ 6x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)+7\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ 6x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) & =7\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ x(6\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)) & =7\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ x & =\frac{7\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{6\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding Exact Solutions of Exponential Equations
canonical_examples.problem: Expressed in terms of $\log_2,$ what value of $x$ satisfies the equation $2^{x+1}=3^x?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we take $\log_2$ on both sides of the equation: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{x+1} & ={3}^{x} \\ {log}_{2}⁡({2}^{x+1}) & ={log}_{2}⁡({3}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\log_b \left( b^c \right) = c$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
x+1 = \log_2 \left(3^{x}\right)
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
x+1 = x \log_2 \left(3\right)
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x{log}_{2}⁡(3) \\ x{log}_{2}⁡(3)-x & =1 \\ x({log}_{2}⁡(3)-1) & =1 \\ x & =\frac{1}{{log}_{2}⁡(3)-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Finding Solutions of Exponential Equations Using the Natural Logarithm
canonical_examples.problem: Expressed in terms of natural logarithms, what value of $x$ satisfies the equation $e^{x+1}=2^x\cdot 5?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $\left(\ln\right)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x+1} & ={2}^{x}\cdot 5 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x+1}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{x}\cdot 5)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\ln \left( e^a \right) = a$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
x+1 =\ln \left(2^{x}\cdot 5\right)
$$

Next, we use the power and product laws of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{x})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x+1 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-1 \\ x(1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-1 \\ x & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-1}{1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Expressed in terms of natural logarithms, determine the value of $x$ that satisfies the equation $5^{x+2}=9^{x-2}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $\left(\ln\right)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{x+2} & ={9}^{x-2} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({5}^{x+2}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({9}^{x-2})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives

$$
(x+2)\ln(5) = (x-2)\ln(9).
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =(x-2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)) & =2(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)) \\ x & =\frac{2(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(9))}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The most general way of solving exponential equations with different bases is to use logarithms on both sides of the equation. 
For example, given the equation

$$
3^{x+1} = 5^{x},
$$

we could apply $\log_3$ on both sides and get

$$
\log_3(3^{x+1}) = \log_3(5^{x}).
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\log_b \left( b^c \right) = c$ to simplify the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & ={log}_{3}⁡({5}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the power law for logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x{log}_{3}⁡(5)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x{log}_{3}⁡(5) \\ x-x{log}_{3}⁡(5) & =-1 \\ x(1-{log}_{3}⁡(5)) & =-1 \\ x & =-\frac{1}{1-{log}_{3}⁡(5)} \\ x & =\frac{1}{{log}_{3}⁡(5)-1}\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** in the first step, we also could have applied $\log_5$ on both sides of our equation, instead of $\log_3.$ Then, the answer would be numerically the same but expressed using $\log_5$ instead of $\log_3.$

\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x{log}_{3}⁡(5) \\ x-x{log}_{3}⁡(5) & =-1 \\ x(1-{log}_{3}⁡(5)) & =-1 \\ x & =-\frac{1}{1-{log}_{3}⁡(5)} \\ x & =\frac{1}{{log}_{3}⁡(5)-1}\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** in the first step, we also could have applied $\log_5$ on both sides of our equation, instead of $\log_3.$ Then, the answer would be numerically the same but expressed using $\log_5$ instead of $\log_3.$

Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we take the common logarithm (log) of both sides of the equation: 10x−2=3xlog⁡(10x−2)=log⁡(3x)

Now, we use the fact that logb⁡(bc)=c to simplify the left-hand side. This gives: x−2=log⁡(3x)

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side: x−2=xlog⁡(3)

Finally, we solve for x, as follows: x−2=xlog⁡(3)x−xlog⁡(3)=2x(1−log⁡(3))=2x=21−log⁡(3)

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding Exact Solutions of Exponential Equations
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we take ${log}_{5}$ on both sides of the equation: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{x+4} & ={2}^{2-x} \\ {log}_{5}⁡({5}^{x+4}) & ={log}_{5}⁡({2}^{2-x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that ${log}_{b}⁡({b}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side:

$$
x+4={log}_{5}⁡({2}^{2-x})
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
x+4=(2-x){log}_{5}⁡(2)
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+4 & =(2-x){log}_{5}⁡(2) \\ x+4 & =2{log}_{5}⁡(2)-x{log}_{5}⁡(2) \\ x+x{log}_{5}⁡(2) & =2{log}_{5}⁡(2)-4 \\ x(1+{log}_{5}⁡(2)) & =2{log}_{5}⁡(2)-4 \\ x & =\frac{2{log}_{5}⁡(2)-4}{1+{log}_{5}⁡(2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the change of base formula, we have

$$
{log}_{5}⁡(2)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}≈0.430\,677.
$$

Finally, we can approximate $x$ as

$$
x≈\frac{2\cdot 0.430\,677-4}{1+0.430\,677}≈-2.194,
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we take ${log}_{5}$ on both sides of the equation: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{y}={4}^{y+1} \\ {log}_{5}⁡({5}^{y}) & ={log}_{5}⁡({4}^{y+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that ${log}_{b}⁡({b}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={log}_{5}⁡({4}^{y+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =(y+1){log}_{5}⁡4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $y,$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =(y+1){log}_{5}⁡4 \\ y & =y{log}_{5}⁡4+{log}_{5}⁡4 \\ y-y{log}_{5}⁡4 & ={log}_{5}⁡4 \\ y(1-{log}_{5}⁡4) & ={log}_{5}⁡4 \\ y & =\frac{{log}_{5}⁡4}{1-{log}_{5}⁡4}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the change of base formula, we have

$$
{log}_{5}⁡(4)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}≈0.861\,353.
$$

Finally, then, we can approximate $y$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}y≈\frac{0.861\,353}{1-0.861\,353}≈6.213,\end{aligned}
$$

to $3$ decimal places.

question.html:
Question 3
?

Given that 5y=4y+1, what is the value of y? Round your answer to 3 decimal places.

a
6.213
b
−5.891
c
1.293
d
7.712
e
0.544
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we take log5 on both sides of the equation:

5y=4y+1log5⁡(5y)=log5⁡(4y+1)

Now, we use the fact that logb⁡(bc)=c to simplify the left-hand side:

y=log5⁡(4y+1)

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

y=(y+1)log5⁡4

Finally, we solve for y, as follows:

y=(y+1)log5⁡4y=ylog5⁡4+log5⁡4y−ylog5⁡4=log5⁡4y(1−log5⁡4)=log5⁡4y=log5⁡41−log5⁡4

Using the change of base formula, we have

log5⁡(4)=ln⁡(4)ln⁡(5)≈0.861353.

Finally, then, we can approximate y as

y≈0.8613531−0.861353≈6.213, to 3 decimal places.
question.knowledge_point: Finding Exact Solutions of Exponential Equations

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding Exact Solutions of Exponential Equations
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, notice that, by multiplying by $5$ on both sides,  the given equation is equivalent to

$$
{3}^{x}=15\cdot {4}^{x}
$$

Now, we take ${log}_{3}$ on both sides of the equation: 

$$
{log}_{3}⁡({3}^{x})={log}_{3}⁡(15\cdot {4}^{x})
$$

Then, we use the fact that ${log}_{b}⁡({b}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={log}_{3}⁡(15\cdot {4}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use  the product law and the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={log}_{3}⁡(15\cdot {4}^{x}) \\  & ={log}_{3}⁡(15)+{log}_{3}⁡({4}^{x}) \\  & ={log}_{3}⁡(15)+x{log}_{3}⁡4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={log}_{3}⁡(15)+x{log}_{3}⁡4 \\ x-x{log}_{3}⁡4 & ={log}_{3}⁡(15) \\ x(1-{log}_{3}⁡4) & ={log}_{3}⁡(15) \\ x & =\frac{{log}_{3}⁡(15)}{1-{log}_{3}⁡4}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the change of base formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{3}⁡(15)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡15}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}≈2.464\,974, \\ {log}_{3}⁡4=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}≈1.261\,860.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can approximate $x$ as

$$
x≈\frac{2.464\,974}{1-1.261\,860}≈-9.413,
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Question 4
?

Given that 3x5=3⋅4x, what is the value of x? Round your answer to 3 decimal places.

a
−6.678
b
−9.413
c
7.891
d
8.901
e
−10.934
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, notice that, by multiplying by 5 on both sides, the given equation is equivalent to 3x=15⋅4x

Now, we take log3 on both sides of the equation:

log3⁡(3x)=log3⁡(15⋅4x)

Then, we use the fact that logb⁡(bc)=c to simplify the left-hand side:

x=log3⁡(15⋅4x)

Next, we use the product law and the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

x=log3⁡(15⋅4x)=log3⁡(15)+log3⁡(4x)=log3⁡(15)+xlog3⁡4

Finally, we solve for x, as follows:

x=log3⁡(15)+xlog3⁡4x−xlog3⁡4=log3⁡(15)x(1−log3⁡4)=log3⁡(15)x=log3⁡(15)1−log3⁡4

Using the change of base formula, we have log3⁡(15)=ln⁡15ln⁡3≈2.464974,log3⁡4=ln⁡4ln⁡3≈1.261860.

Finally, we can approximate x as x≈2.4649741−1.261860≈−9.413, rounded to 3 decimal places.

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding Exact Solutions of Exponential Equations
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we take the common logarithm $(log)$ of both sides of the equation:   

$$
\begin{aligned}{10}^{x+1} & ={3}^{x+2} \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({10}^{x+1}) & =\operatorname{log}⁡({3}^{x+2})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that ${log}_{b}⁡({b}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
x+1=\operatorname{log}⁡({3}^{x+2})
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =(x+2)\operatorname{log}⁡(3) \\ x+1 & =x\operatorname{log}⁡(3)+2\operatorname{log}⁡(3)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x\operatorname{log}⁡(3)+2\operatorname{log}⁡(3) \\ x-x\operatorname{log}⁡(3) & =2\operatorname{log}⁡(3)-1 \\ x(1-\operatorname{log}⁡(3)) & =2\operatorname{log}⁡(3)-1 \\ x & =\frac{2\operatorname{log}⁡(3)-1}{1-\operatorname{log}⁡(3)}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: Expressed in terms of common logarithms, what value of $x$ satisfies the equation ${10}^{x+1}={3}^{x+2}?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we take the common logarithm $(log)$ of both sides of the equation:   

$$
\begin{aligned}{10}^{x+1} & ={3}^{x+2} \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({10}^{x+1}) & =\operatorname{log}⁡({3}^{x+2})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that ${log}_{b}⁡({b}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
x+1=\operatorname{log}⁡({3}^{x+2})
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =(x+2)\operatorname{log}⁡(3) \\ x+1 & =x\operatorname{log}⁡(3)+2\operatorname{log}⁡(3)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x\operatorname{log}⁡(3)+2\operatorname{log}⁡(3) \\ x-x\operatorname{log}⁡(3) & =2\operatorname{log}⁡(3)-1 \\ x(1-\operatorname{log}⁡(3)) & =2\operatorname{log}⁡(3)-1 \\ x & =\frac{2\operatorname{log}⁡(3)-1}{1-\operatorname{log}⁡(3)}\end{aligned}
$$
