Question 5
?

Expressed in terms of common logarithms, what value of x satisfies the equation 10x+1=3x+2?

a
log⁡(3)1+log⁡(3)
b
log⁡(2)−log⁡(3)
c
2log⁡(3)−11−log⁡(3)
d
log⁡(3)−1
e
1+log⁡(3)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we take the common logarithm (log) of both sides of the equation:

10x+1=3x+2log⁡(10x+1)=log⁡(3x+2)

Now, we use the fact that logb⁡(bc)=c to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

x+1=log⁡(3x+2)

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

x+1=(x+2)log⁡(3)x+1=xlog⁡(3)+2log⁡(3)

Finally, we solve for x, as follows:

x+1=xlog⁡(3)+2log⁡(3)x−xlog⁡(3)=2log⁡(3)−1x(1−log⁡(3))=2log⁡(3)−1x=2log⁡(3)−11−log⁡(3)

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $\left(\ln\right)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x+1} & ={2}^{x}\cdot 5 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x+1}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{x}\cdot 5)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\ln \left( e^a \right) = a$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
x+1 =\ln \left(2^{x}\cdot 5\right)
$$

Next, we use the power and product laws of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{x})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x+1 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-1 \\ x(1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-1 \\ x & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-1}{1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
3x-1=\operatorname{ln}⁡({6}^{2x+1}).
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
3x-1=(2x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-1 & =(2x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ 3x-1 & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ 3x-2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) & =1+\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ x(3-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)) & =1+\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ x & =\frac{1+\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)}{3-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Question 12

Find the solution of 3x+5=76−2x.

a
6ln⁡(7)−5ln⁡(3)ln⁡(3)+2ln⁡(7)
b
6ln⁡(7)ln⁡(3)ln⁡(3)+2ln⁡(7)
c
1ln⁡(3)+2ln⁡(7)
d
6ln⁡(3)+5ln⁡(7)ln⁡(7)−ln⁡(3)
e
16ln⁡(7)−5ln⁡(3)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we take the natural logarithm (ln) of both sides of the equation:

3x+5=76−2xln⁡(3x+5)=ln⁡(76−2x)

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives:

(x+5)ln⁡(3)=(6−2x)ln⁡(7)

Finally, we solve for x, as follows:

(x+5)ln⁡(3)=(6−2x)ln⁡(7)xln⁡(3)+5ln⁡(3)=6ln⁡(7)−2xln⁡(7)xln⁡(3)+2xln⁡(7)=6ln⁡(7)−5ln⁡(3)x(ln⁡(3)+2ln⁡(7))=6ln⁡(7)−5ln⁡(3)x=6ln⁡(7)−5ln⁡(3)ln⁡(3)+2ln⁡(7)

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives

$$
(3x-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)=(x+6)\operatorname{ln}⁡(9).
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(3x-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(4) & =(x+6)\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) \\ 3x\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(4) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)+6\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) \\ 3x\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)+6\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) \\ x(3\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)+6\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) \\ x & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)+6\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)}\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{x+3} & ={2}^{5-4x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({5}^{x+3}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{5-4x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =(5-4x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =(5-4x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-4x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+4x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)) & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x & =\frac{5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Find the solution of 5x+3=25−4x.

a
ln⁡(2)+3ln⁡(5)ln⁡(5)−2ln⁡(2)
b
5ln⁡(5)−ln⁡(2)ln⁡(5)+ln⁡(2)

Submit

EXPLANATION

First, we take the natural logarithm (ln) of both sides of the equation:

5x+3=25−4xln⁡(5x+3)=ln⁡(25−4x)

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives:

(x+3)ln⁡(5)=(5−4x)ln⁡(2)

Finally, we solve for x, as follows:

(x+3)ln⁡(5)=(5−4x)ln⁡(2)xln⁡(5)+3ln⁡(5)=5ln⁡(2)−4xln⁡(2)xln⁡(5)+4xln⁡(2)=5ln⁡(2)−3ln⁡(5)x(ln⁡(5)+4ln⁡(2))=5ln⁡(2)−3ln⁡(5)x=5ln⁡(2)−3ln⁡(5)ln⁡(5)+4ln⁡(2)

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{6x+1} & ={6}^{x+7} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{6x+1}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({6}^{x+7})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives

$$
(6x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)=(x+7)\operatorname{ln}⁡(6).
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(6x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) & =(x+7)\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ 6x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)+7\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ 6x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) & =7\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ x(6\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)) & =7\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ x & =\frac{7\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{6\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Expressed in terms of common logarithms, what value of $x$ satisfies the equation ${10}^{x-2}={3}^{x}?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we take the common logarithm $(log)$ of both sides of the equation: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{10}^{x-2} & ={3}^{x} \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({10}^{x-2}) & =\operatorname{log}⁡({3}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that ${log}_{b}⁡({b}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
x-2=\operatorname{log}⁡({3}^{x})
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
x-2=x\operatorname{log}⁡(3)
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-2 & =x\operatorname{log}⁡(3) \\ x-x\operatorname{log}⁡(3) & =2 \\ x(1-\operatorname{log}⁡(3)) & =2 \\ x & =\frac{2}{1-\operatorname{log}⁡(3)}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for x, as follows: x−2=xlog⁡(3)x−xlog⁡(3)=2x(1−log⁡(3))=2x=21−log⁡(3)

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding Exact Solutions of Exponential Equations
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we take the common logarithm $(log)$ of both sides of the equation: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{10}^{x-2} & ={3}^{x} \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({10}^{x-2}) & =\operatorname{log}⁡({3}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that ${log}_{b}⁡({b}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
x-2=\operatorname{log}⁡({3}^{x})
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
x-2=x\operatorname{log}⁡(3)
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-2 & =x\operatorname{log}⁡(3) \\ x-x\operatorname{log}⁡(3) & =2 \\ x(1-\operatorname{log}⁡(3)) & =2 \\ x & =\frac{2}{1-\operatorname{log}⁡(3)}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Expressed in terms of common logarithms, what value of x satisfies the equation 10x−2=3x?

a
21−log⁡(3)
b
1+log⁡(3)
c
−3log⁡(2)
d
12−log⁡(3)
e
log⁡(2)+log⁡(3)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we take the common logarithm (log) of both sides of the equation: 10x−2=3xlog⁡(10x−2)=log⁡(3x)

Now, we use the fact that logb⁡(bc)=c to simplify the left-hand side. This gives: x−2=log⁡(3x)

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side: x−2=xlog⁡(3)

Finally, we solve for x, as follows: x−2=xlog⁡(3)x−xlog⁡(3)=2x(1−log⁡(3))=2x=21−log⁡(3)

solution.reasoning: Taking common logarithms gives x-2=x\log(3), so x(1-\log(3))=2 and x=2/(1-\log(3)), which is option a. No answer key or grade for this question is captured; the worked example concerns a different equation.

Question 1
?

Expressed in terms of common logarithms, what value of x satisfies the equation 10x−2=3x?

a
21−log⁡(3)
b
1+log⁡(3)
c
−3log⁡(2)
d
12−log⁡(3)
e
log⁡(2)+log⁡(3)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we take the common logarithm (log) of both sides of the equation: 10x−2=3xlog⁡(10x−2)=log⁡(3x)

Now, we use the fact that logb⁡(bc)=c to simplify the left-hand side. This gives: x−2=log⁡(3x)

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side: x−2=xlog⁡(3)

Finally, we solve for x, as follows: x−2=xlog⁡(3)x−xlog⁡(3)=2x(1−log⁡(3))=2x=21−log⁡(3)

question.name: Question 2
question.worked_solution:
First, we take ${log}_{5}$ on both sides of the equation: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{x+4} & ={2}^{2-x} \\ {log}_{5}⁡({5}^{x+4}) & ={log}_{5}⁡({2}^{2-x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that ${log}_{b}⁡({b}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side:

$$
x+4={log}_{5}⁡({2}^{2-x})
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
x+4=(2-x){log}_{5}⁡(2)
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+4 & =(2-x){log}_{5}⁡(2) \\ x+4 & =2{log}_{5}⁡(2)-x{log}_{5}⁡(2) \\ x+x{log}_{5}⁡(2) & =2{log}_{5}⁡(2)-4 \\ x(1+{log}_{5}⁡(2)) & =2{log}_{5}⁡(2)-4 \\ x & =\frac{2{log}_{5}⁡(2)-4}{1+{log}_{5}⁡(2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the change of base formula, we have

$$
{log}_{5}⁡(2)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}≈0.430\,677.
$$

Finally, we can approximate $x$ as

$$
x≈\frac{2\cdot 0.430\,677-4}{1+0.430\,677}≈-2.194,
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Given that ${5}^{y}={4}^{y+1},$ what is the value of $y?$ Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
First, we take ${log}_{5}$ on both sides of the equation: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{y}={4}^{y+1} \\ {log}_{5}⁡({5}^{y}) & ={log}_{5}⁡({4}^{y+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that ${log}_{b}⁡({b}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={log}_{5}⁡({4}^{y+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =(y+1){log}_{5}⁡4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $y,$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =(y+1){log}_{5}⁡4 \\ y & =y{log}_{5}⁡4+{log}_{5}⁡4 \\ y-y{log}_{5}⁡4 & ={log}_{5}⁡4 \\ y(1-{log}_{5}⁡4) & ={log}_{5}⁡4 \\ y & =\frac{{log}_{5}⁡4}{1-{log}_{5}⁡4}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the change of base formula, we have

$$
{log}_{5}⁡(4)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}≈0.861\,353.
$$

Finally, then, we can approximate $y$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}y≈\frac{0.861\,353}{1-0.861\,353}≈6.213,\end{aligned}
$$

to $3$ decimal places.

question.html:
Question 3
?

Given that 5y=4y+1, what is the value of y? Round your answer to 3 decimal places.

a
6.213
b
−5.891
c
1.293
d
7.712
e
0.544
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we take log5 on both sides of the equation:

5y=4y+1log5⁡(5y)=log5⁡(4y+1)

Now, we use the fact that logb⁡(bc)=c to simplify the left-hand side:

y=log5⁡(4y+1)

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

y=(y+1)log5⁡4

Finally, we solve for y, as follows:

y=(y+1)log5⁡4y=ylog5⁡4+log5⁡4y−ylog5⁡4=log5⁡4y(1−log5⁡4)=log5⁡4y=log5⁡41−log5⁡4

Using the change of base formula, we have

log5⁡(4)=ln⁡(4)ln⁡(5)≈0.861353.

Finally, then, we can approximate y as

y≈0.8613531−0.861353≈6.213, to 3 decimal places.

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding Exact Solutions of Exponential Equations
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we take ${log}_{5}$ on both sides of the equation: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{y}={4}^{y+1} \\ {log}_{5}⁡({5}^{y}) & ={log}_{5}⁡({4}^{y+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that ${log}_{b}⁡({b}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={log}_{5}⁡({4}^{y+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =(y+1){log}_{5}⁡4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $y,$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =(y+1){log}_{5}⁡4 \\ y & =y{log}_{5}⁡4+{log}_{5}⁡4 \\ y-y{log}_{5}⁡4 & ={log}_{5}⁡4 \\ y(1-{log}_{5}⁡4) & ={log}_{5}⁡4 \\ y & =\frac{{log}_{5}⁡4}{1-{log}_{5}⁡4}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the change of base formula, we have

$$
{log}_{5}⁡(4)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}≈0.861\,353.
$$

Finally, then, we can approximate $y$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}y≈\frac{0.861\,353}{1-0.861\,353}≈6.213,\end{aligned}
$$

to $3$ decimal places.

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: Given that $\frac{{3}^{x}}{5}=3\cdot {4}^{x},$ what is the value of $x?$ Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
First, notice that, by multiplying by $5$ on both sides,  the given equation is equivalent to

$$
{3}^{x}=15\cdot {4}^{x}
$$

Now, we take ${log}_{3}$ on both sides of the equation: 

$$
{log}_{3}⁡({3}^{x})={log}_{3}⁡(15\cdot {4}^{x})
$$

Then, we use the fact that ${log}_{b}⁡({b}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={log}_{3}⁡(15\cdot {4}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use  the product law and the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={log}_{3}⁡(15\cdot {4}^{x}) \\  & ={log}_{3}⁡(15)+{log}_{3}⁡({4}^{x}) \\  & ={log}_{3}⁡(15)+x{log}_{3}⁡4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={log}_{3}⁡(15)+x{log}_{3}⁡4 \\ x-x{log}_{3}⁡4 & ={log}_{3}⁡(15) \\ x(1-{log}_{3}⁡4) & ={log}_{3}⁡(15) \\ x & =\frac{{log}_{3}⁡(15)}{1-{log}_{3}⁡4}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the change of base formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{3}⁡(15)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡15}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}≈2.464\,974, \\ {log}_{3}⁡4=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}≈1.261\,860.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can approximate $x$ as

$$
x≈\frac{2.464\,974}{1-1.261\,860}≈-9.413,
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, notice that, by multiplying by $5$ on both sides,  the given equation is equivalent to

$$
{3}^{x}=15\cdot {4}^{x}
$$

Now, we take ${log}_{3}$ on both sides of the equation: 

$$
{log}_{3}⁡({3}^{x})={log}_{3}⁡(15\cdot {4}^{x})
$$

Then, we use the fact that ${log}_{b}⁡({b}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={log}_{3}⁡(15\cdot {4}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use  the product law and the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={log}_{3}⁡(15\cdot {4}^{x}) \\  & ={log}_{3}⁡(15)+{log}_{3}⁡({4}^{x}) \\  & ={log}_{3}⁡(15)+x{log}_{3}⁡4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={log}_{3}⁡(15)+x{log}_{3}⁡4 \\ x-x{log}_{3}⁡4 & ={log}_{3}⁡(15) \\ x(1-{log}_{3}⁡4) & ={log}_{3}⁡(15) \\ x & =\frac{{log}_{3}⁡(15)}{1-{log}_{3}⁡4}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the change of base formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{3}⁡(15)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡15}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}≈2.464\,974, \\ {log}_{3}⁡4=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}≈1.261\,860.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can approximate $x$ as

$$
x≈\frac{2.464\,974}{1-1.261\,860}≈-9.413,
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Question 4
?

Given that 3x5=3⋅4x, what is the value of x? Round your answer to 3 decimal places.

a
−6.678
b
−9.413
c
7.891
d
8.901
e
−10.934
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, notice that, by multiplying by 5 on both sides, the given equation is equivalent to 3x=15⋅4x

Now, we take log3 on both sides of the equation:

log3⁡(3x)=log3⁡(15⋅4x)

Then, we use the fact that logb⁡(bc)=c to simplify the left-hand side:

x=log3⁡(15⋅4x)

Next, we use the product law and the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

x=log3⁡(15⋅4x)=log3⁡(15)+log3⁡(4x)=log3⁡(15)+xlog3⁡4

Finally, we solve for x, as follows:

x=log3⁡(15)+xlog3⁡4x−xlog3⁡4=log3⁡(15)x(1−log3⁡4)=log3⁡(15)x=log3⁡(15)1−log3⁡4

Using the change of base formula, we have log3⁡(15)=ln⁡15ln⁡3≈2.464974,log3⁡4=ln⁡4ln⁡3≈1.261860.

Finally, we can approximate x as x≈2.4649741−1.261860≈−9.413, rounded to 3 decimal places.

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: Expressed in terms of common logarithms, what value of $x$ satisfies the equation ${10}^{x+1}={3}^{x+2}?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we take the common logarithm $(log)$ of both sides of the equation:   

$$
\begin{aligned}{10}^{x+1} & ={3}^{x+2} \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({10}^{x+1}) & =\operatorname{log}⁡({3}^{x+2})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that ${log}_{b}⁡({b}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
x+1=\operatorname{log}⁡({3}^{x+2})
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =(x+2)\operatorname{log}⁡(3) \\ x+1 & =x\operatorname{log}⁡(3)+2\operatorname{log}⁡(3)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x\operatorname{log}⁡(3)+2\operatorname{log}⁡(3) \\ x-x\operatorname{log}⁡(3) & =2\operatorname{log}⁡(3)-1 \\ x(1-\operatorname{log}⁡(3)) & =2\operatorname{log}⁡(3)-1 \\ x & =\frac{2\operatorname{log}⁡(3)-1}{1-\operatorname{log}⁡(3)}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Expressed in terms of common logarithms, what value of x satisfies the equation 10x+1=3x+2?

a
log⁡(3)1+log⁡(3)
b
log⁡(2)−log⁡(3)
c
2log⁡(3)−11−log⁡(3)
d
log⁡(3)−1
e
1+log⁡(3)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we take the common logarithm (log) of both sides of the equation:

10x+1=3x+2log⁡(10x+1)=log⁡(3x+2)

Now, we use the fact that logb⁡(bc)=c to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

x+1=log⁡(3x+2)

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

x+1=(x+2)log⁡(3)x+1=xlog⁡(3)+2log⁡(3)

Finally, we solve for x, as follows:

x+1=xlog⁡(3)+2log⁡(3)x−xlog⁡(3)=2log⁡(3)−1x(1−log⁡(3))=2log⁡(3)−1x=2log⁡(3)−11−log⁡(3)

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding Exact Solutions of Exponential Equations
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we take the common logarithm $(log)$ of both sides of the equation:   

$$
\begin{aligned}{10}^{x+1} & ={3}^{x+2} \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({10}^{x+1}) & =\operatorname{log}⁡({3}^{x+2})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that ${log}_{b}⁡({b}^{c})=c$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
x+1=\operatorname{log}⁡({3}^{x+2})
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =(x+2)\operatorname{log}⁡(3) \\ x+1 & =x\operatorname{log}⁡(3)+2\operatorname{log}⁡(3)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =x\operatorname{log}⁡(3)+2\operatorname{log}⁡(3) \\ x-x\operatorname{log}⁡(3) & =2\operatorname{log}⁡(3)-1 \\ x(1-\operatorname{log}⁡(3)) & =2\operatorname{log}⁡(3)-1 \\ x & =\frac{2\operatorname{log}⁡(3)-1}{1-\operatorname{log}⁡(3)}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Expressed in terms of common logarithms, what value of x satisfies the equation 10x+1=3x+2?

a
log⁡(3)1+log⁡(3)
b
log⁡(2)−log⁡(3)
c
2log⁡(3)−11−log⁡(3)
d
log⁡(3)−1
e
1+log⁡(3)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we take the common logarithm (log) of both sides of the equation:

10x+1=3x+2log⁡(10x+1)=log⁡(3x+2)

Now, we use the fact that logb⁡(bc)=c to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

x+1=log⁡(3x+2)

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

x+1=(x+2)log⁡(3)x+1=xlog⁡(3)+2log⁡(3)

Finally, we solve for x, as follows:

x+1=xlog⁡(3)+2log⁡(3)x−xlog⁡(3)=2log⁡(3)−1x(1−log⁡(3))=2log⁡(3)−1x=2log⁡(3)−11−log⁡(3)

solution.reasoning: Taking common logarithms gives x+1=(x+2)\log(3). Collecting terms yields x(1-\log(3))=2\log(3)-1, so x=(2\log(3)-1)/(1-\log(3)), option c. No Math Academy answer key or grade for this question is captured.

x+1=(x+2)log⁡(3)x+1=xlog⁡(3)+2log⁡(3)

First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2x-1} & =3\cdot {8}^{x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2x-1}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3\cdot {8}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{a})=a$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives

$$
2x-1=\operatorname{ln}⁡(3\cdot {8}^{x}).
$$

Next, we use the power and product laws of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-1 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+\operatorname{ln}⁡({8}^{x}) \\ 2x-1 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-1 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) \\ 2x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)+1 \\ 2x-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(8) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+1 \\ x(2-\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+1 \\ x & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+1}{2-\operatorname{ln}⁡(8)}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+1 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{x-1}).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+1 & =(x-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\end{aligned}

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+1 & =(x-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ 3x+1 & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ 3x-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-1 \\ x(3-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)) & =-(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+1) \\ x & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+1}{3-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: Expressed in terms of natural logarithms, what value of $x$ satisfies the equation ${e}^{x+2}=5\cdot {6}^{x}?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x+2} & =5\cdot {6}^{x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x+2}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5\cdot {6}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{a})=a$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
x+2=\operatorname{ln}⁡(5\cdot {6}^{x})\,
$$

Next, we use the power and product laws of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+\operatorname{ln}⁡({6}^{x}) \\ x+2 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ x-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-2 \\ x(1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-2 \\ x & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-2}{1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

Expressed in terms of natural logarithms, what value of x satisfies the equation ex+2=5⋅6x?

a
ln⁡(5)−21−ln⁡(6)
b
ln⁡(5)ln⁡(6)
c
ln⁡(5)2+ln⁡(6)
d
ln⁡(5)1−ln⁡(6)
e
ln⁡(5)−2ln⁡(6)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we take the natural logarithm (ln) of both sides of the equation:

ex+2=5⋅6xln⁡(ex+2)=ln⁡(5⋅6x)

Now, we use the fact that ln⁡(ea)=a to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

x+2=ln⁡(5⋅6x)

Next, we use the power and product laws of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

x+2=ln⁡(5)+ln⁡(6x)x+2=ln⁡(5)+xln⁡(6)

Finally, we solve for x, as follows:

x+2=ln⁡(5)+xln⁡(6)x−xln⁡(6)=ln⁡(5)−2x(1−ln⁡(6))=ln⁡(5)−2x=ln⁡(5)−21−ln⁡(6)

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding Solutions of Exponential Equations Using the Natural Logarithm
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x+2} & =5\cdot {6}^{x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x+2}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5\cdot {6}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{a})=a$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
x+2=\operatorname{ln}⁡(5\cdot {6}^{x})\,
$$

Next, we use the power and product laws of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+\operatorname{ln}⁡({6}^{x}) \\ x+2 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ x-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-2 \\ x(1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-2 \\ x & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-2}{1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

question.html:
Question 9
?

Expressed in terms of natural logarithms, what value of x satisfies the equation ex+2=5⋅6x?

a
ln⁡(5)−21−ln⁡(6)
b
ln⁡(5)ln⁡(6)
c
ln⁡(5)2+ln⁡(6)
d
ln⁡(5)1−ln⁡(6)
e
ln⁡(5)−2ln⁡(6)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we take the natural logarithm (ln) of both sides of the equation:

ex+2=5⋅6xln⁡(ex+2)=ln⁡(5⋅6x)

Now, we use the fact that ln⁡(ea)=a to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

x+2=ln⁡(5⋅6x)

Next, we use the power and product laws of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

x+2=ln⁡(5)+ln⁡(6x)x+2=ln⁡(5)+xln⁡(6)

Finally, we solve for x, as follows:

x+2=ln⁡(5)+xln⁡(6)x−xln⁡(6)=ln⁡(5)−2x(1−ln⁡(6))=ln⁡(5)−2x=ln⁡(5)−21−ln⁡(6)
question.knowledge_point: Finding Solutions of Exponential Equations Using the Natural Logarithm

solution.reasoning: Taking natural logarithms gives x+2=\ln(5)+x\ln(6). Therefore x(1-\ln(6))=\ln(5)-2, yielding option a. No Math Academy answer key or grade for this question is captured.

feedback.problem: Expressed in terms of natural logarithms, what value of $x$ satisfies the equation ${e}^{x+2}=5\cdot {6}^{x}?$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x+2} & =5\cdot {6}^{x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x+2}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5\cdot {6}^{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{a})=a$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

$$
x+2=\operatorname{ln}⁡(5\cdot {6}^{x})\,
$$

Next, we use the power and product laws of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+\operatorname{ln}⁡({6}^{x}) \\ x+2 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ x-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-2 \\ x(1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-2 \\ x & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-2}{1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that ln⁡(ea)=a to simplify the left-hand side. This gives:

x+2=ln⁡(5⋅6x)

Next, we use the power and product laws of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

x+2=ln⁡(5)+ln⁡(6x)x+2=ln⁡(5)+xln⁡(6)

Finally, we solve for x, as follows:

x+2=ln⁡(5)+xln⁡(6)x−xln⁡(6)=ln⁡(5)−2x(1−ln⁡(6))=ln⁡(5)−2x=ln⁡(5)−21−ln⁡(6)

question.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{3x-1} & ={6}^{2x+1} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{3x-1}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({6}^{2x+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{a})=a$ to simplify the left-hand side. This gives

$$
3x-1=\operatorname{ln}⁡({6}^{2x+1}).
$$

Next, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify the right-hand side:

$$
3x-1=(2x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-1 & =(2x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ 3x-1 & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ 3x-2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) & =1+\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ x(3-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)) & =1+\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ x & =\frac{1+\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)}{3-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)}\end{aligned}
$$

question.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{4x+1} & ={6}^{7x+5} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({5}^{4x+1}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({6}^{7x+5})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives

$$
(4x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)=(7x+5)\operatorname{ln}⁡(6).
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(4x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =(7x+5)\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ 4x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =7x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)+5\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ 4x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-7x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x(4\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-7\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)) & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x & =\frac{5\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-7\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 12
question.problem: Find the solution of ${3}^{x+5}={7}^{6-2x}.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{x+5} & ={7}^{6-2x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{x+5}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({7}^{6-2x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+5)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =(6-2x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+5)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =(6-2x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(7) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+5\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =6\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)-2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(7) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(7) & =6\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)-5\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\ x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)) & =6\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)-5\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\ x & =\frac{6\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)-5\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)}\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding Solutions of Exponential Equations Using the Natural Logarithm: Advanced Cases
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{x+5} & ={7}^{6-2x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{x+5}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({7}^{6-2x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+5)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =(6-2x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+5)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =(6-2x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(7) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+5\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =6\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)-2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(7) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(7) & =6\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)-5\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\ x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)) & =6\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)-5\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\ x & =\frac{6\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)-5\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 12
?

Find the solution of 3x+5=76−2x.

a
6ln⁡(7)−5ln⁡(3)ln⁡(3)+2ln⁡(7)
b
6ln⁡(7)ln⁡(3)ln⁡(3)+2ln⁡(7)
c
1ln⁡(3)+2ln⁡(7)
d
6ln⁡(3)+5ln⁡(7)ln⁡(7)−ln⁡(3)
e
16ln⁡(7)−5ln⁡(3)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we take the natural logarithm (ln) of both sides of the equation:

3x+5=76−2xln⁡(3x+5)=ln⁡(76−2x)

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives:

(x+5)ln⁡(3)=(6−2x)ln⁡(7)

Finally, we solve for x, as follows:

(x+5)ln⁡(3)=(6−2x)ln⁡(7)xln⁡(3)+5ln⁡(3)=6ln⁡(7)−2xln⁡(7)xln⁡(3)+2xln⁡(7)=6ln⁡(7)−5ln⁡(3)x(ln⁡(3)+2ln⁡(7))=6ln⁡(7)−5ln⁡(3)x=6ln⁡(7)−5ln⁡(3)ln⁡(3)+2ln⁡(7)

solution.reasoning: Taking natural logarithms gives (x+5)\ln(3)=(6-2x)\ln(7). Therefore x(\ln(3)+2\ln(7))=6\ln(7)-5\ln(3), yielding option a. No Math Academy answer key or grade for this question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 12
feedback.problem: Find the solution of ${3}^{x+5}={7}^{6-2x}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{x+5} & ={7}^{6-2x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{x+5}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({7}^{6-2x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+5)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =(6-2x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+5)\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =(6-2x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(7) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+5\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) & =6\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)-2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(7) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(7) & =6\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)-5\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\ x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)) & =6\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)-5\operatorname{ln}⁡(3) \\ x & =\frac{6\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)-5\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(7)}\end{aligned}
$$

question.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{4}^{3x-1} & ={9}^{x+6} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({4}^{3x-1}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({9}^{x+6})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives

$$
(3x-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)=(x+6)\operatorname{ln}⁡(9).
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(3x-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(4) & =(x+6)\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) \\ 3x\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(4) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)+6\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) \\ 3x\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)+6\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) \\ x(3\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)+6\operatorname{ln}⁡(9) \\ x & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)+6\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(9)}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =(5-4x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Question 14
?

Find the solution of 5x+3=25−4x.

a
ln⁡(2)+3ln⁡(5)ln⁡(5)−2ln⁡(2)
b
5ln⁡(5)−ln⁡(2)ln⁡(5)+ln⁡(2)
c
15ln⁡(2)−3ln⁡(5)
d
1ln⁡(5)+4ln⁡(2)
e
5ln⁡(2)−3ln⁡(5)ln⁡(5)+4ln⁡(2)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we take the natural logarithm (ln) of both sides of the equation:

5x+3=25−4xln⁡(5x+3)=ln⁡(25−4x)

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives:

(x+3)ln⁡(5)=(5−4x)ln⁡(2)

Finally, we solve for x, as follows:

(x+3)ln⁡(5)=(5−4x)ln⁡(2)xln⁡(5)+3ln⁡(5)=5ln⁡(2)−4xln⁡(2)xln⁡(5)+4xln⁡(2)=5ln⁡(2)−3ln⁡(5)x(ln⁡(5)+4ln⁡(2))=5ln⁡(2)−3ln⁡(5)x=5ln⁡(2)−3ln⁡(5)ln⁡(5)+4ln⁡(2)

last_observation.name: Question 14
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding Solutions of Exponential Equations Using the Natural Logarithm: Advanced Cases
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{x+3} & ={2}^{5-4x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({5}^{x+3}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{5-4x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =(5-4x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =(5-4x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-4x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+4x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)) & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x & =\frac{5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 14
?

Find the solution of 5x+3=25−4x.

a
ln⁡(2)+3ln⁡(5)ln⁡(5)−2ln⁡(2)
b
5ln⁡(5)−ln⁡(2)ln⁡(5)+ln⁡(2)
c
15ln⁡(2)−3ln⁡(5)
d
1ln⁡(5)+4ln⁡(2)
e
5ln⁡(2)−3ln⁡(5)ln⁡(5)+4ln⁡(2)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we take the natural logarithm (ln) of both sides of the equation:

5x+3=25−4xln⁡(5x+3)=ln⁡(25−4x)

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives:

(x+3)ln⁡(5)=(5−4x)ln⁡(2)

Finally, we solve for x, as follows:

(x+3)ln⁡(5)=(5−4x)ln⁡(2)xln⁡(5)+3ln⁡(5)=5ln⁡(2)−4xln⁡(2)xln⁡(5)+4xln⁡(2)=5ln⁡(2)−3ln⁡(5)x(ln⁡(5)+4ln⁡(2))=5ln⁡(2)−3ln⁡(5)x=5ln⁡(2)−3ln⁡(5)ln⁡(5)+4ln⁡(2)
question.knowledge_point: Finding Solutions of Exponential Equations Using the Natural Logarithm: Advanced Cases

solution.reasoning: Taking natural logarithms gives (x+3)\ln(5)=(5-4x)\ln(2). Thus x(\ln(5)+4\ln(2))=5\ln(2)-3\ln(5), yielding option e. No Math Academy answer key or grade for this question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 14
feedback.problem: Find the solution of ${5}^{x+3}={2}^{5-4x}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{x+3} & ={2}^{5-4x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({5}^{x+3}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{5-4x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =(5-4x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =(5-4x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+3\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-4x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+4x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)) & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(5) \\ x & =\frac{5\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 15
question.worked_solution:
First, we take the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{6x+1} & ={6}^{x+7} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{6x+1}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({6}^{x+7})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the power law of logarithms to simplify both sides of the equation. This gives

$$
(6x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)=(x+7)\operatorname{ln}⁡(6).
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(6x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) & =(x+7)\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ 6x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)+7\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) \\ 6x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-x\operatorname{ln}⁡(6) & =7\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ x(6\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)) & =7\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\ x & =\frac{7\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}{6\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(6)}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Simplify $\frac{\sqrt{32{z}^{5}}}{\sqrt{8{z}^{3}}}$ given that $z>0.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring the quotient under a single radical and then simplify the result:

$$
\sqrt{\frac{9{b}^{4}}{16}}=\frac{\sqrt{9{b}^{4}}}{\sqrt{16}}=\frac{\sqrt{9{b}^{4}}}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}}}=\frac{\sqrt{9{b}^{4}}}{4}
$$

Now, notice that the expression inside the radical is a perfect square. So, we can continue simplifying by writing the expression as this perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{9{b}^{4}}}{4} & = \\ \frac{\sqrt{(3{b}^{2})^{2}}}{4} & = \\ \frac{|3{b}^{2}|}{4} & = \\ \frac{|3|\cdot |{b}^{2}|}{4} & = \\ \frac{3\cdot |{b}^{2}|}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

A squared number is always positive or zero, and the absolute value of any positive (or zero) number is itself, so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3\cdot |{b}^{2}|}{4} & = \\ \frac{3\cdot {b}^{2}}{4} & = \\ \frac{3{b}^{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Simplify $\sqrt{\frac{9}{64{q}^{2}}}$ given that $q>0.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we put the numerator and denominator under separate radicals and then simplify the result:

$$
\sqrt{\frac{9}{64{q}^{2}}}=\frac{\sqrt{9}}{\sqrt{64{q}^{2}}}=\frac{\sqrt{{3}^{2}}}{\sqrt{64{q}^{2}}}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{64{q}^{2}}}
$$

Now, notice that the expression inside the radical is a perfect square. So, we can continue simplifying by writing the expression as this perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{64{q}^{2}}} & = \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{(8q)^{2}}} & = \\ \frac{3}{|8q|} & = \\ \frac{3}{|8|\cdot |q|} & = \\ \frac{3}{8\cdot |q|}\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we are told that $q>0,$ so we have $|q|=q.$ Therefore, the final answer is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{8\cdot |q|} & = \\ \frac{3}{8\cdot q} & = \\ \frac{3}{8q}.\end{aligned}
$$

4.Simplifying a Radical Expression With Domain Restrictions?

Simplify 964q2 given that q>0.

E

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we bring the quotient under a single radical and then simplify the result:

$$
\frac{\sqrt{32{z}^{5}}}{\sqrt{8{z}^{3}}}=\sqrt{\frac{32{z}^{5}}{8{z}^{3}}}=\sqrt{4{z}^{2}}
$$

Now, notice that the expression inside the radical is a perfect square. So, we can continue simplifying by writing the expression as this perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{4{z}^{2}} & = \\ \sqrt{{2}^{2}{z}^{2}} & = \\ \sqrt{{(2z)}^{2}} & = \\ |2z| & = \\ |2|\cdot |z| & = \\ 2\cdot |z| & \end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we are told that $z>0,$ so we have $|z|=z.$ Therefore, the final answer is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot |z| & = \\ 2\cdot z & = \\ 2z.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we put the numerator and denominator under separate radicals and then simplify the result:

$$
\sqrt{\frac{9{b}^{4}}{16}}=\frac{\sqrt{9{b}^{4}}}{\sqrt{16}}=\frac{\sqrt{9{b}^{4}}}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}}}=\frac{\sqrt{9{b}^{4}}}{4}
$$

Now, notice that the expression inside the radical is a perfect square. So, we can continue simplifying by writing the expression as this perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{9{b}^{4}}}{4} & = \\ \frac{\sqrt{(3{b}^{2})^{2}}}{4} & = \\ \frac{|3{b}^{2}|}{4} & = \\ \frac{|3|\cdot |{b}^{2}|}{4} & = \\ \frac{3\cdot |{b}^{2}|}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

A squared number is always positive or zero, and the absolute value of any positive (or zero) number is itself, so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3\cdot |{b}^{2}|}{4} & = \\ \frac{3\cdot {b}^{2}}{4} & = \\ \frac{3{b}^{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Simplify $\frac{\sqrt{32{z}^{5}}}{\sqrt{8{z}^{3}}}$ given that $z>0.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we bring the quotient under a single radical and then simplify the result:

$$
\frac{\sqrt{32{z}^{5}}}{\sqrt{8{z}^{3}}}=\sqrt{\frac{32{z}^{5}}{8{z}^{3}}}=\sqrt{4{z}^{2}}
$$

Now, notice that the expression inside the radical is a perfect square. So, we can continue simplifying by writing the expression as this perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{4{z}^{2}} & = \\ \sqrt{{2}^{2}{z}^{2}} & = \\ \sqrt{{(2z)}^{2}} & = \\ |2z| & = \\ |2|\cdot |z| & = \\ 2\cdot |z| & \end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we are told that $z>0,$ so we have $|z|=z.$ Therefore, the final answer is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot |z| & = \\ 2\cdot z & = \\ 2z.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{4{z}^{2}} & = \\ \sqrt{{2}^{2}{z}^{2}} & = \\ \sqrt{{(2z)}^{2}} & = \\ |2z| & = \\ |2|\cdot |z| & = \\ 2\cdot |z| & \end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot |z| & = \\ 2\cdot z & = \\ 2z.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.worked_solution:
First, we put the numerator and denominator under separate radicals and then simplify the result:

$$
\sqrt{\frac{9{b}^{4}}{16}}=\frac{\sqrt{9{b}^{4}}}{\sqrt{16}}=\frac{\sqrt{9{b}^{4}}}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}}}=\frac{\sqrt{9{b}^{4}}}{4}
$$

Now, notice that the expression inside the radical is a perfect square. So, we can continue simplifying by writing the expression as this perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{9{b}^{4}}}{4} & = \\ \frac{\sqrt{(3{b}^{2})^{2}}}{4} & = \\ \frac{|3{b}^{2}|}{4} & = \\ \frac{|3|\cdot |{b}^{2}|}{4} & = \\ \frac{3\cdot |{b}^{2}|}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

A squared number is always positive or zero, and the absolute value of any positive (or zero) number is itself, so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3\cdot |{b}^{2}|}{4} & = \\ \frac{3\cdot {b}^{2}}{4} & = \\ \frac{3{b}^{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: Simplify $\sqrt{\frac{9}{64{q}^{2}}}$ given that $q>0.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we put the numerator and denominator under separate radicals and then simplify the result:

$$
\sqrt{\frac{9}{64{q}^{2}}}=\frac{\sqrt{9}}{\sqrt{64{q}^{2}}}=\frac{\sqrt{{3}^{2}}}{\sqrt{64{q}^{2}}}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{64{q}^{2}}}
$$

Now, notice that the expression inside the radical is a perfect square. So, we can continue simplifying by writing the expression as this perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{64{q}^{2}}} & = \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{(8q)^{2}}} & = \\ \frac{3}{|8q|} & = \\ \frac{3}{|8|\cdot |q|} & = \\ \frac{3}{8\cdot |q|}\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we are told that $q>0,$ so we have $|q|=q.$ Therefore, the final answer is

$$

Simplify 964q2 given that q>0.

a
34q2
b
34q
c
98q2
d
38q
e
98q
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we put the numerator and denominator under separate radicals and then simplify the result: 964q2=964q2=3264q2=364q2

Now, notice that the expression inside the radical is a perfect square. So, we can continue simplifying by writing the expression as this perfect square: 364q2=3(8q)2=3|8q|=3|8|⋅|q|=38⋅|q|

Lastly, we are told that q>0, so we have |q|=q. Therefore, the final answer is 38⋅|q|=38⋅q=38q.

feedback.problem: Simplify $\sqrt{\frac{9}{64{q}^{2}}}$ given that $q>0.$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we put the numerator and denominator under separate radicals and then simplify the result:

$$
\sqrt{\frac{9}{64{q}^{2}}}=\frac{\sqrt{9}}{\sqrt{64{q}^{2}}}=\frac{\sqrt{{3}^{2}}}{\sqrt{64{q}^{2}}}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{64{q}^{2}}}
$$

Now, notice that the expression inside the radical is a perfect square. So, we can continue simplifying by writing the expression as this perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{64{q}^{2}}} & = \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{(8q)^{2}}} & = \\ \frac{3}{|8q|} & = \\ \frac{3}{|8|\cdot |q|} & = \\ \frac{3}{8\cdot |q|}\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we are told that $q>0,$ so we have $|q|=q.$ Therefore, the final answer is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{8\cdot |q|} & = \\ \frac{3}{8\cdot q} & = \\ \frac{3}{8q}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: A $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ Given that the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are $13$ and $8,$ find the length of the ellipse's semi-major axis.
questions.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$

Since the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ is $13,$ we obtain

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}=13\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=\sqrt{13}.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is $\sqrt{13}.$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem: A $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ Given that the singular values of $A$ are ${\sigma }_{1}=10$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=2\sqrt{5},$ find the length of the semi-major axis of the ellipse.
questions.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are called the *singular values* of $A.$ Since the largest singular value of $A$ is ${\sigma }_{1}=10,$ the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ must be ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}={10}^{2}.$ So, we obtain that

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}={10}^{2}\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=10.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is ${\sigma }_{1}=10.$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225355/assets/d4947e37239d2ac2950b536d7afc2d0810ea713c437b7095a43e123d50ff2b34.png)

A $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A,$ what are the nonzero singular values of $A?$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\,…,{v}_{n}\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of ${R}^{n}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}\ge …\ge {\lambda }_{n}.
$$

Then,

- ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{1},$

- ${\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{2},$

- $⋯$

In our example, we see that

- $||A{v}_{1}||=8={\sigma }_{1},$ and

- $||A{v}_{2}||=5={\sigma }_{2}.$

Therefore, the nonzero singular values of $A$ are ${\sigma }_{1}=8$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=5.$

questions.name: Question 12
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225355/assets/63d5de8c08559ecc88b4fd7e2184204a1e6ea2f8a9e8ca6af7959e2354876e3f.png)

A $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A,$ which of the following is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $9$ of ${A}^{T}A?$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\,…,{v}_{n}\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of ${R}^{n}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}\ge …\ge {\lambda }_{n}.
$$

Then,

- ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{1},$

- ${\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{2},$

- $⋯$

In our example, we see that

- $||A{v}_{1}||=5={\sigma }_{1},$ which means that ${\lambda }_{1}={5}^{2}=25,$ and

- $||A{v}_{2}||=3={\sigma }_{2},$ which means that ${\lambda }_{2}={3}^{2}=9.$

Therefore, an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=9$ of ${A}^{T}A$ is ${v}_{2}.$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225355/assets/6be1f51600ae7b42ad0c4c8f67eb8f3ba3570606ec4e3e5e75c65df397aab060.png)

A $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A,$ what are the nonzero singular values of $A?$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\,…,{v}_{n}\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of ${R}^{n}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}\ge …\ge {\lambda }_{n}.
$$

Then,

- ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{1},$

- ${\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{2},$

- $⋯$

In our example, we see that

- $||A{v}_{1}||=7={\sigma }_{1},$ and

- $||A{v}_{2}||=5={\sigma }_{2}.$

Therefore, the nonzero singular values of $A$ are ${\sigma }_{1}=7$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=5.$

- $||A{v}_{2}||=4={\sigma }_{2},$ which means that ${\lambda }_{2}={4}^{2}=16.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Semi-Major Axis of the Image of the Unit Sphere
canonical_examples.problem: A $2 \times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\big\{ \mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ from $\mathbb{R}^3$ onto an ellipse in $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Given that the eigenvalues of $A^T A$ are $7, 2,$ and $0,$ find the length of the ellipse's semi-major axis.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\big\{ \mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ from $\mathbb{R}^3$ onto the ellipse $\big\{ A\mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $A\mathbf{x}$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where $\mathbf{x}^T (A^T A) \mathbf{x}$ is the quadratic form with the matrix $A^T A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $\| \mathbf{x} \| =1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix $A^T A.$

Since the largest eigenvalue of $A^T A$ is $7,$ we obtain

$$
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \|^2 \big\} = 7
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \| \big\}  = \sqrt{7}.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is $\sqrt{7}.$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Semi-Major Axis of the Image of the Unit Sphere

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Semi-Major Axis of the Image of the Unit Sphere Given the Corresponding Singular Values
canonical_examples.problem: A $2 \times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\big\{ \mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ from $\mathbb{R}^3$ onto an ellipse in $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Given that the singular values of $A$ are $\sigma_1=4,$ $\sigma_2=2,$ and $\sigma_3 = 0,$ find the length of the semi-major axis of the ellipse.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\big\{ \mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ from $\mathbb{R}^3$ onto the ellipse $\big\{ A\mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $A\mathbf{x}$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where $\mathbf{x}^T (A^T A) \mathbf{x}$ is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix $A^T A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $\| \mathbf{x} \| =1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix $A^T A.$ 

The square roots of the eigenvalues of $A^T A$ are called the *singular values* of $A.$ Since the largest singular value of $A$ is $\sigma_1=4,$ the largest eigenvalue of $A^T A$ must be $\lambda_1 = \sigma_1^2=4^2.$ So, we obtain that

$$
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \|^2 \big\} = 4^2
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \| \big\} = 4.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is $\sigma_1=4.$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Semi-Major Axis of the Image of the Unit Sphere Given the Corresponding Singular Values

canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225355/assets/094b6043b9cce7f3ac2a7cc32fa53785d3fbf5b490ce853474f89bb4afa8291a.png)

A $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\big\{ \mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ from $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto an ellipse in $\mathbb{R}^2.$ The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that $\mathbf v_1$ and $\mathbf v_2$ are unit eigenvectors of $A^TA,$ find an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $36$ of $A^T A?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\left\{\mathbf v_1, \mathbf v_2\,\ldots, \mathbf v_n\right\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of $\mathbb R^n$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $A^T A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
\lambda_1\geq \lambda_2\geq \ldots \geq \lambda_n.
$$

Then,

- $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{\lambda_1}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_1,$

- $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{\lambda_2}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_2,$

- $\cdots$

In our example, we see that

- $||A\mathbf v_1|| = 8 = \sigma_1,$ which means that $\lambda_1 = 8^2 = 64,$ and

- $||A\mathbf v_2|| = 6 = \sigma_2,$ which means that $\lambda_2 = 6^2 = 36.$

Therefore, an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda_2 = 36$ of $A^T A$ is $\mathbf{v}_2.$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Let's suppose we are given the matrix

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225355/assets/18f57c05cb79918e17401427e3419648791562a5d38116582e0d396e20db1069.svg)

Then, the corresponding linear transformation 

$$
\mathbf x \mapsto A \mathbf x
$$

maps the unit circle $\big\{ \mathbf x \, | \, \|\mathbf x\|=1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb R^2$ onto an ellipse $\big\{ A\mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2,$ as shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225355/assets/c163f7714d0e2045db37438b7ea66a2dc8ac92cfbe309a0d24c898bbfac8c295.png)

 

How can we find the maximum possible value of $\|A \mathbf x\|?$ Geometrically, this is equivalent to finding the semi-major axis of our ellipse.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225355/assets/866052291b0d7a416988c0c42fa99eec1d1bfd3b1344cf3cf2eb0a09457ae38d.png)

First, we note the following:

- The value of $\mathbf x$ that maximizes $||A\mathbf x||$ also maximizes $||A\mathbf x||^2.$

- If $\mathbf v$ is a column vector, then $||\mathbf v||^2 = \mathbf v^T \mathbf v\mathbin{:}$

Therefore, we can re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $A\mathbf{x}$ on our ellipse as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x\end{aligned}
$$

  

Note that $\mathbf{x}^T (A^T A) \mathbf{x}$ is a quadratic form with the matrix $A^T A.$ Therefore, the maximum value of this quadratic form for $\| \mathbf{x} \| =1$ equals the largest eigenvalue of the matrix $A^T A.$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & 6 \\ 6 & 10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^TA\mathbin{:}$  

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}10-\lambda  & 6 \\ 6 & 10-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )^{2}-36 & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )^{2} & =36 \\ 10-\lambda  & =\pm 6 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,16\end{aligned}
$$

Since the largest eigenvalue of $A^T A$ is $16,$ we obtain

$$
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \|^2 \big\} = 16
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \| \big\} = \sqrt{16} = 4.
$$

 

Therefore, the length of the semi-major axis of our ellipse equals $4.$

tutorials.content:
Let's suppose we are given the matrix

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225355/assets/18f57c05cb79918e17401427e3419648791562a5d38116582e0d396e20db1069.svg)

Then, the corresponding linear transformation 

$$
\mathbf x \mapsto A \mathbf x
$$

maps the unit circle $\big\{ \mathbf x \, | \, \|\mathbf x\|=1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb R^2$ onto an ellipse $\big\{ A\mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2,$ as shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225355/assets/c163f7714d0e2045db37438b7ea66a2dc8ac92cfbe309a0d24c898bbfac8c295.png)

 

How can we find the maximum possible value of $\|A \mathbf x\|?$ Geometrically, this is equivalent to finding the semi-major axis of our ellipse.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225355/assets/866052291b0d7a416988c0c42fa99eec1d1bfd3b1344cf3cf2eb0a09457ae38d.png)

First, we note the following:

- The value of $\mathbf x$ that maximizes $||A\mathbf x||$ also maximizes $||A\mathbf x||^2.$

- If $\mathbf v$ is a column vector, then $||\mathbf v||^2 = \mathbf v^T \mathbf v\mathbin{:}$

Therefore, we can re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $A\mathbf{x}$ on our ellipse as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x\end{aligned}
$$

  

Note that $\mathbf{x}^T (A^T A) \mathbf{x}$ is a quadratic form with the matrix $A^T A.$ Therefore, the maximum value of this quadratic form for $\| \mathbf{x} \| =1$ equals the largest eigenvalue of the matrix $A^T A.$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & 6 \\ 6 & 10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^TA\mathbin{:}$  

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}10-\lambda  & 6 \\ 6 & 10-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )^{2}-36 & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )^{2} & =36 \\ 10-\lambda  & =\pm 6 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,16\end{aligned}
$$

Since the largest eigenvalue of $A^T A$ is $16,$ we obtain

$$
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \|^2 \big\} = 16
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \| \big\} = \sqrt{16} = 4.
$$

 

Therefore, the length of the semi-major axis of our ellipse equals $4.$

tutorials.name: The Singular Values of a Matrix
tutorials.problem:
Let $A$ be an $m\times n$ matrix. Then, $A^T A$ is always a symmetric, positive semi-definite matrix. In particular, $A^TA$ can be orthogonally diagonalized, and its eigenvalues are non-negative real numbers.

The **singular values** of  $A$ are defined as the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T A.$ The $i$th singular value of $A$ is denoted $\sigma_i\mathbin{:}$

- $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{\lambda_1}$

- $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{\lambda_2}$

- $\sigma_3 = \sqrt{\lambda_3}$

$\:\vdots$

- $\sigma_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}$

We usually list the singular values in *decreasing* order. 

Now, we know that $A^TA$ is orthogonally diagonalizable. Therefore, if

$$
\left\{\mathbf v_1, \mathbf v_2\,\ldots, \mathbf v_n\right\}
$$

is an *orthonormal* basis of $\mathbb R^n$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A^T}{A}$ with the corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
\lambda_1\geq \lambda_2\geq \ldots \geq \lambda_n,
$$

then it can be shown that

- $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{\lambda_1}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_1,$

- $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{\lambda_2}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_2,$

$\:\vdots$

- $\sigma_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_n.$

Furthermore:

- $\sigma_1$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x,$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_1$

- $\sigma_2$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x$ that are orthogonal to $\mathbf v_1,$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_2$

- $\sigma_3$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x$ that are orthogonal to $\mathbf v_1$ *and* $\mathbf v_2,$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_3$

$\:\vdots$

- $\sigma_n$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x$ that are orthogonal to $\mathbf v_1,\mathbf v_2,\ldots,\mathbf v_{n-1},$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_n$

Let's take a look at a concrete example.

tutorials.problem:
We've seen that for the matrix $A,$ given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225355/assets/9c11e176876a767543250d5b18038cae7b14a36a692a6f14474da6b4312a48b9.svg)

the eigenvalues of $A^TA$ are $\lambda_1=16$ and $\lambda_2=4.$ It's easy to show that the corresponding unit eigenvectors of $A^T A$ are 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225355/assets/7c44b67b766ea8385f4d7780523ee560bd3e215a0cee42db9baf208da471ccdd.svg) 

The singular values of $A$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{16}=4, \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting all of this information together gives us the following diagram. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225355/assets/238f4ae60c783dd786476a339f012ef1b4ca82bcac7aa3f3ef4445726938ef3a.png)

 

Note that our ellipse's semi-major and semi-minor axes are $\sigma_1 = 4$ and $\sigma_2 =2,$ respectively.

tutorials.content:
We've seen that for the matrix $A,$ given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225355/assets/9c11e176876a767543250d5b18038cae7b14a36a692a6f14474da6b4312a48b9.svg)

the eigenvalues of $A^TA$ are $\lambda_1=16$ and $\lambda_2=4.$ It's easy to show that the corresponding unit eigenvectors of $A^T A$ are 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225355/assets/7c44b67b766ea8385f4d7780523ee560bd3e215a0cee42db9baf208da471ccdd.svg) 

The singular values of $A$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{16}=4, \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting all of this information together gives us the following diagram. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225355/assets/238f4ae60c783dd786476a339f012ef1b4ca82bcac7aa3f3ef4445726938ef3a.png)

 

Note that our ellipse's semi-major and semi-minor axes are $\sigma_1 = 4$ and $\sigma_2 =2,$ respectively.

tutorial.problem:
Let's suppose we are given the matrix

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225355/assets/575b639f926dd7585dcc4ceed2a2c19c08b4260919f6b772202d4d8415170787.svg)

Then, the corresponding linear transformation 

$$
\mathbf x \mapsto A \mathbf x
$$

maps the unit circle $\big\{ \mathbf x \, | \, \|\mathbf x\|=1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb R^2$ onto an ellipse $\big\{ A\mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2,$ as shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225355/assets/c163f7714d0e2045db37438b7ea66a2dc8ac92cfbe309a0d24c898bbfac8c295.png)

 

How can we find the maximum possible value of $\|A \mathbf x\|?$ Geometrically, this is equivalent to finding the semi-major axis of our ellipse.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225355/assets/866052291b0d7a416988c0c42fa99eec1d1bfd3b1344cf3cf2eb0a09457ae38d.png)

First, we note the following:

- The value of $\mathbf x$ that maximizes $||A\mathbf x||$ also maximizes $||A\mathbf x||^2.$

- If $\mathbf v$ is a column vector, then $||\mathbf v||^2 = \mathbf v^T \mathbf v\mathbin{:}$

Therefore, we can re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $A\mathbf{x}$ on our ellipse as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x\end{aligned}
$$

  

Note that $\mathbf{x}^T (A^T A) \mathbf{x}$ is a quadratic form with the matrix $A^T A.$ Therefore, the maximum value of this quadratic form for $\| \mathbf{x} \| =1$ equals the largest eigenvalue of the matrix $A^T A.$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & 6 \\ 6 & 10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^TA\mathbin{:}$  

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}10-\lambda  & 6 \\ 6 & 10-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )^{2}-36 & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )^{2} & =36 \\ 10-\lambda  & =\pm 6 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,16\end{aligned}
$$

Since the largest eigenvalue of $A^T A$ is $16,$ we obtain

$$
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \|^2 \big\} = 16
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \| \big\} = \sqrt{16} = 4.
$$

 

Therefore, the length of the semi-major axis of our ellipse equals $4.$

Therefore, we can re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $A\mathbf{x}$ on our ellipse as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x\end{aligned}
$$

  

Note that $\mathbf{x}^T (A^T A) \mathbf{x}$ is a quadratic form with the matrix $A^T A.$ Therefore, the maximum value of this quadratic form for $\| \mathbf{x} \| =1$ equals the largest eigenvalue of the matrix $A^T A.$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & 6 \\ 6 & 10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^TA\mathbin{:}$  

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}10-\lambda  & 6 \\ 6 & 10-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )^{2}-36 & =0 \\ (10-\lambda )^{2} & =36 \\ 10-\lambda  & =\pm 6 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,16\end{aligned}
$$

Since the largest eigenvalue of $A^T A$ is $16,$ we obtain

$$
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \|^2 \big\} = 16
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \| \big\} = \sqrt{16} = 4.
$$

 

Therefore, the length of the semi-major axis of our ellipse equals $4.$

a

13
c

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ATA.

max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖2}=13⟹max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖}=13.

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is 13.

A 2×3 matrix A maps the unit sphere {x|‖x‖=1} from R3 onto an ellipse in R2. Given that the eigenvalues of ATA are 7, 3, and 0, find the length of the ellipse's semi-major axis.

a
7
b
7
c
0
d
5
e
52
Submit
Correct

The matrix A maps the unit sphere {x|‖x‖=1} from R3 onto the ellipse {Ax|‖x‖=1} in R2.

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point Ax on our ellipse, as follows:

‖Ax‖2=(Ax)T(Ax)=(xTAT)(Ax)=xT(ATA)x,

where xT(ATA)x is the quadratic form with the matrix ATA.

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ATA.

Since the largest eigenvalue of ATA is 7, we obtain

max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖2}=7⟹max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖}=7.

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is 7.

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$

$$

tutorial.name: The Singular Values of a Matrix
tutorial.problem:
Let $A$ be an $m\times n$ matrix. Then, $A^T A$ is always a symmetric, positive semi-definite matrix. In particular, $A^TA$ can be orthogonally diagonalized, and its eigenvalues are non-negative real numbers.

The **singular values** of  $A$ are defined as the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix $A^T A.$ The $i$th singular value of $A$ is denoted $\sigma_i\mathbin{:}$

- $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{\lambda_1}$

- $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{\lambda_2}$

- $\sigma_3 = \sqrt{\lambda_3}$

$\:\vdots$

- $\sigma_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}$

We usually list the singular values in *decreasing* order. 

Now, we know that $A^TA$ is orthogonally diagonalizable. Therefore, if

$$
\left\{\mathbf v_1, \mathbf v_2\,\ldots, \mathbf v_n\right\}
$$

is an *orthonormal* basis of $\mathbb R^n$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A^T}{A}$ with the corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
\lambda_1\geq \lambda_2\geq \ldots \geq \lambda_n,
$$

then it can be shown that

- $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{\lambda_1}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_1,$

- $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{\lambda_2}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_2,$

$\:\vdots$

- $\sigma_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_n.$

Furthermore:

- $\sigma_1$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x,$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_1$

- $\sigma_2$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x$ that are orthogonal to $\mathbf v_1,$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_2$

- $\sigma_3$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x$ that are orthogonal to $\mathbf v_1$ *and* $\mathbf v_2,$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_3$

$\:\vdots$

- $\sigma_n$ is the maximum value of $||A\mathbf x||$ over all *unit* vectors $\mathbf x$ that are orthogonal to $\mathbf v_1,\mathbf v_2,\ldots,\mathbf v_{n-1},$ and is attained on the unit eigenvector $\mathbf v_n$

Let's take a look at a concrete example.

tutorial.content:
We've seen that for the matrix $A,$ given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225355/assets/d0bc1a894bd4becb168f55f5ac4f97ee91451add907911034beef7b7728a14d2.svg)

the eigenvalues of $A^TA$ are $\lambda_1=16$ and $\lambda_2=4.$ It's easy to show that the corresponding unit eigenvectors of $A^T A$ are 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225355/assets/ca86ebe2257e15723c0a9704bd27f1b22c12b532b9f09ee844609674d2bebf5e.svg) 

The singular values of $A$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{16}=4, \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting all of this information together gives us the following diagram. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14225355/assets/238f4ae60c783dd786476a339f012ef1b4ca82bcac7aa3f3ef4445726938ef3a.png)

 

Note that our ellipse's semi-major and semi-minor axes are $\sigma_1 = 4$ and $\sigma_2 =2,$ respectively.
tutorial.title: Associating Singular Values With an Ellipse's Principal Axes

observed_steps.name: Example: Finding the Semi-Major Axis of the Image of the Unit Sphere Given the Corresponding Singular Values
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Semi-Major Axis of the Image of the Unit Sphere
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\big\{ \mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ from $\mathbb{R}^3$ onto the ellipse $\big\{ A\mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $A\mathbf{x}$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where $\mathbf{x}^T (A^T A) \mathbf{x}$ is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix $A^T A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $\| \mathbf{x} \| =1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix $A^T A.$ 

The square roots of the eigenvalues of $A^T A$ are called the *singular values* of $A.$ Since the largest singular value of $A$ is $\sigma_1=4,$ the largest eigenvalue of $A^T A$ must be $\lambda_1 = \sigma_1^2=4^2.$ So, we obtain that

$$
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \|^2 \big\} = 4^2
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \| \big\} = 4.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is $\sigma_1=4.$

question.html:
Question 6
?

A 2×3 matrix A maps the unit sphere {x|‖x‖=1} from R3 onto an ellipse in R2. Given that the singular values of A are σ1=3, σ2=22, and σ3=0, find the length of the semi-major axis of the ellipse.

a
3
b
3
c
8
d
9
e
22
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The matrix A maps the unit sphere {x|‖x‖=1} from R3 onto the ellipse {Ax|‖x‖=1} in R2.

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point Ax on our ellipse, as follows:

‖Ax‖2=(Ax)T(Ax)=(xTAT)(Ax)=xT(ATA)x,

where xT(ATA)x is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ATA.

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ATA.

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ATA are called the singular values of A. Since the largest singular value of A is σ1=3, the largest eigenvalue of ATA must be λ1=σ12=32. So, we obtain that

max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖2}=32⟹max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖}=3.

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is σ1=3.

observed_steps.name: Question 7
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Semi-Major Axis of the Image of the Unit Sphere Given the Corresponding Singular Values
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are called the *singular values* of $A.$ Since the largest singular value of $A$ is ${\sigma }_{1}=12,$ the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ must be ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}={12}^{2}.$ So, we obtain that

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}={12}^{2}\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=12.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is ${\sigma }_{1}=12.$

question.html:
Question 9
?

A 2×2 matrix A maps the unit circle {x|‖x‖=1} from R2 onto an ellipse in R2. Given that the singular values of A are σ1=6 and σ2=23, find the length of the semi-major axis of the ellipse.

a
6
b
3
c
6
d
12
e
23
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The matrix A maps the unit circle {x|‖x‖=1} from R2 onto the ellipse {Ax|‖x‖=1} in R2.

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point Ax on our ellipse, as follows:

‖Ax‖2=(Ax)T(Ax)=(xTAT)(Ax)=xT(ATA)x,

where xT(ATA)x is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ATA.

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when ‖x‖=1, is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ATA.

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ATA are called the singular values of A. Since the largest singular value of A is σ1=6, the largest eigenvalue of ATA must be λ1=σ12=62. So, we obtain that

max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖2}=62⟹max‖x‖=1{‖Ax‖}=6.

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is σ1=6.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are called the *singular values* of $A.$ Since the largest singular value of $A$ is ${\sigma }_{1}=6,$ the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ must be ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}={6}^{2}.$ So, we obtain that

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}={6}^{2}\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=6.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is ${\sigma }_{1}=6.$
